Also on Sunday, Jeffries dismissed President Trump’s repeated promises to pay Americans $5,000 if Republicans win in November’s high-stakes midterm elections.

“It wasn't a serious proposal that was presented by Donald Trump. He's broken every promise that he's presented. Donald Trump promised to actually lower costs on day one. Costs haven't gone down. They've gone up,” Jeffries said Sunday.

“If we win the midterms, we will, on the other hand, provide a, let's call it Trump dividend, $5,000 for every adult citizen in our country," Trump said Thursday at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.
Jeffries also challenged other claims made by the Trump during the convention, including the president asking voters to “pretend” he is on ballot in November.
“I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot,” Trump said on Wednesday.

“Mr. President, we don't have to pretend. You are actually on the ballot. Your failed economy is on the ballot. The cost of living crisis is on the ballot. The fact that you've gotten us involved in a reckless and costly war of choice in the Middle East that has skyrocketed gas prices, that's on the ballot,” Jeffries said on "This Week."
Throughout the primary cycle, progressive Democrats have scored wins in key races, posing questions for the Democratic caucus looking to take control in November.

“You’ve taken some heat from progressives in the party, including from many who align with the Democratic Socialists. Are you confident that you'll actually be speaker if the Democrats win? Stephanopoulos asked Jeffries.

“Well, we're focused right now on taking back control of the House of Representatives. That is the only mission that's important, so we can lower the high cost of living, lower the cost of gas, lower the cost of groceries, lower the cost of housing, certainly fight to make health care affordable for every single American and combat the unprecedented corruption that's been unleashed on the American people and beginning on day one, hold the crooks accountable," Jeffries said in response.

Stephanopoulos also pressed Jeffries on his late August meeting with the president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Jeffries defended the meeting, claiming that “there are going to be times that you have to speak with people on the other side of the aisle.”

title: Millions dropped from SNAP food assistance as funding faces September uncertainty
summary: SNAP funding could face a major shake-up at the end of September unless Congress passes a resolution to delay major changes included in the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill.
story: Starting Oct. 1, states will have to cover 75% of program administrative costs.

Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) funding could face a major shake-up at the end of September unless Congress passes a resolution to delay major changes included in H.R. 1, commonly known as the GOP's One Big Beautiful Bill.

Starting Oct. 1, states will have to pick up 75% of the administrative costs of running the program, with the funding burden of providing benefits to participants set to shift from the federal to state level over the next few years.
State and national food assistance groups are calling on Congress to pass a resolution delaying the implementation of this cost shift, to give states more time to prepare for the bigger bill.
The federal food assistance program faced a funding lapse last fall, and experts are now warning of an uncertain future.

Nationwide, roughly 5 million Americans have lost access to SNAP since the Republican-backed budget bill became law, including more than 1.5 million children, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.

Much of the decline can be attributed to changes in work requirements and administrative hurdles in applying, coupled with a major cost shift that states will have to bear if they want SNAP to remain fully funded, Dottie Rosenbaum, director of federal SNAP policy at the CBPP, told ABC News.
Under the law, the upper age limit for able-bodied adults without dependents who must meet work requirements was raised from 54 to 64.
Additionally, exemptions were changed for parents and other family members responsible for a dependent, lowering the qualifying age from 18 to 14.

"The declines we're seeing in SNAP participation so far are far deeper and far faster than the Congressional Budget Office predicted at the time the law was enacted, and it's especially alarming that more than one and a half million children have been cut," Rosenbaum said.

"We're hearing increasing reports ... of people struggling to put food on the table, of people facing untenable choices between, you know, paying their rent and buying groceries and other essentials, putting gas in their cars," Rosenbaum added.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the impact of the new work requirements. The administration has publicly supported the idea in the past.

"The American dream is not being on [a] food stamp program. ... The American dream is not being on all these programs. That should be a hand up, not a handout," Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in an interview on Fox Business in January.
Alongside the new work requirements, the budget outlined a major shift in costs from the federal government to the states.
Beyond each state's responsibility to pay 75% of SNAP's administrative costs starting in October, states are set to pay a percentage of the benefit costs tied to its error rate in the coming years.
The error rate measures underpayments and overpayments, resulting in mandatory additional payments ranging from 5% to 15% for most states.

The benefit cost shift will take effect as early as 2027 and could lead to cuts or major changes in other state-run programs as states try to make up the difference, food assistance leaders told ABC News.
These changes, some already implemented and others on the horizon, have forced food banks to step in and fill the gaps while lawmakers debate a more stable funding structure.
Impacts already seen

In Arizona, the state "took immediate action on error reduction efforts after H.R. 1 became law," the Arizona Dept. of Economic Security said. This included expanding documentation requirements, establishing a preauthorization review process and continuous income monitoring. More than 400,000 SNAP recipients lost access to the program thereafter, according to the CBPP.

"Which meant that the number of people visiting food banks increased by about the same amount," Terri Shoemaker, executive vice president of the Arizona Food Bank Network, said, crediting the state's changes in SNAP for the substantial drop in participation.

"We know that [the Arizona Department of Economic Security] is trying to get its arms around accuracy and reporting, but at the same time, we also know that there are people who were impacted by those changes who shouldn't have been," Shoemaker said.
When the changes began in Arizona, Shoemaker said, communities rallied to donate food to people who had lost access to SNAP. Still, she added, the response is not sustainable.

"For every one meal that Arizona food banks provide for families, SNAP usually provides about five," Shoemaker said. "Nationally, that statistic is more like one [meal from food banks] for every nine [meals from SNAP]. But if you think about that and food banks trying to fill that gap, it's just a scale and scope that is so vast that food banks are going to have a hard time keeping up."
In neighboring New Mexico, the impact can also be seen.

"Find out where your food bank distributes food and check out the length of a line," said Jill Dixon, the executive director of the Food Depot -- a collection of food banks covering northern New Mexico. "We have one in front of our building on the first and third Thursday of every month. That line usually extends over a mile and a half by the time it opens at 7 a.m."
The Food Depot distributed more than 8 million meals across much of New Mexico in 2025.
"These are people. They're not lines. It's not boxes of food. It's not anonymous. It's deeply personal, and it's right at the center of our community," Dixon said.

"We're going to see some hard times ahead," she added. "Long term, we really have a reckoning of how we're going to go about making sure that people are fed in a moment when it is incredibly hard to make ends meet."
Predominantly Republican states hit

In predominantly Republican states, the impact is similar. Louisiana has seen the second largest per-capita decline, with 21% of the state's SNAP recipients no longer having access to SNAP according to the CBPP.

Food Bank of North Central Arkansas CEO Jeff Quick said his state is facing a burden too large to bear without major changes. "We will never be able to food bank our way out of food insecurity," Quick said.

"At best, I think we may be unprepared or unable to cover the cost to continue SNAP in Arkansas, and again, if that worst-case scenario were to happen, it could have an estimated $1.2 billion negative economic impact on our state," he added.
Quick also said work requirements have hit harder in Arkansas, adding that a worker earning the state's $11-an-hour minimum wage may still be ineligible for SNAP benefits.

"We don't want to see anyone go hungry, and regardless of who you are or how you vote or how you legislate, we're all on the same path," Quick said. "We got to put great minds together around common causes to find solutions to hunger."
The White House did not comment on whether the administration supports delaying the cost shift.
What's next?

Food bank organizations at the state and national levels are asking Congress to pass a resolution delaying the cost shift and allowing states more time to lower their error rates before taking on the additional costs.
"States need more time," Rosenbaum said. "They need more time to work to lower their error rate and improve their payment accuracy in a way that doesn't limit access to benefits."
Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman released a version of the farm bill that would delay the cost shift of SNAP, though it has not advanced through the opposite chamber.
Lawmakers return to Washington from August recess on Sept. 14.

title: Some 9/11 families call on Trump to hold Saudis accountable during NYC ceremony
summary: Some family members of 9/11 victims used the 25th anniversary ceremonies to openly call on the president to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for the attacks.
story: Family members openly called on the president to hold Saudi Arabia accountable.
Some family members of 9/11 victims used the 25th anniversary ceremonies to openly call on the federal government to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for the attacks.

During the ceremonial reading of the names at ground zero Friday, Terry Strada, the widow of 9/11 victim Tom Strada, received cheers after she admonished prior administrations, including the past presidents seated before her, for failing to get answers about the Saudi government's alleged role in the attacks.
"Administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," she said.

A coalition of victims' families are suing the Saudi government over their alleged role and have continued to pursue evidence they say points to deep Saudi complicity. The Saudis deny that claim and are fighting the suit in court.
Many of the 9/11 hijackers were Saudi nationals, according to the FBI.
The Saudis have repeatedly denied having any role in facilitating the attacks and replied in court that they remain "an ally of the United States [and] a sworn enemy of Al Qaeda."

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told ABC News last week that "President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, and his team is working diligently to identify records that are responsive to these families' request."
Strada, the national chair of the advocacy group 9/11 Families United, said that presidential administrations broke "promises both public and private ... it has been one betrayal after another."
President Donald Trump "can still change that," she added.

"Tell the Saudis to stop lying," she said. "Tell them if they want to be friends with the USA they cannot continue to deny all of this -- all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through."
Trump attended a ceremony at the Pentagon at the time of the Manhattan ceremony. Strada urged Vice President JD Vance, who attended the ceremony, to "carry that message back" to Washington.
"How can it be, 25 years, and still we have no justice for the role Saudi Arabia played in your murder?" Strada asked as many attendees applauded in approval.
Strada wasn't the only family member who called on Trump to provide more scrutiny of the Saudi government.
A nephew of 9/11 victim Lisa Marie Terry also brought up the alleged Saudi involvement in the attacks after he finished reading some of the names.
"President Trump, you are our last hope. Release the unredacted files that implicate Saudi Arabia while what's left of the victims' families are still alive to see it," he said to cheers.

In statement released Friday afternoon, a White House spokesperson said, "President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, which is why he authorized the declassification and release of hundreds of pages of documents related to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001."

"The President will always pay tribute to the American heroes we lost in the tragic September 11 attacks, their beautiful family members, and to the acts of heroism that defined that fateful day when the unbreakable spirit of the American people prevailed," the statement said.
On Friday, the CIA released 71 presidential briefs related to the 9/11 attacks, ranging in dates from 1998 to Sept. 12, 2001.

"The products trace the story of CIA analysts' evolving understanding of al-Qa'ida and efforts to highlight and warn of Osama Bin Ladin's attack plotting despite sparse, vague, and imperfect information," the agency said in a statement.

Brett Eagleson, the president of 9/11 Justice, the coalition of victims' families suing the Saudi government over its alleged role in the attacks, welcomed the documents' release but pointed out that the records omit key documents they've requested as part of their suit.

Most notably missing are phone records belonging to Omar al Bayoumi, a Saudi national, Eagleson said in a statement. According to a lawsuit filed by the some of the 9/11 families, Bayoumi allegedly provided logistical and financial support to two of the hijackers.
"Families have asked both past and current administrations to release the records that will help expose the full truth," Eagleson said.

"It is time for the Trump administration and Congress to do their part in helping the 9/11 Families get the justice we have fought for by holding the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia accountable for its proven role in the attacks that changed all of our lives so deeply and irreparably 25 years ago," he added.

In July, New York Republican Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, joined by Democratic Reps. Dan Goldman and Jerry Nadler, wrote a letter to a little-known but powerful advisory panel called the Public Interest Declassification Board, housed within the National Archives. It carries the power to consider requests for sensitive government secrets and make recommendations to the president about whether to declassify them.

The lawmakers' request, sent at the behest of the 9/11 families, bemoaned the "repeated obstacles" attorneys for the families have faced "in obtaining access to these materials from U.S. law enforcement and intelligence agencies."
Attorneys for the families believe those records could help them better understand the timing and nature of 9/11 hijackers' communications and key events in the hijackers' planning of the attacks.

The board responded weeks later, writing that it was "actively engaged in interagency consultations to determine what equities, if any, may remain in relation to these records." It urged patience as "those discussions continue."
The U.S. has long been a strategic partner with the Saudi Arabia for decades.

Trump has had a close relationship with the Saudi government in both of his terms and last November invited Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to the White House for a state visit. It was the first time MBS visited the U.S. in seven years.
Trump defended MBS when he was asked by ABC News chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce about the anger from 9/11 families over the visit.
"As far as this gentleman is concerned, he's done a phenomenal job," Trump said of the prince.
MBS responded, "I feel painful about families of 9/11 in America, but we have to focus on reality."
The prince alleged that Osama bin Laden used Saudis to destroy the relationship between the kingdom and the United States.
"We've been working to prove [bin Laden] wrong and continuing developing our nation. It is critical for the safety of the world," he said.
-ABC News' Cindy Smith and Nicholas Kerr contributed to this report.

title: 9/11 then and now: Photos show how the World Trade Center area has changed
summary: Photos from the Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the World Trade Center and photos taken in 2026 show how New York City's Lower Manhattan has changed in 25 years.
story: A look at how Lower Manhattan has evolved in the 25 years since Sept. 11.

New York City has changed in many ways in the 25 years since the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. The area surrounding the former site of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan may be among the most transformed parts of the city since that tragic day in 2001.
New photographs taken by ABC News ahead of Sept. 11 show just how much the neighborhood has changed – or in some cases, remained largely the same – over the last quarter century.

Top: A nighttime view of the Manhattan skyline with the twin towers of the World Trade Center, taken in January 2001 from across the Hudson River in Weehawken, New Jersey. Bottom: One World Trade Center and the Tribute in Light shine across the Manhattan skyline on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: The wreckage of World Trade Center 2 (South Tower), World Trade Center 3, and World Trade Center 4 building, at Ground Zero on Sept. 12, 2001. Bottom: The same intersection, looking west at the corner of Church Street and Cortlandt Street, with all-new development at the location that was once World Trade Center Plaza, about a block away from where the twin towers stood. Taken on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: Dust and debris cover the area and cloud the air on Washington Street, looking north at Rector Street, just a few blocks from the site of the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. Bottom: The same block 25 years later, with a nearly direct view of One World Trade Center, on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: A Burger King restaurant at the corner of Church Street and Liberty Street, just blocks from Ground Zero, became a temporary NYPD headquarters in the days after the terrorist attacks. Photographed on Sept. 12, 2001. Bottom: A Burger King remains at the same location 25 years later, with not much change to the exterior. Taken on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: A destroyed NYPD patrol car sits among the wreckage and debris on Church Street, in front of what was once a Brooks Brothers clothing store, directly across from the former World Trade Center Plaza. Taken in the days following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Bottom: The same retail space on the ground level of One Liberty Plaza is now home to a Chopt Creative Salad Co. restaurant. The stairs and general architecture remain the same. Photographed on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: A closer look at the devastated former Brooks Brothers store, just a day after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center, which was just across the street at the time. Bottom: The same steps and storefront photographed on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: Wreckage and debris looking west on Vesey Street from Church Street, between the former World Trade Center 5 building (left) and a federal office building housing a U.S. post office (right). Photographed on the morning of Sept. 12, 2001. Bottom: The same intersection looks vastly different 25 years later, with only the post office building remaining. Photographed on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: The 1982 sculpture “Double Check” by John Seward Johnson II in Zuccotti Park (named Liberty State Park at the time), became a makeshift memorial in the days after the terrorist attacks, as the park was just across the street from the former World Trade Center Plaza. Bottom: The sculpture has been moved several times in the years following the attacks and now sits on a bench at the corner of Liberty Street and Broadway, just across from Zuccotti Park. Photographed on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: Associated Press photographer Amy Sancetta pushes her bicycle on John Street, at the corner of Nassau Street, still covered in dust and debris a few days after Sept. 11, 2001. Bottom: The same intersection, just three blocks from where the twin towers once stood, 25 years later.

Top: Police seal off Dey Street, just west of Broadway, one block from the former World Trade Center Plaza, five days after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Bottom: The same block 25 years later shows the Fulton Center transit and retail complex (left) which opened in 2014, and 195 Broadway (right), a skyscraper that opened in 1916. Photographed on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: An NYPD officer wearing a protective mask stands guard near the New York Stock Exchange in the financial district in the days following the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. Bottom: Similar view of the New York Stock Exchange, looking north on Broad Street, at Exchange Place, 25 years later. Photographed on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: The original St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church, the only house of worship destroyed in the terrorist attacks, sat just below the twin towers. The original structure was built in the 1830s as a private home and later purchased by Greek immigrants and converted into a church by the early 1900s. Bottom: Located in the same spot on Cedar Street, the new St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church and National Shrine was rebuilt in 2014 and completed in 2022. Photographed on Sept. 4, 2026.

Top: The twin towers of the World Trade Center and the Manhattan skyline seen behind the Brooklyn Bridge on Sept. 8, 2001, just three days before the terrorist attacks. Bottom: The Manhattan skyline from a similar angle on Aug. 5, 2026, including One World Trade Center seen behind the Brooklyn Bridge.

title: Triplets carry on father's FDNY legacy after 9/11
summary: The triplet sons of an FDNY firefighter who responded to the Sept. 11 attacks are following in his footsteps and honoring the legacy he left behind.
story: A firefighter father's 9/11 sacrifice is inspiring his triplet sons to serve.
NEW YORK -- The triplet sons of an FDNY firefighter who responded to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks are not identical, but they share a common past and will soon share a common future.
They're three of the thousands of children who lost a parent 25 years ago on Sept. 11 or in the years after due to 9/11-related illnesses.

William Gormley's sons - Raymond, Billy and Kevin - were just 3 years old when their father rushed to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001. While many children lost parents that day, the brothers grew up with their father, only later learning the toll his work at Ground Zero had taken on his health.

"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways," Raymond said while sitting on a couch between his two brothers. "The same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything. No one understands me like these two understand me."
But for Kevin, Raymond and Billy didn't learn about what happened from the history books, they lived it and they always had each other to rely on.
"This is a huge point my father always made, he said, 'These are your people. You were born with them, and this is what you got til the end,'" Kevin said.
They don't remember what happened on Sept. 11, since they were so young.
"Now, 25 years later, we're understanding the full grasp of what happened that day," Raymond said.
William Gormley rushed to the twin towers after they were struck. Unlike many children, they didn't lose their dad that day. The reality of the work he did hit later in life.
Firefighter Gormley worked on the pile for months, looking for survivors and later, for the remains of victims.
"It makes you feel some pride knowing your father went in there selflessly to help others and do the best he could," Kevin said.

The family said the long-term effects of his work became apparent over time. Growing up, the brothers accompanied their father to numerous doctor appointments but did not fully understand the severity of his health problems.
"They never really told us anything really," Billy said. "But as kids we'd go to hospital waiting rooms in summer for doctors' appointments. But not knowing the severity."

Raymond added, "Growing up he had skin cancer, sinus issues. So growing up as a kid, I personally never really understood what that came from. It wasn't until he was diagnosed with bladder cancer in 2016 that we put two together and realized it was from his time spent at Ground Zero."
William Gormley died of bladder and lung cancer in 2017. According to a report, he was one of more than 400 fire and EMS workers who have died from 9/11-related illnesses.
Asked whether his father would have made the same decision knowing what is now known about the dangers faced at Ground Zero, Raymond said there was no doubt.
"One hundred percent, without hesitation," he said. "Not only him, but every single person he went down with that day would go down to the pile again, without a doubt."
Today, a street in Brooklyn bears William Gormley's name, near the firehouse where he worked.
Despite their father's advice to seek work outside the fire service, the brothers found themselves drawn to the profession.
"My father would always say, 'When you get older, get a job where you sit behind a desk and write checks for people,'" Kyle said.
"He'd always say, 'Work with your brain, not your hands,'" Raymond added.

He went on to say, "So I'm a firefighter right now, an FDNY firefighter working at the same house he worked at, Ladder 174. So it's full circle really, it's crazy from him telling me to work with your brain, not your hands, and it's crazy I'm sleeping in the same bed he did 20 years ago."
Billy hopes to join the fire service soon.
"So I'm an EMT with the fire department at the moment," he said. "Waiting to join fire as well."
Kevin has also applied to become a firefighter.
"You hope one day, you can fill those shoes," he said.
The report said Billy and Kevin could join the fire academy as soon as this month.
The brothers said they were inspired not only by their father, but also by the support they received from firefighters after his death.

"Once I saw the camaraderie, everyone coming together, people driving us around, his old coworkers taking care of us, the laughs, the tears," Raymond said. "After that in my mind, it was something I would really like to do."
"Yeah, what they did was incredible how they took care of us, made sure everything was in order," another brother added.
And this didn't just have an impact on the three brothers, it impacted the entire family, including their big sister, Bridget.
"I think there's a beauty in that it was never forced down their throats," said Bridget. "My dad was never like, 'You're going to be a fireman!' Our dad was like, 'You're NOT going to be a fireman!'"

Bridget has also dedicated her work to preserving the stories of those affected by Sept. 11. She works with 9/11 survivors and produced a documentary about the dangers of toxic dust exposure. It's called, "Dust: Lingering Legacy of 9/11."
"Along the way, I got to know my father's friends better," she said. "I mean, I lost my dad, but I've got [sic] thousands of uncles now."

For the Gormley siblings, the events of Sept. 11 continue to shape their lives and careers. They say their shared experiences and bond have helped them navigate a loss that has defined much of their lives.
"Just being there for someone on their worst day, being their hope when there's no hope is really something special, something we take a lot of pride in," Raymond said.

"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways, the same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything, no one understands me like these two understand me," one of the brothers said.
As they continue their careers in public service, the brothers say they are carrying forward the values their father exemplified, together.

title: A 9/11 widow reflects on 25 years of grief and what comes next
summary: "I felt this duty to give back, and I still do," Marian Fontana says.
story: When the 9/11 attacks unfolded, 25 years ago, most Americans remember exactly where they were at the moments hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a remote field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

Marian Fontana was in Brooklyn and had plans to celebrate her eighth wedding anniversary that day with her husband, Dave Fontana, a New York City firefighter. He stayed past his shift and like so many other firefighters, rushed to Lower Manhattan when the first plane struck, she said.
"And I dropped my son off for his second day of kindergarten," Marian Fontana said. "He was five. And I sat, I called [Dave] and said, 'you know, are you ready to go?'"
Fontana said there was a change of shifts around the time of the attack.
After the attacks, rows of media trucks were set up along West Side Highway, more than a mile from Ground Zero where first responders and crews searched for victims.

Frank Schramm, a professional photographer, says he grabbed his camera and began documenting scenes around the city. Looking back, he says it was one of the few ways to mark history before the era of smartphones and social media.
Reporters and photographers were often the "first witnesses of 9/11," he said, "and in a way they, by being there, were speaking to the world about what was going on."
For millions of Americans, the attacks were not something they experienced directly but witnessed on a TV screen. Regardless, the experience still left its mark.
Mindy Notheis says she was getting ready for work at her home in St. Louis, Missouri.

"And the first plane hit, there was tons of confusion and then the second plane hit and everybody knew that something was drastically wrong and then you just saw --within a matter of what, an hour? -- the towers fall," she said.

Notheis says she recently visited the 9/11 Memorial in Lower Manhattan with her niece -- who wasn't even born when the attacks happened -- paying their respects to the thousands of names inscribed in the bronze around the twin reflecting pools where the towers once stood.
She says she has made it a point to bring her other nieces and nephews to see the 9/11 Memorial and Museum over the years.
New York City, its residents and families who lost loved ones showed resilience in those initial days, weeks and months that followed.
After the attacks, relatives of victims, political leaders and the public have gathered at the 9/11 ceremonies in Lower Manhattan. But many other families have marked the anniversary in private.
Marian Fontana and her son, Aidan, who's now 30, say they will go to the beach to pay tribute to Dave.

"It's a mixed bag because I'm grateful that people remember, and yet sometimes it's really hard to go back there," Marian Fontana said. "It's very traumatic. And so I've really always let my son decide what we do on that day, and I think because it's been such a public event that we've been part of, he always chooses a very private."

Marian Fontana says after 25 years of raising her son and grieving, she can start thinking about what's next. She says that includes getting back to activities like comedy and writing, along with launching a podcast called "Firehouse Files," which features firsthand accounts from firefighters and first responders.

"I wanted to give back for the huge generosity that was shown to me after 9/11 and this overwhelming flow of generosity from the world," she said. "And I felt this duty to give back, and I still do. But there was a point at which I was kind of sacrificing my own, you know, my own well-being. So I'm kind of spending this next chapter kind of focusing on myself, returning to theater, returning to the things I love, and really trying to make this last chapter a happy one."
Michelle Franzen is a correspondent and anchor for ABC News and ABC Radio

title: Remembering the FDNY chaplain who raced to the Twin Towers on 9/11 to pray
summary: Twenty-five years after he rushed to help others on 9/11, FDNY Chaplain Father Mychal Judge's legacy of faith and compassion continues to inspire.
story: As chaos unfolded on Sept. 11 FDNY Chaplain Father Mychal Judge ran toward it.

NEW YORK -- FDNY Chaplain Mychal Judge raced to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001 from his midtown Engine Company One / Ladder Company 24. As the chaos unfolded, he prayed for the people trapped, for the rescuers and for humanity. His legacy of hope and service live on a quarter century after his death when the south tower collapsed.
"Today we will bury Mychal Judge," Father Michael Duffy said in a homily delivered after the chaplain's death. "We will bury his body, but not his spirit."
Judge, described as a close friend of Duffy and the first official victim of the 9/11 terror attacks, raced to the twin towers as the chaos unfolded.

"I pray for him every day," Duffy said. "And I think whenever there's excitement around or a fire truck or an ambulance or somebody need consolation, I think, 'Mychael Judge would be right there with them.'"

A French film crew happened to be profiling the FDNY that day and captured Father Judge's final moments inside the lobby of the north tower. He was praying for people jumping from the fire and smoke on the upper floors when the south tower collapsed, sending forth a tsunami of concrete and steel.
Duffy recalled learning of Judge's death while at his soup kitchen in Philadelphia.
"I had no doubt that when the plane hit the building, that he would be there," Duffy said.
An image of Judge's body being carried from the rubble became one of the enduring symbols of the attacks.

"That kind of is an icon that represents 2,000 people," Duffy said. "And the helplessness of goodness being overcome by evil and all those 2,000 people who died and how they were loved by their friends and families."
He went on to say, "I think that that picture symbolized it, that brought it concretely, that's why we feel empty."
The two men first met in the 1970s as Franciscan priests assigned to the same parish in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Duffy said Judge became a mentor without officially being a mentor.
Duffy also remembered Judge's humility.

"He had no airs about him, like he was better or standoffish," Duffy said. "So if you want to share what's really going on in your life, you want to gravitate to the most receptive person and that was him."

Born in Brooklyn, Judge shined shoes near the Church of St. Francis of Assisi on 31st Street before joining the Franciscan order. He was appointed FDNY chaplain in 1992 and ministered to people from all walks of life.
"There's another part of him that I don't know if too many people know that about him, he loved to be where the action was," Duffy said.
Four days after Judge's death, Duffy traveled to New York to deliver the homily at his funeral, as Judge had wanted. Thousands gathered at the church on 31st Street.
Even in death, Duffy said Judge left behind a message of service and compassion.
"We will bury his hands, but not his good works," said Duffy, repeating the lines from his homily at Judge's funeral. "We come to bury his heart, but not his love. Never his love."
Months after 9/11, Father Judge's gear and helmet were recovered. They are now on display at the New York City Fire Museum, alongside the FDNY memorial.

title: 25 years after 9/11, many first responders and survivors navigate health effects
summary: It’s estimated 400,000 people were exposed to toxins, risk of physical injury and stressful conditions from 9/11 and the aftermath, according to the WTC Health Program.
story: When Michael O'Connell found out he had been accepted into the New York City Fire Department, he was elated. O'Connell had started his career as a police officer, but he always had more of an interest in becoming a firefighter.
"It was more my speed," O'Connell told ABC News. "It was like camaraderie, team, unity. It's where I wanted to be."

O'Connell was sworn into the FDNY as a probationary firefighter. Just four months later, he was deployed to lower Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001, following the terrorist attack at the World Trade Center.
For several weeks, O'Connell said he didn't go home. He went back-and-forth between his firehouse and ground zero, extinguishing fires amid the rubble and engaging in search-and-rescue operations.

O'Connell started hearing about fellow firefighters who worked at the site being diagnosed with asthma or cancer but didn't experience any health problems himself until New Year's Day 2007, when he says he woke up in severe pain.
"My body inflamed two times the size of what it was," O'Connell said. "I didn't know what was going on ... and I had like bruises and blisters all over my body."

O'Connell said he was eventually diagnosed with sarcoidosis, a multi-system inflammatory disease that typically affects the lungs, skin and lymph nodes, and his doctors believe is linked to his exposure to toxins at ground zero.

It's estimated that 400,000 people were exposed to toxic dust, smoke and debris; risk of physical injury; and physically and emotionally stressful conditions from 9/11 and the aftermath, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.

At least 69 cancers -- including breast, prostate, skin and head and neck -- have been certified as being linked to 9/11 as have airway and digestive disorders, musculoskeletal disorders and mental health conditions, according to the WTC Health Program.

More than 9,400 people have died from 9/11-related illnesses -- according to recently published data from the WTC Health Program -- which is three times higher than the 2,977 who died in the attacks in New York, at the Pentagon and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Data from the WTC Health Program shows about 50,000 cancer diagnoses have been certified.

Many of these people are members of the FDNY and NYPD who responded to the attacks or assisted in cleanup operations, but they also include civilians -- those who lived, worked, went to school or passed through the area.

"The truth is, 9/11 didn't end on 9/11," Michael Barasch, managing partner at Barasch & McGarry, a law firm that specializes in helping 9/11 responders and survivors get compensation and health benefits, told ABC News. "I personally lost dozens of clients, mostly firefighters and police officers, on 9/11, but I have lost thousands of clients since."

"9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept. 11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
Responding to ground zero

On the morning of 9/11, Thomas Wilson, an NYPD sergeant, was investigating a burglary of an elderly couple in Brooklyn when calls came in over his radio that an object had hit the World Trade Center. Wilson replied that he was heading to the Williamsburg Bridge.
"I said goodbye to that couple, 'I'll come see you later on to take that report,'" Wilson told ABC News. "Never did see them again."

Wilson said he shut down the Williamsburg Bridge on the Manhattan side while his colleague shut down the Brooklyn side. The assignment went from facilitating the movement of vehicles over the bridge to securing it as people fled from Manhattan over the bridge on foot.
"I don't know how many thousands upon thousands of people crossed the bridge that day," Wilson said. "I'm still haunted. Covered in dust. ... That mass exodus out of Manhattan still sticks with me."
When O'Connell, the firefighter, got down to the site, he said he was instructed to help shut down the water mains, and then he climbed on the rubble to assist in search and rescue.

Throughout the day, O'Connell remembers hearing alarms. He said that attached to the Scott Air-Pak, a self-contained breathing apparatus that firefighters wear, is a Personal Alert Safety System (PASS) Alarm, which sits on the chest and tracks movement.
If a firefighter stays still for 20 to 30 seconds, it emits a loud beep to help colleagues locate them.

"That's all you heard were those alarms when we first got there. Nothing but PASS Alarms," O'Connell said. "As a fireman, when you hear it, you're meant to act and try your best to get to that person. You couldn't. They were underneath that pile."
John Feal, a demolition supervisor at ground zero who arrived on site on Sept. 12, also remembers the PASS Alarms going off.

"I don't care who you are, you're not programed ... to see that kind of devastation of that magnitude," he told ABC News. "I've never witnessed anything like that in my life, nor do I wish I ever see anything like that again."
Cleanup efforts

Wilson said he contributed to recovery efforts at ground zero, where he says he spent about 350 hours, and later as a sifter at Fresh Kills Landfill on Staten Island, which was temporarily reopened as a sorting ground for some of the ground zero rubble.
Wilson said he almost never thought about the dust and toxins he was inhaling.
"My mindset was just get the job done," Wilson said. "... Got to do what you got to do to keep things moving along."
At the landfill, Wilson said he was issued a disposable suit with boots, a hood, gloves and a respirator, but said the shifts were 12 hours, and that some respirator filters have an eight-hour limit.

Ivonne Sanchez, former FDNY emergency medical technician, arrived at ground zero after the towers fell and said she spent about 20 straight hours at the site. She said the dust was so thick that she couldn't get her bearings.

For the next several months, Sanchez worked on body identification and recovery efforts. She said she was motivated to continue responding at ground zero with the hope that she would find her friend, who died in the attacks.
Sanchez said she didn't receive a mask until October, when the site was visited by Occupational Safety and Health Administration inspectors for mandatory mask fittings.
O'Connell, the firefighter, said he didn't have a mask for the first few days until he received a painter's mask.

"You'd put them on but, quite honestly, you can't work with a painter's mask on for 24 hours straight and be a part of Bucket Brigade and talk to your guys and drink water," he said. "You're always pulling it on and off. Nobody was thinking, 'What's coming of this? Are we gonna get sick because we're breathing this stuff in?' That wasn't in anybody's head."
First responders begin falling ill
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this week that more than 170,000 pages related to the attacks were being made public, including about air quality.

Among the documents revealed is the "Harding Memo," an October 2001 memo from then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that indicated the city knew of the air quality dangers and the legal liability, even though the city publicly declared the air was safe.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) also told the public at the time that the air around ground zero was safe to breathe. In an interview with The Guardian in 2016, Christine Todd Whitman, who was EPA administrator during 9/11, apologized for "whatever we got wrong" but denied that she knowingly lied about the air quality or knew at the time it was dangerous.

In Lower Manhattan, the collapse of the Twin Towers led to a massive dust cloud that filled the air and blanketed city blocks with ash, debris, metal, glass, asbestos, benzene and other harmful particles, according to the WTC Health program. Fires within the debris pile burned through the end of December 2001 with flare-ups in 2002.
The city did not immediately respond to ABC News' request on potential toxins first responders were exposed to in the aftermath or allegations by agencies at the time that the air was safe.

Medical research is ongoing about the potential links between 9/11-related toxic exposure and certain cancers and illnesses. Dozens of cancers and conditions have a certified link, but scientists are still learning about the cumulative effects of breathing in a "toxic cocktail," how long it may take for certain cancers to develop -- if they do at all -- and how chemical exposure and trauma can accelerate physical decline and life expectancy.

Sanchez, the EMT, said she would often go home after a day at ground zero coughing, bleeding from her nose or vomiting. Sanchez retired in 2002 after recovery efforts ended due to an injury at the site, which she said caused lower back pain and nerve damage that she said she manages to this day.

In the years after 9/11, Sanchez said she developed chronic sinusitis and asthma. In 2014, in her early 40s, she said she began experiencing severe hot flashes. Sanchez said she went to the doctor four weeks later and was diagnosed with breast cancer that spread to her lymph nodes.
"It was Stage II and ... it was very aggressive," Sanchez said.

Sanchez said she had a lumpectomy in August 2014 and a mastectomy in December 2014. While Sanchez says her cancer is currently in remission, she said she has also developed seven or eight stomach ulcers that have caused gastrointestinal problems from her time at ground zero.

Wilson, the police officer, said he also developed cancer. Wilson was diagnosed with an aggressive neck cancer that had spread to his tongue and skeletal muscle after going to the doctor for sinus issues and tongue pain, he said.
Wilson said he underwent a procedure called a hemiglossectomy, which involved removing part of his tongue, along with a neck dissection to remove the neck tumor and 39 lymph nodes.
Doctors used a skin graft from the wrist to replace part of Wilson's tongue as well as an artery from his arm to implant in his neck, he said.

To this day, Wilson said he continues to take medication for his thyroid, experiences fibrosis in his neck, attends swallow therapy and sleeps with an oxygen machine due to severe asthma. He said he also suffers from osteoradionecrosis in his jaw, a serious condition in which bone dies after being exposed to radiation therapy.
Wilson said he also started seeing a mental health specialist two years ago.
"I had a lot to unpack," he said. "It eases me and it helps me get back, and I know I had a lot of anxiety; I still do."
O'Connell, the firefighter, learned he had developed sarcoidosis when his wife was pregnant with the couple's first child, he said.

"I just [thought], this is the first child I'm gonna have. Maybe the only. I just want to get to that day. Get me to the day so I can see this baby and see you and her together, and then I'm good," O'Connell said.

O'Connell said he received drugs, including cancer medications and steroids as treatment. He said he was told there was never a case of sarcoidosis in the history of the FDNY until he was diagnosed but, since then, there have been many more cases, according to O'Connell.
O'Connell returned to work but said he had to retire as a lieutenant in 2010 after experiencing flare-ups while he was in the line of duty.
"That's your family. ... It's a house of 50 guys, and we do everything together," he said. "It's a family and leaving that is one of the worst things that's ever happened in my life."
Many first responders have died from their illnesses, including William Gormley, a firefighter with the New York City Fire Department.

His daughter, Bridget Gormley, said from 9/11 until his death, he had a persistent cough. She said her father was also riddled with skin cancer following his time at ground zero and was going to the doctor two or three times a year to remove cancerous tissue from several areas including his back, arms and nose.
In Christmas 2016, William Gormley was diagnosed with bladder cancer. The cancer spread to his lungs, and he died in June 2017.

"I think my father was well aware that it was caused from being downtown, ground zero, in the pit, in a pile," Bridget Gormley told ABC News. "He and his friends would joke, 'This is all going to kill us one day.' Very gallows humor, but I think they knew."
"I couldn't wrap my head around it': Civilians develop illnesses as well
9/11-related illnesses didn't just affect the first responders but also civilians, including people who were working in the area at the time.

Barbara Mohan, office administrator and paralegal at Barasch & McGarry, said she first realized something was wrong in 2016, when she tripped on an uneven sidewalk walking across City Hall Park on her way to the office and fell on her knee.
Mohan said she went to a hospital, where doctors determined she hadn't broken or fractured any bones. Within a week or two, Mohan said she started to get pain in her hip.

She said she went to an orthopedist, who diagnosed her with bursitis -- inflammation of a small fluid-filled sac that cushions the bones, tendons and muscles near joints -- and recommended physical therapy.

"The more I went to physical therapy, the more it hurts," Mohan told ABC News. "Another X-ray, and then [the orthopedist] sent me for an MRI, and it showed a lesion on my hip bone, kind of the top of the femur."

The doctor referred Mohan to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, she said, where she was diagnosed with large B-cell lymphoma, a subtype of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma that affects the lymphatic system.

Mohan, who had been working in an office just blocks away from the World Trade Center since 1996 -- and returned to work three weeks later -- was told by colleagues at the firm that they believed her cancer was linked to her 9/11 exposure.
"I just couldn't wrap my head around it," she said. "I just got cancer. I guess I never associated it to [9/11] ever, not once. And I work here, two blocks away."

Barasch, the attorney, said he also developed cancer. In 2018, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, which is the second most common cancer in the 9/11 community, and then years later, he was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer, when doctors noticed irregular coloring under his thumb.

"Of course, I knew right away it was caused by my exposure," Barasch said. "I was here on 9/11, caught in the dust cloud, moved back three weeks later. ... So, I knew, because this is what I do for a living, I suspect the average civilian has no idea."
The fight for benefits

Feal, the demolition supervisor, said he was injured at ground zero on Sept. 17, 2001, when a falling piece of steel landed on his left foot. He said he developed gangrene, then sepsis, and eventually required a partial amputation.

He said he was denied compensation from the first 9/11 Victims' Compensation Fund (VCF) created by Congress because his injury occurred outside of a 96-hour window of eligibility for rescue workers. Feal was injured about 123 hours after the attack.

A spokesperson for the VCF told ABC News that questions about denied compensation under the first VCF "should be directed to those who implemented the program and formulated the regulations," and pointed to remarks VCF Special Master Allison Turkel provided during a press briefing last week.

The denial spurred Feal to become an advocate for 9/11 first responders. Feal founded the FealGood Foundation to help ground zero workers receive assistance, spread awareness and advocate, including lobbying members of Congress.

"I had nothing to prove. I had a documented injury," Feal said. "All of those men and women, uniform and non-uniform, and those people that [went] to work, that went to school in lower Manhattan, they had to prove they got sick from 9/11."

Feal and several first responders suffering from 9/11-related illnesses lobbied Congress in the late 2000s to help pass the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act of 2010, which provides health monitoring and aid to the first responders, volunteers and survivors of the attacks. This also led to the establishment of the WTC Health Program.

James Zadroga was an NYPD officer who responded to recovery efforts at ground zero and died in 2006 of a respiratory disease. Two separate autopsies reportedly linked his death to inhaling toxic substances at ground zero and he was the first NYPD officer whose death was attributed to exposure at the site.
Turkel said during the press briefing last week that the VCF has received more than 112,000 claims and has awarded more than $18.56 billion to over 77,000 claimants since reopening in 2011.

The Zadroga Act expired in 2015, and Feal and first responders went down again to Washington, D.C. O'Connell, the firefighter, testified before Congress, as did late night host Jon Stewart in a clip that went viral.
"What Jon did in those eight-and-a-half, nine minutes in front of Congress that America saw really moved the needle," Feal said.
In December 2015, the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Reauthorization Act passed, which extended medical benefits to affected individuals until 2090.
25 years later

The first responders -- O'Connell, Wilson and Sanchez -- often conduct outreach, including speaking at schools, sharing with students their experiences at Ground Zero and their work to ensure first responders receive health care and compensation.

"I think [9/11 is] an historical event, but also, we're still living with ... many of the repercussions that happened that day," Wilson said. "So, I would like to see more schools make sure they're teaching about it."

The 9/11 Memorial & Museum announced earlier this year it will add a seventh moment of silence and a bell toll at this year's 25th commemoration ceremony to honor those who have died of illnesses related to their time at or near the World Trade Center site.

For the past 24 years, there have been six moments of silence followed by bell tolls: two to mark the times when the planes struck the World Trade Center towers; one to mark when a plane struck the Pentagon; one to mark when a plane crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania; and two to mark the collapses of the Twin Towers.
Knowing what they know now, and having suffered their various illnesses, O'Connell, Wilson and Sanchez all said they would respond to ground zero the way they did a quarter-century ago.
"I wouldn't change a thing," O'Connell said. "I can't say anything else but that. Nothing, not a thing."

title: An Iranian commercial ship is struck near Strait of Hormuz with 1 dead, Iranian media say
summary: State-run media in Iran say an Iranian commercial vessel has been struck off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with one person killed and four wounded
story: State-run media in Iran say an Iranian commercial vessel has been struck off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with one person killed and four wounded

CAIRO -- An Iranian cargo vessel was struck early Sunday off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with one person killed and four wounded, Iranian state media said, a day before Tehran seeks to brief regional countries on its contested efforts to manage shipping traffic there.

The events were a deadly reminder of the underlying challenge to global shipping even as attention turns to a new threat, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen now perched on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.

State-run IRNA news agency quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a “terrorist enemy.” There was no immediate comment by the U.S. military, which has struck Iranian-flagged vessels during its blockade of Iranian ports — while facing a new threat from Iranian ballistic missiles launched at its warships.

Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor said a vessel was hit by a projectile while transiting the strait, later adding that a fire had broken out and local authorities were evacuating those on board.
Qeshm Island, about 14 miles (22 kilometers) from the port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Hours before the attack, Iran’s government remained defiant. “Our people can’t be bullied into submission. Iran won’t surrender,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a U.S.-aimed social media post.

Monday's meeting returns regional attention to the Strait of Hormuz days after the Houthis swept down Yemen's Red Sea coast to apply new pressure to a growing alternative for global shipping. While the Houthis say they are targeting only neighboring Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting the rebels, markets are wary.
Global prices of oil, natural gas and related products have been sent even higher.

Commercial ship traffic remains low in the Strait of Hormuz as attacks continue on what was seen as an international waterway before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28. The U.S. has asserted that plenty of oil is getting out as its military helps to guide ships along Oman's coast, at the risk of attack.

Iran has said foreign ministers from regional countries will meet Monday to discuss efforts by Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, to manage shipping on it. However, Bahrain has already said it will not attend, citing a lack of diplomatic relations with Tehran.
It was not clear what other nations would be there, and there was no new statement from Iran on Sunday.

Since early in the war, Iran has expressed interest in having ships pay fees for transit. It has said traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman’s.

But Iran has said reaching an agreement with Oman on the strait doesn’t mean it will open for shipping. “The waterway would be opened up on the condition that the U.S. will terminate its blockade,” Iran’s president told broadcaster India Today TV on Saturday.

There was some measure of optimism in the region about the planned meeting, with hope that Gulf nations might use it to assert a collective response to a war they had no part in starting. For months, they have faced Iranian attacks that Tehran has claimed target U.S. military assets on their lands.

“Oman is hoping that by presenting this agreement with a reasonable level of regional buy-in, the Trump administration will be forced to recognize that the future of the strait will be decided by regional countries,” Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, who heads the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a think tank focused on Iran’s economy, said on social media.
Anna reported from Jerusalem.

title: Wisconsin congressman swims to safety after plane makes emergency landing in a lake
summary: U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, a candidate for Wisconsin governor, wiped away tears and laughed as he shared how thankful he is to survive following a harrowing late-night emergency landing into a lake of the small plane he was riding in
story: U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, a candidate for Wisconsin governor, wiped away tears and laughed as he shared how thankful he is to survive following a harrowing late-night emergency landing into a lake of the small plane he was riding in

WAUSAU, Wis. -- U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, a candidate for Wisconsin governor, wiped away tears and laughed while sharing how thankful he was Sunday to survive a harrowing late-night emergency landing into a lake of the small plane he was riding in.

The pilot “said we are going down,” Tiffany, a Republican, told reporters at a downtown Wausau firehouse. “'Pull your seat belt tight.' I gave it a yank and pulled it good and tight. It was probably about 10 seconds later ... we hit the water.”

Tiffany said he and the pilot, Leonard Boltz, remained on top of the plane in Lake Wausau until it began sinking before deciding to try and swim to shore. He said they swam about 100 to 150 feet (30 to 45 meters) until they reached water shallow enough to stand in.
“We’re really fortunate that God was looking after us last night," said the 68-year-old Tiffany.

The Marathon County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement that the emergency landing happened just before 9 p.m. Saturday. Boltz called 911 after the pair got out of the plane. They were rescued by emergency responders in a fire department airboat just after 9 p.m.

“The gravity of this is probably just hitting me at this point,” Tiffany said Sunday. "We were making jokes every step of the way last night, though we knew it was a serious situation, we tried to keep it light through the whole thing.”
David Crowley, the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, wished Tiffany a “quick recovery” in a post on X and lauded the “heroism of the pilot.”
Tiffany said he was returning from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner when the single-engine, four-seat Beechcraft Bonanza aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport.
Tiffany said he suffered a cut above his right eye that required 12 stitches. Boltz, who Tiffany said is a retired Air Force pilot, also suffered cuts and received four stitches.
He said the incident will not impact his gubernatorial campaign.
A no-wake buoy was placed near the plane, which remained in the lake, and boaters were being asked to avoid the area until the plane can be removed, the sheriff's office said.

A Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson said the agency would investigate the incident. A National Transportation Safety Board spokesperson said that agency is waiting for the FAA to assess the plane as to whether the damage was substantial enough for it to get involved.

title: Ukrainians embed with US forces during drills to teach the latest in drone warfare
summary: The U.S. Army is actively incorporating drone tactics learned from Ukrainian troops
story: The U.S. Army is actively incorporating drone tactics learned from Ukrainian troops

NUREMBERG, Germany -- A lone American soldier stood on a dusty road in Germany, fussing with a controller. Moments later, a drone, with wings that stretched almost as wide as his arms, whirred to life and shot into the sky.

The soldier was taking part in a U.S. Army training exercise designed to showcase and experiment with tactics and equipment picked up from the Ukrainians, whose pioneering drone warfare has helped them against Russia's forces more than 4 1/2 years into the war.

The annual American exercises, held in the Bavarian foothills over the past several weeks, demonstrate how close the relationship has become between U.S. and Ukrainian forces as American troops look to incorporate drone capabilities and tactics into their own units.

Brig. Gen. Terry Tillis, who leads the Germany-based Army training unit, recently told reporters that they have 1,900 drones and they represent “the latest things that we’ve learned from Ukrainian efforts in this war.”

The Associated Press received rare access to the training ground in Germany and troops conducting the exercises, gaining insight into how the United States is pairing with and learning from Ukraine. The effort has taken on more urgency as the U.S. tries to counter Iranian drone attacks in that more than 6-month-old conflict.

The U.S. military has become more comfortable highlighting the level of cooperation it receives from Ukrainian forces, and officials say the Army has made strides in getting drones into soldiers' hands. But leaders have not offered a clear answer to how America's largest military service will adapt its tactics to any conflict where drones are omnipresent.

An Army official said that while there is universal agreement on the need to incorporate drones into the ranks, Army leaders still need to decide how to structure those ground forces for drone warfare and not just use drones to aid in tasks that soldiers already do.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Army units are integrating one-way attack drones all the way down to the company level, but there needs to be more than just “adding drones to an infantry battalion.”

Aiding such efforts are large annual exercises such as Saber Junction, which runs for nearly four weeks in August and September in Germany. The Army unit heading up the U.S. forces is the 173rd Airborne Brigade.

Tillis, the brigadier general, said some soldiers from the brigade were sent to Ukraine at the start of the year to learn from the country that has been on the cutting edge of drone warfare since Russia invaded in February 2022.
During the Army exercises, Tillis said late last month that the Ukrainians “are embedded with them, they’ll help advise, assist and then help them employ” the technology.

About a dozen Ukrainian military personnel traveled to Germany to participate in this year's exercise. They are providing insights on electronic warfare, drone warfare and lessons learned from ongoing combat operations, the U.S. Army said.

Roughly 50% of the 173rd Airborne Brigade's engagements with opposing troops during the exercise “were drone contact first,” Anthony Miller, the Army’s chief technology officer, told reporters this week.
Even as that collaboration yields more insights, it comes as the Army has faced a parade of departures of top leaders who have championed these drone experiments.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth suddenly ousted the Army’s top uniformed officer, Gen. Randy George, in April and replaced him with Gen. Christopher LaNeve. LaNeve has had an ascendant career under the Republican administration, going from commanding an Army formation in South Korea to effectively leading the nation's largest military service as acting chief of staff in about two years.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, the service’s top civilian leader and a George ally, also departed early this month. Both George and Driscoll were champions of quickly adapting the Army to use drone technology.
Trump has named Adam Telle, a civilian leader in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, as the acting Army secretary.

A couple of weeks before Driscoll's departure, LaNeve ordered an Army unit experimenting in drone warfare — a smaller formation within the 173rd Airborne Brigade — to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion after nearly a year of work.

The Army has argued that returning the unit to a more traditional mission was always part of the plan, but there was an expectation under the previous leadership that the battalion would continue its work.

While the loss of the specialized unit appears to be a blow to drone warfare efforts, the Army official noted that it was never clear whether such units were going to be the path forward in the long term.

The official said both the specialized battalion and the regular engagements with the Ukrainians are not part of a larger effort to mimic Ukraine but to help the Army imagine how the U.S. would employ its own formation built around the way the American military wages war.
With more resources, the Ukrainians also would be using drones in a different way, the official said.

Ukraine two years ago created a separate branch of the armed forces, called the Unmanned Systems Forces, just for drone warfare. But drones also have become so deeply embedded across Ukraine’s military that it is hard to find a unit that does not use them in some form — from reconnaissance to strikes — with artillery and other traditional weapons now often operating in tandem with drones overhead.
Similarly, the Army’s chief technology officer said he has discouraged the idea of centralizing drone knowledge in one unit or formation.

“We’ve pushed back on having something like a drone corps since its inception because our theory of the case is if you centralize that in one place, what you lose is the ability to actually scale that learning and send that out to the rest of the Army,” Miller told reporters Wednesday.

Miller also pointed to the 173rd Airborne Brigade's performance in the exercises in Germany as proof that spreading drone integration efforts “across the brigade and across the Army was the right move.”

title: Alaska drops voter misconduct cases against American Samoans who wrongly checked 'US citizen' box
summary: Alaska prosecutors are dropping voter misconduct cases against a group of residents born in American Samoa after a state appeals court threw out felony charges against a woman who wrongly checked a box saying she was a U.S. citizen
story: Alaska prosecutors are dropping voter misconduct cases against a group of residents born in American Samoa after a state appeals court threw out felony charges against a woman who wrongly checked a box saying she was a U.S. citizen

ANCHORAGE, Alaska -- Alaska prosecutors are dropping voter misconduct cases against a group of residents born in American Samo a after a state appeals court threw out felony charges against a woman who wrongly checked a box saying she was a U.S. citizen.

The state’s Department of Law announced the decision Friday, after a three-judge Court of Appeals panel ruled a week earlier that state law requires proof that defendants who erroneously filled out voter registration forms had a “consciousness of wrongdoing” and intended to break the law.

The panel found flaws with a state trooper’s questioning of Tupe Smith, the woman involved in the case that was thrown out, as well as with the grand jury process that led to her indictment. It overturned a lower court’s decision that had kept the charges against her alive.

Acting Alaska Attorney General Cori Mills said in a statement that after reviewing the decision and applying the facts, prosecutors concluded that they could not prove cases against Smith and the other s beyond a reasonable doubt. Her husband, Michael Pese, had also been charged.
“We respect the role of the courts in interpreting Alaska law and will faithfully execute our duty to apply the law and carefully evaluate our prosecutorial decisions,” Mills said.
In a statement last week, Smith’s lawyer Whitney Brown heralded the Court of Appeals decision, saying it “establishes an important safeguard against imposing felony liability for an honest mistake.”

The court “made clear that Alaska law requires more than simply showing that a statement was false — the State must prove a person acted with a consciousness of wrongdoing,” Brown said. “That distinction makes a world of difference to Ms. Smith and helps ensure that Alaska’s voter-misconduct statute is applied as the legislature intended going forward.”
Neil Weare, part of the legal team representing Smith and Pese, said Saturday that the decision to drop charges “raises questions about why this prosecution was even brought to begin with.”

“It’s clear that all along, they really had no evidence of any consciousness of wrongdoing on the part of Michael, Tupe or the other defendants,” said Weare, co-director of the nonprofit Right to Democracy.

In all, 11 people from the small community of Whittier, about 50 miles (80 kilometers) southeast of Anchorage, were charged with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship either when registering or trying to vote. Messages seeking comment were left for their lawyers.

American Samoa is the only U.S. territory where residents are not automatically granted citizenship by being born on American soil and instead are considered U.S. nationals. Paths to citizenship exist, such as naturalization, though that process can be expensive and cumbersome.
American Samoans can serve in the military, obtain U.S. passports and vote in elections in American Samoa, but they cannot hold public office in the U.S. or participate in most U.S. elections.

Smith was arrested after winning election to a regional school board in 2023. She has said she relied on erroneous information from election officials in Whittier when she identified herself as a U.S. citizen on voter registration forms.

Smith said she marks herself as a U.S. national on paperwork. But when there was no such option on voter registration forms, she was told by city representatives that it was appropriate to mark herself as a citizen, according to court papers.

Prosecutors contended that Smith falsely and deliberately claimed citizenship, pointing to warnings on voter registration forms she filled out in 2020 and 2022 that noncitizens “are not eligible to vote.”

The Court of Appeals panel said in its ruling that toward the end of a police interview, a state trooper asked Smith “a long compound question that implied that Smith actually knew she was not eligible to vote” but wanted to be involved in the school board.

When Smith, whose native language is not English, did not respond right away, another state trooper clarified, “He’s asking you,” and the first trooper again presented his question, which the panel describe as “a lengthy and complex statement containing four individual questions.”
Smith answered “Yes,” the panel said, leading to her arrest and indictment on two counts of felony voter misconduct.

title: The secret ballot has been an article of faith in US elections. That's being tested in Georgia
summary: There's a flaw in Georgia’s voting equipment that can allow voters to be matched to their ballots after they’ve been cast
story: There's a flaw in Georgia’s voting equipment that can allow voters to be matched to their ballots after they’ve been cast

ATLANTA -- Security researchers say rapid advances in artificial intelligence are making it more critical to address a flaw in Georgia's voting equipment that can allow voters to be matched to their ballots after they have been cast.

The system's vulnerability has been drawing increased attention, with election security advocates criticizing state election officials for failing to fix it before the November elections. Georgia election officials say they have taken steps to address the potential harm, but some advocates say the state is not going far enough.

The vulnerability does not allow votes to be changed or cast doubt on election results, but it could let someone see how others voted. That is important because ballot secrecy is a fundamental right under the state constitution and violations could create an opening for legal challenges.
While the flaw has been known for a few years, the widespread adoption of AI tools and the blistering pace of its sophistication have election security experts raising alarms.

This is "a bit of a wake-up call because it illustrates how much more easily vulnerabilities can be exploited now that AI can do all of the technical work for you,” said J. Alex Halderman, a voting technology specialist at the University of Michigan who was part of the team that exposed the flaw.

Other jurisdictions across the country use the same voting equipment made by Dominion Voting Systems, a company that has since been sold and renamed Liberty Vote. But many have applied a software update to fix the flaw, and some other states do not allow the public release of records that are needed to exploit it, said Mark Lindeman, policy and strategy director at Verified Voting, a nonpartisan group focused on election technology.

Georgia, a presidential battleground with one of the nation's most closely watched U.S. Senate races this year, is the only place where the system is used statewide. Lindeman said that, combined with an open records law that has allowed access to key documents, creates a “perfect storm."
"It’s really embarrassing that this is still a possibility,” Lindeman said.
Georgia voters make their selections on touchscreen voting machines that print paper ballots voters insert into scanners to tally the votes.

Such cast-vote records detail the votes from each ballot. Those records and electronic ballot images created by the scanners are randomized. But the software flaw allows them to be put back in the order they were cast, according to a report by researchers who discovered it in 2022.
Along with other publicly available data, that information could be used to match voters to their ballots, the researchers wrote.

Max Springer, a Princeton University researcher who was not involved in the original research and studies AI, said he gave a publicly available AI assistant that research. He said it was able to reverse the shuffling of electronic ballot records from Georgia's May primary and then tell him what other records it would need to match names to ballots.

He then gave the AI assistant the early voting list for the counties he examined and the cast-vote record file, which could be obtained through a public records request. It was able to create “buckets of ballots and potential voters,” he wrote in a blog post. In many instances, that made it possible to match voters to their ballots.
In cases where ambiguity remained, he wrote, he got the public audit log for the ballot scanners and precinct check-in records and was able to match most ballots to specific voters.
“AI coding tools are essentially supercharging laymen people to exploit vulnerabilities,” Springer said in an interview.

Georgia's Constitution says elections “shall be by secret ballot” and state law requires voting machines to “permit voting in absolute secrecy so that no person can see or know any other elector’s votes.”

A lack of ballot secrecy can make it easier to buy or sell votes and increase the danger of coercion to vote a certain way by family members, political organizations, employers or government officials. It also is information that could be invaluable to political campaigns.

Gabriel Sterling, special projects manager in the secretary of state’s office, pushed back on the concerns. He said it would be easier to use mail ballots if vote-buying or coercion was the goal and that it likely would be cheaper for campaigns to just increase outreach to voters who fit a certain profile than try to identify voters this way.

State Election Board member Salleigh Grubbs proposed a rule during the board’s August meeting that would have required the secretary of state’s office to apply the software update recommended by the manufacturer by Tuesday.
“Each (voter) has one vote, and no one is entitled to know how it was cast,” Grubbs said. “That privacy protects more than the individual voter. It protects the integrity of the entire election.”

In a letter to the election board, an agency lawyer argued that the update has not been certified by the secretary of state, the implementation would take months and the legislature has not provided necessary funding. The board rejected Grubbs' proposal. Some members said they did not believe they had the authority to order the secretary of state to act and they raised concerns about the short timeline before the November midterms.

Board member Sara Tindall Ghazal, who voted against the proposal, said it is “intensely frustrating” that the software update has not been applied. But she pointed out that it is a felony to reveal how someone voted, which should serve as a deterrent.
“I hate the fact that it’s even physically possible, but there are very, very severe penalties if somebody were to actually do this,” she said.
