title: Former Bond girl says next 007 should be 'another gorgeous man' as James Bond decision looms
summary: Alison Papworth weighed in on who should play James Bond in the iconic film franchise. The actress appeared in "For Your Eyes Only" and "Octopussy."
story: Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.
The search for the next 007 is underway, and former Bond girl Alison Papworth has a clear message: Leave one thing untouched.

"What do I hope? I know they’re about to announce the next Bond, aren’t they?" the actress, who also works as a director for a London-based design and consultancy firm, told Fox News Digital. "And we’re all waiting with bated breath.

"If they’re true to the books, I hope it’s a man," she said. "A man, just a man. Yes, I think it would be very strange if it were a woman. Don’t you? It would be a totally different thing. So, I hope it’s another man, another gorgeous man."
AMAZON ANNOUNCES SEARCH FOR NEXT JAMES BOND IS UNDERWAY, AS HOLLYWOOD CASTING CHOICES COME UNDER SCRUTINY
Alison Papworth, right, was a Bond girl in "For Your Eyes Only" and "Octopussy," starring Roger Moore as 007. (Globe Photos/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)
Papworth’s comments came before Gary Oldman said on "The Morning Show" that his "Slow Horses" costar Jack Lowden could be the next James Bond.

"Jack, it’s been rumored that he’s on the shortlist," Oldman said on the Canadian talk show. "We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So, my fingers are crossed for Jack."

According to Deadline, Oldman later clarified his comments, saying, "There’s six people on a shortlist. I heard a rumor that they’ve picked James Bond, but they haven’t announced it yet, which is their prerogative. So, I do not know [who has got the part], but I’m hoping it’s Jack."
Jack Lowden attends the "Ella McCay" U.K. special screening at Picturehouse Central in London Nov. 24, 2025. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Amazon MGM Studios gained creative control of the James Bond franchise in 2025 after forming a joint venture with longtime Bond producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli.
WATCH: BOND GIRL ALISON PAPWORTH REVEALS HER HOPE FOR THE NEXT 007

In May, the studio announced the search for the next James Bond was underway. Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next installment, with Steven Knight writing the screenplay. Daniel Craig last played 007 in 2021's "No Time to Die."
People magazine reported that Paul Mescal, Jacob Elordi and Jack O'Connell are among the actors rumored to be in the running to take over the iconic role.

Producer Barbara Broccoli and producer Michael G. Wilson attend the world premiere of "No Time to Die" at the Royal Albert Hall in London, on Sept. 28, 2021. (Getty Images for EON Productions, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Studios, and Universal Pic)
The upcoming release will be the 26th Bond film in the more than 60-year-old franchise.
Daniel Craig was the last actor to play James Bond. (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)
Papworth appeared in 1981’s "For Your Eyes Only" and 1983’s "Octopussy," both of which starred Roger Moore.
"He was an absolute gentleman," she said. "Yes, I know everybody says it. I only have fabulous, fabulous memories of him being funny, telling the best jokes. Very dry, very droll.
Actor Roger Moore stands on the set of "Octopussy." (Corbis via Getty Images)

"One thing I really remember about him, when we were in India, there was a stuntman. I think it was a stuntman. He used to smuggle beef drippings in his luggage for Roger because he loved it. It was very funny, and it stuck in my mind all those years later."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Actor Roger Moore is seen here in London with seven of the women who appeared in "Octopussy." Back row, from left: Carolyn Seaward, Janine Andrews and Tina Robinson. Front row, from left: Joni Flynn, Alison Worth (who now goes by Papworth), Carole Ashby and Mary Stavin. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Being a Bond girl had its benefits. Papworth recalled being flown first class to Rio de Janeiro, where vodka was flowing for the cast, and she tried caviar for the first time. In between filming, she would observe Moore playing Backgammon at picture-worthy destinations.
But life on set wasn't always as luxurious.
Alison Papworth (seen here with her husband) is one of the few women who have appeared in more than one Bond film. (Courtesy of Alison Papworth)

"It was the middle of winter doing the scenes for 'Octopussy' where we were fighting in the castle," Papworth recalled. "We learned to stunt fight, and it was supposed to be in India. But we were at Pinewood Studios, and it was below freezing. All the girls had these red bodysuits on with big capes. We were so cold, we had thermals on underneath. So, we probably looked about five pounds heavier."
Sir Roger Moore, who starred as James Bond, died May 23, 2017, at the age of 89. (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

Papworth didn’t expect to appear in two Bond films. She recalled a publicity director once telling her, "Once you’ve done a Bond movie, you get thrown on the Bond Girl scrap heap." But Broccoli, daughter of longtime Bond producer Albert "Cubby" Broccoli, had a different idea.
"You can imagine my surprise when I got the call from Barbara Broccoli saying, 'You’re on the next one, Alison,'" she said. "And it stayed with me. Bond has stayed with me. It’s changed my life.

"My two best friends, I met one on 'For Your Eyes Only,' Vanya Seager; she was another Bond girl. And I met my other best friend, Carole Ashby, on 'Octopussy.' Carol was there when my baby was born. Vanya and I, we speak every day. I speak to them both every day.
Alison Papworth, seen here with her husband, went on to become an interior designer. (Courtesy of Alison Papworth)
"So, without Bond, I wouldn’t have those two incredible bonds."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Poster art for the 1983 James Bond film "Octopussy," directed by John Glen. (Alamy Stock Photo)
After appearing in two Bond movies, Papworth continued acting and modeling. By the time she reached her 30s, however, her modeling career was "leveling out."

"My husband had lots of properties, and I’d always loved interior design," she said. "I’m totally self-taught, but I’m passionate about it. And he just started giving me properties to do, and that developed into our business, which has been running successfully for all these years. I still love it. And after he died, I carried on. He taught me well."
Alison Papworth vacationed this summer with close friend Joan Collins, right. (Instagram.com/joancollinsdbe/)

Today, Papworth is a director at Camhall Design & Consultancy, an interior design company based in the U.K. It has completed projects in London, New York, Boston and the Bahamas. She also helped launch Lustre & Lustre London, which offers "luxury cleaning services."
Today, Alison Papworth heads Camhall Design & Consultancy, an interior design company based in the U.K. (Courtesy of Alison Papworth)

Papworth and her close pal, Joan Collins, also teamed up to raise funds for Shooting Star Children's Hospices. According to the organization's site, it supports, "babies, children and young people with life-limiting conditions, and their families, across south-west London, north-west London and Surrey."
Papworth still has fond memories of her time bringing the Bond stories to life.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Roger Moore meets the press with cast members from the James Bond film "Octopussy" June 1, 1983. (Getty Images)

"I love show business," she said. "I really do. It’s fabulous. And maybe I’m lucky that I’m not super famous, so I can have a private life. I’m not like my dear friend Joan who gets stopped everywhere. I’m lucky because I can dip in and out of it.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ringo Starr hosts a charity fashion show in September 1986 featuring models Jilly Johnson, Cheryl Hart, Alison Worth, Carolyn Seaward, Camella and Carole Ashby. (Alamy)

"I still do signings," Papworth continued. "It went quiet through my 30s and 40s. And then, I don’t know. Bond fans are very good at tracking you down. I started to get invites to do signings. I remember doing my first signing in Birmingham at this huge exhibition center. My husband and my kids came because I was a first-time signer. There were all 'Star Wars,' 'Doctor Who,' astronauts, boxers and little me."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Family Affair’ star Kathy Garver says failed remake ‘sucked,’ reveals what went wrong
summary: Kathy Garver called the 2002 "Family Affair" remake terrible, saying Gary Cole and Tim Curry couldn't replicate the original cast's deep warmth.
story: The ‘Family Affair’ star explains why the 2002 remake starring Tim Curry ‘sucked’ for ‘many reasons.’
Kathy Garver is not holding back about the failed 2002 remake of "Family Affair."

In a new interview with Fox News Digital, Garver — who is gearing up to celebrate the 60th anniversary of "Family Affair" by hosting a special marathon featured on Catchy Comedy — explained why the reboot lacked the chemistry, warmth and familial bond that made the classic show so beloved.
"Excuse my language, but it sucked," Garver, who portrayed Cissy in the original series, said. "And it did for many reasons."
'FAMILY AFFAIR' STAR TALKS 'SURVIVING CISSY,' SEEING ANISSA JONES FOR THE LAST TIME AND ALLEGED SITCOM CURSE
Kathy Garver, who played Cissy in the original "Family Affair" series, said the 2002 remake "sucked." (Everett Collection; Mark Gunter/Getty Images for ACCA Journal)
The original "Family Affair" premiered in 1966 and followed bachelor Bill Davis as he unexpectedly became the guardian of his late brother and sister-in-law's three children: Cissy, Buffy and Jody.
Brian Keith played Bill, while Sebastian Cabot portrayed the family’s butler, Mr. French.

The 2002 remake featured Gary Cole as Bill Davis and Tim Curry as Mr. French. Although Garver praised both actors, she said they brought entirely different qualities to the characters audiences had already grown attached to.
KELSEY GRAMMER ADMITS IT'S 'EXHAUSTING' WHEN MOVIES TRY TO ALTER HISTORY TO FIT MODERN TASTES
"I think it’s very difficult to do a remake," Garver said. "When they see Gary Cole, they say, ‘Well, that’s not Uncle Bill.’"
Cole was "great in ‘NCIS,’" Garver said, but "as you know, he’s no Brian Keith."
Keith’s appeal, she explained, came from the contrast between his tough exterior and his tenderness toward the children.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The cast of the television series "Family Affair" Aug. 10, 1966. Pictured from left are Anissa Jones as Buffy, Brian Keith as Bill Davis, Kathy Garver as Cissy, Sebastian Cabot as Mr. French and Johnny Whitaker as Jody. (Getty Images)
Brian Keith was "this macho guy, the ex-Marine," Garver said. "And here he is, this loving dad."
TIM CURRY'S CAUSE OF DEATH REVEALED
Garver also felt Curry’s portrayal of Mr. French was too far removed from Cabot’s understated performance.
"Tim Curry had a whole different take on it," she said. "It was very good, but it wasn’t in a situation-comedy vein. It was like the Tim Curry show.
"And, so, that didn’t quite mesh with Sebastian Cabot, who was a wonderful actor."
Garver described Curry’s Mr. French as "loud and boisterous," while Cabot’s version was "much more low-key."
Caitlin Wachs, Gary Cole and Tim Curry appear in the 2002 episode of "Family Affair," which aired Sept. 26, 2002. (Courtesy Everett Collection)
ORIGINAL 'LITTLE HOUSE' VILLAIN RETURNS FOR REBOOT WITH WARNING FOR NEW NELLIE
Cabot’s performance was also rooted in his character’s love for the children, Garver said, something she felt the remake failed to convey.
"He, too, did everything in love," she said. "And, basically, he loved the children. And I think that was missing from Tim Curry."
WATCH: ‘FAMILY AFFAIR’ STAR KATHY GARVER SAYS FAILED REMAKE ‘SUCKED,’ REVEALS WHAT WENT WRONG
The actress said the original cast members brought an authentic sense of family to the show because their characters genuinely cared for one another.
"Each individual person on the original ‘Family Affair’ had a family that they loved," Garver said.
‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS
Garver credited that emotional connection with helping the show stand out from other sitcoms of its era.
"I think it was a groundbreaker," she said. "It was the first of its kind — a single father, or a single uncle, single relative, that all of a sudden gets three orphan children."

The series also benefited from its production quality, according to Garver. She noted that "Family Affair" was among the early television sitcoms filmed in color and that many of the cast and crew members came from the movie industry.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
The actress is gearing up to celebrate the beloved show's 60th anniversary by hosting a special marathon on Catchy Comedy.  (Getty Images)
"So, it was a real quality kind of show," she said.
Garver said the original series also featured "relatable characters" and storylines that continue to resonate with audiences.

"It has stories that endure today," she said. "And, so, it remains relatable, I believe, because it’s a family. And how — what do I do with the family? How do I deal with these problems? And it shows you that."
She also believed the warmth of the original series was reflected in the way the characters interacted with one another.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
(L-R) Diane Brewster, Anissa Jones, Kathy Garver and Johnnie Whitaker in a scene from the TV series "Family Affair" in 1967. (Bettmann/Contributor)
"People really like each other — what a concept," Garver said. "People aren’t yelling and screaming at them. You have this very calm person that’s listening to you."
Garver said the original cast’s chemistry was also visible in their performances.
"Our creator, Ed Hartman, who was just a fabulous writer, creator and producer, told me, ‘Kathy, it’s in the eyes. You act through your eyes. What is coming through them?’
Garver said she would be opposed to a sequel.  (Getty Images)
"I think that warmth is something that’s sustained."
For Garver, the enduring appeal of "Family Affair" comes down to the emotional comfort it continues to provide viewers.
She described the show as "a comfort" and compared watching it to "taking a bite of the comfort cake."
"It’s not all this chaos, but something that’s beautiful and lovely and watchable," Garver said.

Catchy Comedy Network will celebrate the sitcom’s 60th anniversary with a special programming event Sunday, Sept. 13. Garver will host the marathon and share memories of portraying Cissy throughout all five seasons.

title: Zachary Levi calls California a ‘failed state’ that is ‘literally and figuratively on fire’ after Texas move
summary: Zachary Levi calls California a "failed state" after leaving Hollywood for Texas. The "Chuck" actor is starring in Guy Moshe's new action thriller "The Fix" opposite Liam Neeson.
story: In an interview with his ‘The Hit’ co-star Liam Neeson, Zachary Levi shared his vision for building a ‘better Hollywood.’
Zachary Levi isn't holding back about why he packed up and left his home state of California for Texas.
In 2017, the 45-year-old actor, who is starring in the upcoming action thriller "The Fix," sold his home in Los Angeles and bought a ranch outside Austin.
During a recent interview with Fox News Digital alongside his "The Fix" co-star Liam Neeson, Levi candidly opened up about why he left the Golden State.
KIRK CAMERON PRAISES NASHVILLE'S 'GOOD VALUES' AFTER DITCHING CALIFORNIA OVER COST OF LIVING, POLITICS
"I grew up in California. I love California. It is a failed state," he said. "It is literally and figuratively on fire."
Zachary Levi called California a "failed state" after moving to Texas.  (Getty Images)

Along with his disillusionment with California, the "Chuck" star explained that his departure was rooted in a long-standing desire to rethink how the entertainment industry operates from the inside out.
NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE'

"Ever since I started working in Hollywood and I saw how broken it all was, I felt very compelled by God to go build a better Hollywood — like a new United Artists kind of studio — where it's owned and operated by the artists, where we can cut out all the middlemen, where we all can do really well, build a community," Levi said.

"And then not just a place to work," he continued. "People can live there, and kids can go to school there. And we have an organic farm, and, like, all of the things that I think everybody really wants these days."
WATCH: Zachary Levi calls California a 'failed state' after moving to Texas
'FRIDAY NIGHT LIGHTS' STAR ADRIANNE PALICKI SAYS TEXAS GAVE HER SOMETHING HOLLYWOOD COULDN'T

"We look at the regular world around us, and we see it burning. And we're like, 'Can we do this better? I feel like we can do this better," Levi added. "So, that all culminated in nine years ago, me finding 75 acres outside of Austin, Texas, to buy, to develop, to turn into this magical kind of idea. That's why I left."
Levi is fulfilling his vision by building Wyldwood Studios, a $100 million film and lifestyle campus on his 75-acre property in Bastrop County outside Austin.
PARAMOUNT ESCALATES THREAT TO LEAVE CALIFORNIA AS DEM AG'S ANTITRUST LAWSUIT STALLS WARNER BROS MERGER

Designed as a hybrid production hub and creative retreat, the multi-phase project pairs soundstages and production offices with housing and wellness spaces. Wyldwood is expected to open its first two soundstages in 2027.
The actor is building a $100 million film and lifestyle campus on his 75-acre property. (Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)
Looking back on his decision to move, Levi explained that walking away from his life in California meant trading idyllic weather and close personal ties for a bigger mission.
‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STARS JEP AND JESSICA ROBERTSON SAY ‘A LOT OF PRAYER’ LED THEM TO LEAVE LOUISIANA FOR TEXAS

"I left behind a lot of community and family and perfect weather in Southern California, but when you weigh it all out — and you must — you have to come to these points in your life, and you go, 'Is all of that really worth the thing that I know I'm supposed to go build in the future to make a better world?' And, to me, that calling on my life was more important," he said.
"Fortunately, Austin's awesome. It's great, you know?" Levi continued. "It can get kinda hot in the summer and kinda cold in the wintertime, but I can deal with it.
"There's no thing as bad weather, just the wrong clothing."
Levi is starring in the new action-thriller "The Fix." (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)
"The Fix" marks a sharp departure for Levi, who is best known for starring in lighter projects like the action-comedy series "Chuck" and the superhero film franchise "Shazam!"
TAYLOR SHERIDAN TAKES SWIPE AT LOS ANGELES AFTER BUILDING TV EMPIRE FROM TEXAS

Directed by Guy Moshe, the movie follows a group of war-torn, disgraced former CIA operatives, led by Tucker (Levi) and mentored by his long-time lead Larry (Neeson), who are left disillusioned in the chaotic wake of the 2021 U.S. military withdrawal from Afghanistan.

After a high-stakes mission goes disastrously wrong, the team embarks on a rogue, high-risk mission in Tehran. Seeking both a life-changing score and a chance at personal redemption, the group attempts to pull off a daring rescue operation while confronting their own past choices.
TAYLOR SHERIDAN'S $330M FOUR SIXES RANCH PURCHASE FORCED HIM OUT OF RETIREMENT PLANS
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Levi explained that he was drawn to the project because he wanted to take on a different character type than those that he had previously played.
Liam Neeson plays his longtime lead and mentor in the movie. (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)

"I wanted to do something fun, gritty, darker, in comparison to other roles that I've played in the past, and this gave me that and then some, because there was all of the great spycraft and twists and turns and revelations throughout the story, as well as this human foundation," he said.

"'Who are these people in real life? Why are they doing the things that they're doing? What is this redemption that they are trying to seek?' The moral ambiguity of all of that, of, like, who's really the good guy and who's the bad guy. I think these are really cool themes to explore. And I got to do them with the Liam Neeson."
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Neeson also explained why he joined the movie's cast, heaped praise on Levi along with Moshe, who co-wrote the screenplay with Mark Bacci.
"It is a terrific script," he said. "Really, really good, talented director and writer.
"He's a wonderful actor," Neeson added of Levi. "I'm not just saying that because he's here, but he is wonderful."
Along with Levi and Neeson, "The Fix" also stars Annet Mahendru, Grant Harvey, Augusto Aguilera, Elnaaz Norouzi and Wes Chatham.
Levi said he was drawn to the project because he wanted to play a "gritty, darker" role. (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Moshe explained that he believed from the outset that Levi was a natural fit for the project and wasn't surprised by how hard the actor pushed himself physically for the role.

"When I met him, I immediately asked myself, ‘How am I the first one to see what a great action star this guy can be?’ Like a 6-4, handsome, commanding, almost like old movie star type of kind of presence," Moshe said.

"But to me with Zach, the nice thing about him is which people, I think, don't know as much about him — he's very much of an outdoors person," he continued. "He lives in Austin, Texas, on the ranch. He likes rafting. He likes to be outside. He likes to hike. I mean, he's a very physical person in real life."
WATCH: ‘The Fix’ director Guy Moshe says Hollywood overlooked Zachary Levi as an action star

"And he embraced it and was every bit a collaborator from day one," Moshe added. "So, I wouldn't say surprised, but rather validated maybe is the word that I could use. Like, I believed that this would be the case when I met him, and he clearly exceeded my expectations even here."
Moshe told Fox News Digital Levi brought a raw, real-world edge to the set that surprised even the filmmakers.

"Let's just say I found myself in the streets of Tbilisi in a fistfight with Zach and I throwing punches ith people in the middle of the street, which is maybe not something I should advertise," Moshe said. "But I don't know if people would expect that of him. But, like, he's quite a man's man in that capacity.

"He's done all these movies where it's like the four-quadrant family films, all that kind of stuff, whatever, but he's certainly, I think, a much more intense person in real life in certain ways that people might not be familiar with."
Neeson praised his co-star as a "wonderful" actor.   (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)

Norouzi also praised Levi during her interview with Fox News Digital. In "The Fix," the Iranian-born German actress plays Zara, a woman recruited to pose as the Persian wife of Tucker to help cover his cover story as a businessman while his team executes their high-stakes mission in Tehran.
During the course of the movie, Zara and Tucker develop an emotional and romantic relationship amid the surrounding danger.

Norouzi told Fox News Digital Levi is a "fantastic actor," adding, "And you do want to be opposite him as the leading lady."
The former "The Traitors" contestant went on to say that Levi was an "awesome" screen partner.
WATCH: ‘The Fix’ star Elnaaz Norouzi says rare chemistry with co-star Zachary Levi made scenes 'really good'

"Honestly, he's one of those guys who just lets you be and lets you do," she said. "But whenever I would, like — whenever he would feel like I need something from him in the scene to either understand the scene better or to get that chemistry, he would just give it to me.

Nelson was spotted during a rare outing in West Hollywood. (Splash News)
Nelson rose to fame in the 1980s as a member of the infamous Brat Pack, which was a nickname given to a group of young actors who frequently appeared in movies together throughout the decade.
The term was a play on the Rat Pack, which referred to a group of Las Vegas entertainers who often performed together in the 1950s and '60s, including Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr.

The term was coined by writer David Blum, who named the group of actors in a June 1985 article for New York Magazine, after both "St. Elmo's Fire" and "The Breakfast Club" were released in the same year and featured many of the same cast members.

title: Pink hits back amid backlash for criticizing Macklemore's pro-Palestinian concert remarks
summary: Pink doubles down on criticism of Macklemore after his "Free Palestine" chants and anti-Israel song performance at a concert, sharing an emotional statement as a Jewish mom.
story: Fox News correspondent CB Cotton reports on rapper Macklemore facing backlash over anti-Israel comments while performing at an Ed Sheeran concert on ‘Fox Report.’
Pink is doubling down on her criticism of Macklemore following his pro-Palestinian comments during a recent concert.

On Sept. 4, Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, and he used his time onstage to perform his anti-Israel song, "Hind's Hall." He repeatedly chanted "Free Palestine" while a slideshow played on the screen behind him, showing footage from the war in Gaza.

Several fans were upset by the performance, including an Instagram page called "Stop Antisemitism." The page shared a video criticizing Macklemore, calling the move "awful." Pink reposted the video to her own Instagram story, which started a new wave of backlash from people criticizing her for seemingly being pro-Israel.
MICHAEL RAPAPORT SLAMS ‘CLOWN’ MACKLEMORE FOR ANTI-ISRAEL PERFORMANCE
Pink has been receiving backlash after reposting a video criticizing Macklemore following his comments on Palestine and Israel. (John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images; Kristy Sparow/Getty Images)
Initially, Pink didn't explicitly share her opinion on the matter, but on Sept. 11, she took to Instagram to explain her thoughts in an emotional statement.
"I’ve been quiet in my own words for a week, which you know isn’t like me. So here they are," she began.
The "So What" singer explained that she'd reposted the video that was critical of Macklemore, which "said things in words I didn’t write, and I wouldn’t have chosen all of them."
She maintained that "a repost isn't a statement," then wrote, "I’d rather be disagreed with for what I actually said than hated for what anybody else wrote, so let me say it."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Pink spoke about her reaction to the Macklemore controversy as a Jewish woman. (Scott Dudelson/Getty Images)

"I was born a Jew," she continued. "I didn’t pick it, and I’ve never hidden it. And this week a whole lot of people decided what I believe without asking me, without checking a single thing I’ve ever said or done, because a repost and the word 'Jew' were apparently enough to fill in the rest. But let me fill it in... myself."

"Of course I don’t speak for Israel, or for any government. I never have. What I said in October 2023 is still exactly what I believe: Hamas is a terrorist organization. Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations. Protecting innocent life comes first, everywhere, and nobody should ever celebrate the death of a child. Anybody’s child."
JERRY SEINFELD GIVES BLUNT THREE-WORD RESPONSE TO INFLUENCER ASKING FOR A 'FREE PALESTINE'

She detailed the work she's done with UNICEF over the years, spending time with children "on both sides of that fence," and said, "I’m not going to litigate a complex war in an Instagram caption, and I’m not going to recite anybody’s slogan to earn back a follower."

Pink went on to explain that what she was "reacting to" was Macklemore himself. She recalled him performing his song "Same Love" at the Grammys in 2014, and how she cheered on the message, but "Four months later Macklemore put on a hooked nose, a black beard and a bowl cut, performed in it, and called it a 'random costume.'"
Pink recalled a performance Macklemore did years ago that was perceived as antisemitic. (Kieran Frost/Redferns)

"Every Jew I know knew exactly what it was. The same love, it turned out, had a guest list, and we weren’t on it. But he apologized, and I let it go, because that’s what we do. We let it go. title: Mackenzie Phillips shocks with 15-year celibacy confession as Sharon Stone, Teri Hatcher rethink romance
summary: Mackenzie Phillips revealed on a podcast that she has been celibate for 15 years, joining Sharon Stone and Teri Hatcher in new Hollywood trend.
story: While walking the carpet at the Golden Globe Awards, Sharon Stone told Fox News Digital "you get to choose how you view the world."
Mackenzie Phillips revealed that her past extroverted life is nothing like her current status.

"I would get home, and I would have no words left, you know, and so in order to get up and do it again the next day, I had to be alone to recharge," she said, per People. "Which is, by the way, why — am I going to say this out loud? — I have been celibate for 15 years."
'AMERICAN PIE' STAR SHANNON ELIZABETH SWEARS OFF DATING, SAYS ONLYFANS IS 'THE ONLY RELATIONSHIP I NEED'
Mackenzie Phillips, Sharon Stone and Teri Hatcher have each pursued lifestyles that don't include dating. (Getty Images)

"And the parts of me that were injured or wounded, I can care for them myself," she said before noting that she doesn't date. "I have my little friend in the bedside drawer."
Bertinelli admitted that she also experienced "periods of celibacy" and hasn't been physically intimate in "almost two years now."
Phillips first married music manager Jeff Sessler for two years before their divorce in 1981. She then married guitarist Shane Fontayne for 14 years before their split in 2000.

"I'm a really good girlfriend, but I haven't been a girlfriend in a long time," Stone said during an appearance on the "Mayim Bialik's Breakdown" podcast. "And I've been a girlfriend to bad boyfriends, and I've been a girlfriend to good boyfriends."
CHRISTIE BRINKLEY SAYS SHE'S RETHINKING SOULMATES AFTER FOUR MARRIAGES

While the "Basic Instinct" star revealed her dating patterns, she also noted that she's now looking for "someone that's my companion, not just someone to have sex with."

title: Dr. Drew blasts Ryan Reynolds for calling 1980s a 'brutal' era: 'What happened to fun?'
summary: Dr. Drew fires back at Ryan Reynolds' claim that the 1980s were "brutal," arguing the actor confused the decade with the more turbulent 1970s.
story: Celebrity physician Dr. Drew Pinsky tells Fox News Digital why trendy "resets" can hide addiction, not cure it.
Ryan Reynolds has a bone to pick with the 1980s — but Dr. Drew Pinksy isn't buying it.

The "Deadpool" star recently shared a decidedly un-nostalgic view of the decade, arguing that the passage of time has allowed people to romanticize an era that was far more turbulent than the movies, music and pop culture of the time might suggest.

"What's interesting about when you get far enough away from a time period that's quite distinct, I think there's always a lovely feeling associated with it. It's almost like you pave over all the trauma with, like, puppy dogs and ice cream," Reynolds said during an interview with Variety.
POLITICIAN SPENCER PRATT CALLS OUT ACTOR RYAN REYNOLDS FOR CONDEMNING 1980S NOSTALGIA
Dr. Drew Pinsky challenged Ryan Reynolds’ gloomy assessment of the 1980s and questioned whether the decade was really as "brutal" as the actor claimed. (Getty Images)
"And the '80s was a brutal, brutal time for people. It was a f---ing mess... and people forget that. It was a tremendous strife. Sociopolitical tensions everywhere."
Reynolds pointed to the lingering shadow of the Cold War and the Cuban Missile Crisis, noting that the latter had occurred only a couple of decades earlier.
"So, you know, it's a... it's a tumultuous period, but you look back at it now, and you're like, 'Oh, yeah. "Top Gun." Cocaine!' Like, 'No!' It was really scary," he said.

title: Army veteran nicknamed ‘Xena’ after daring missions with Green Berets trades combat gear for pinup glamour
summary: Army veteran Lindsey Schmidt earned the nickname "Xena" while accompanying Green Berets on Iraq missions as the only woman in her battalion.
story: Pin-Ups for Vets 2027 calendar model Lindsey Schmidt recalls how her role as an Arabic linguist helped gather intelligence during military missions.

Lindsey Schmidt spent nine years in the Army, including time accompanying Green Berets on missions in Iraq. Now the veteran nicknamed "Xena" is slipping into red lipstick and stilettos to tell a different side of her story.
The Virginia resident is now appearing in the Pin-Ups For Vets’ 21st annual fundraiser calendar for 2027, which features 13 female veterans from across the country photographed in vintage styles.

"The whole reason I even joined the military was because of 'Saving Private Ryan,'" Schmidt told Fox News Digital. "So it was a full-circle moment to go back into that World War II era.  And it's so great to see a spotlight on female veterans in this way, especially highlighting femininity."
USAF VETERAN WHO DONATED 2 ORGANS POSES AS ‘40S PINUP MODEL
Lindsey Schmidt is featured in Pin-Ups For Vets' 2027 calendar. (Shane Karns)

"I know a lot of us don't feel super feminine when we're in uniform, but to be a part of this group of women who are so accomplished and have been through a lot of obstacles and challenges, it's really special to be a part of it," Schmidt added.
Popular American movie actress Betty Grable models a bathing suit in the most famous pinup photo of World War II. (Getty Images)

The award-winning nonprofit, founded in 2006 by California resident Gina Elise, raises money to support hospitalized and deployed troops. It produces World War II-inspired bombshell calendars featuring veterans as models. Elise previously told Fox News Digital she was inspired by Hollywood actress Betty Grable, whose swimsuit snap was distributed to GIs during World War II.
"When the opportunity arose to serve in the war of my generation, I didn’t hesitate. I wanted to be part of something bigger than myself." (Shane Karns)

Proceeds from the calendar support hospital visits, care packages for deployed troops, ongoing donations of rehabilitation equipment to VA hospitals, and goods for homeless veterans and those transitioning to housing.

To date, Pin-Ups For Vets has donated nearly $140,000 worth of rehab equipment to veterans and military hospitals, according to the organization. It has also visited more than 25,000 ill and injured veterans at their bedsides in more than 135 hospitals and state veterans' homes.
WATCH: PIN-UPS FOR VETS CALENDAR MODEL HOPES TO INSPIRE YOUNG WOMEN

Growing up, Schmidt said she was always deeply patriotic. But after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, she knew she wanted to serve in what she called "the war of my generation." She went on to serve as an Arabic linguist and interrogator.
Lindsey Schmidt graduated from the Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center in Monterey, California, in 2004. (Courtesy of Lindsey Schmidt/Pin-Ups For Vets)

"I actually wanted to learn Russian first," Schmidt said with a laugh. "I thought Russian just sounded cool. But it was 2002, and we needed Arabic. So I went with Arabic. And I'm so glad now that I did."

The movie "Saving Private Ryan," directed by Steven Spielberg, features Barry Pepper as Private Jackson, Tom Hanks as Capt. John Miller and Matt Damon as Private James Francis Ryan. The film had a theatrical release on July 24, 1998. (CBS via Getty Images)
Schmidt soon learned that earning her place wouldn't come easy.

"It was very divided," she explained. "Initially, I wasn't even supposed to go on deployment. They told me no many, many times, but I am persistent and creative. I found a way to get myself onto the deployment. And there were definitely mixed reactions. Some of them saw the value in my skill set. Some of them just thought it was more risk than it was worth."
Lindsey Schmidt is seen here in Birmingham, Alabama, date unknown. (Courtesy of Lindsey Schmidt/Pin-Ups For Vets)

"Some of them told me to my face, 'You don't belong here. We don't want any females,' which isn't fun to hear, but I appreciated that because at least I knew where I stood with those guys," she recalled. "The other ones who were nice, I was just like, 'I'm not sure what your angle is here,' but I kept my head down. I worked hard. I didn't cause any drama. And after a little while, the guys that were opposed to having me there, they all came around eventually."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Lindsey Schmidt is seen here near the Tigris River, not far from Saddam Hussein's palace in 2006. (Courtesy of Lindsey Schmidt/Pin-Ups For Vets)

Schmidt said she deployed to Iraq as the only woman in her battalion, where not everyone believed she belonged. But then suddenly, one soldier who had been outspoken about not wanting her there asked to borrow her helmet. Hours later, he returned it with "Xena" painted across the back — a nod to the legendary warrior princess.

Schmidt later learned the nickname had quietly spread among the troops after they watched her accompany Green Berets on missions while many remained at the forward operating base. At that moment, she said, she knew she had earned their respect and been accepted as one of the team.
Lucy Lawless stars in "Xena: Warrior Princess," directed by Rick Jacobson in 1995. (Alamy Stock Photo)

"Being the only female to accompany the guys on the missions, it was an adventure," she said. "It felt very validating to be able to go out as one of the team members. The objective was always clear before I went on, but getting to go inside and actually getting intel from women and children that they weren't able to otherwise, it felt really cool."
Lindsey Schmidt is seen here training in Helena, Montana, in 2005. (Courtesy of Lindsey Schmidt/Pin-Ups For Vets)

"I would go out on missions with the ODAs, those are the teams of Green Berets, and they separate the women and children from the men," she said. "And our guys, culturally, are not able to talk to the women. And so, by having a female on the objective, I could speak to them, and I could ask them about their husbands and what's really going on behind the scenes and gather intelligence that the guys would not have access to otherwise."
Schmidt said Iraqi women were curious about the female American soldier who was armed yet spoke their language. They would quickly recognize her.
Lindsey Schmidt was transformed into a 1940s pin-up model. (Shane Karns)

"They just started rattling off Arabic, asking me a million questions," Schmidt recalled. "Like, 'We know you speak Arabic. We know you have this information. Talk to us. What's going on?' There was a lot of curiosity, a lot of hesitance. But I think they may saw that, 'Hey, if you talk to me, I can help your situation. If you don't talk to me, there's nothing I can do for you.'"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Lindsey Schmidt is seen here in Iraq. "I served as an interrogator and Arabic linguist in Army Special Operations, and I’m endlessly grateful for the experiences that came with it. I deployed to Iraq and Djibouti in uniform, and later to Afghanistan as a defense contractor." (Courtesy of Lindsey Schmidt/Pin-Ups For Vets)
One interrogation still vividly stands out to Schmidt.

On missions, Schmidt was almost unrecognizable. Clad in full combat gear with her hair pulled back in a tight bun, she accompanied Green Berets on the field. But inside the interrogation room, she traded her uniform for civilian clothes.
The 2027 Pin-Ups for Vets calendar features 13 female veterans. (Shane Karns)
"This particular mission, I was there," Schmidt recalled. "I saw the guy being detained."
Lindsey Schmidt at a palace in Iraq, circa 2006. (Courtesy of Lindsey Schmidt/Pin-Ups For Vets)
During the interrogation, Schmidt asked the detainee to explain how he had been captured. He launched into what Schmidt said she knew was a fabricated story.
"That's not how you were detained," she told him. "Tell me the truth."
He just smirked.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Lindsey Schmidt was a high school cheerleader who was fascinated by World War II history. (Courtesy of Lindsey Schmidt/Pin-Ups For Vets)
Then Schmidt reached up and pulled back her hair.
"Imagine no hair," she said. "Imagine me in uniform. I was there."
Schmidt said the man's eyes widened. He instantly recognized the interrogator who had witnessed his capture.
"I kind of enjoyed that," she said. "And then, the rest of the questioning went a little bit different after that."
The 2027 Pin-Ups For Vets calendar is available now. (Pin-Ups For Vets)
Asked what Americans take for granted, Schmidt didn't hesitate.
"Everything."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
That is the message she hopes to carry now as a model.
James Oliver, who served in the Army from 1967 to 1971, looks over Gina Elise's calendar during her visit to the Denver VA Medical Center on Dec. 14, 2011. (Denver Post via Getty Images)

"Our freedom, our ability, especially for women, especially coming back from the Middle East, just being able to drive by myself, vote, get a job, have a mortgage and credit cards, that I do not take for granted," she explained. "Just basic comforts of being at home. People complain about things, and I just roll my eyes now, thinking we have it so good; you guys don't even understand. But I think just appreciating the opportunities we have."
Gina Elise (wearing a red polka dress) is seen with some of the models from the 2027 Pin-Ups For Vets calendar. (Shane Karns)

"The opportunity is the largest one for me," she continued. "We can be anyone we want to be, we can go anywhere we want to go, do what we want to do, and not everyone in the world has that freedom. Just being able to do anything that I want to do without a man. I can go about my life, and I do not need a male guardian there with me to do it. I think a lot of women here don't understand what life is really like for others. I'm grateful that I had exposure to it, so that it all makes me more appreciative."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Liam Neeson, 74, says he likely still has ‘a couple’ more action movies left in him
summary: Liam Neeson says he may have "a couple" more action movies left in him as he and Zachary Levi explore forgiveness and redemption in "The Fix."
story: The 74-year-old talked to Fox News Digital about his latest CIA thriller "The Fix."
Liam Neeson isn’t hanging it up yet.
The 74-year-old said he thinks may have "a couple" more action movies in him.
"Maybe a couple left, you know," Neeson told Fox News Digital when asked if he’ll transition away from action films in the near future. "Maybe… I hope I have a couple left."
WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HE'S 'TAKING CARE OF BUSINESS' AT 95: 'THE LEAST OF ALL I WANT DO IS DIE'
Liam Neeson is seen in his new film "The Fix." (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)
The "Taken" star joked to Variety last year that he didn’t want to be doing stunts while pushing a walker.
His newest action flick, "The Fix," in which he plays an ex-CIA operative alongside Zachary Levi, hit theaters Friday.
In "The Fix," Neeson said, "There's this incredible thread of humanity that these men, these extraordinary men, have to eventually analyze or work out what makes them tick."

Levi said he "wanted to do something fun, gritty, darker, in comparison to other roles that I've played in the past, and this gave me that and then some, because there was all of the great spycraft and twists and turns and revelations throughout the story, as well as this human foundation."
Neeson touched on the theme of redemption, which is explored in the film.
Zachary Levi stars alongside Neeson in the new film. (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)

"I'd like to think we all need and want second chances, you know," he told Fox News Digital. "We're humans. We've all made mistakes in our personal lives and stuff, you know? It's extraordinary to be forgiven, and it's an extraordinary thing to really forgive someone. It really is very, very special. So, you know, I'm 74 years of age. I've had quite a few things happen to me that several of which seriously I have been forgiven for, which is just amazing, and then I can return that."
Levi compared a lack of forgiveness to "drinking poison, hoping that the other person will die."
"Forgiveness is grace, mercy, understanding, empathy," he said. "These are things that we don't explore enough as human beings."

The 46-year-old said that people are often encouraged to look at others as an "evil monster. And by the way, people do evil things. People do monstrous things. And yet, still, I believe that they are children of God. And yet, still, I believe they are worthy of second, third, fourth chances, right?"

He explained that there needs to be boundaries, but a lack of forgiveness is "eating us alive as human beings, as a society, in this country and around the world because we're not able to just see the other as a child of God."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
In "The Fix," Neeson plays a former CIA operative while Levi plays his protégé. (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)

"The greatest definition of love I've ever heard is to will the good of the other," he added. "It doesn't mean you have to like them at all. It doesn’t mean you have to agree with their decisions at all, but you want them to find the light. You want them to be redeemed. You want that because we all need redemption. We all need forgiveness."

In the film, Levi plays another former CIA operative who is Neeson’s protégé, and he said it was a relief "that I was not wrong to want to meet one of my idols, you know, like everybody says 'don't meet your idols,' and I get it."
The "Shazam" actor revealed that he’s met some of his idols in the past who didn’t live up to his image of them, "but fortunately, you get these wonderful, beautiful exceptions."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Director Guy Moshe told Fox News Digital that he had been looking for a while for a movie in which he could lend his perspective as an Israeli military veteran, but he said he didn’t want it to be a reenactment of something that really happened.
Guy Moshe is seen on the set of "The Fix." (Courtesy of Inaugural Entertainment)

"So when one of the producers came to me with this hook, you know, this idea of this urban legend or like CIA lore or whatever, like money hidden in a wall in Tehran since ‘79, which may or may not be a true thing, I thought, ‘What an interesting way of sort of like hooking a story around a group of guys in that field.’"
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

He said it was about a year and a half after the U.S. pulled out of Afghanistan, and "I could feel what those American soldiers must be feeling after a 20-year war, handing the keys back to the Taliban or something."
Moshe said he had been serving in the Gulf when "we gave back the keys to the PLO after the Oslo agreement."

"I just knew there and then I’ve got to do this," he explained. "I want to start the film in the evacuation from Afghanistan, and I want to give these people some sort of a journey to a mental redemption rather than specific redemption for something, so to fix what was broken in them."
Liam Neeson attends the "Taken 2" premiere in 2012. (Getty Images)

Ultimately, Moshe said "The Fix" is "about a father who wonders if he wants his son to grow up to be like him, even though outwardly the father is the image of the hero that we like to look at," referring to the mentor/mentee relationship of Neeson and Levi's characters.
The director said he thinks Neeson has succeeded as an action hero because he’s "real."

"We identify the most, especially in the action genre, we identify with real people, with a person that we feel conveys something that we believe is a real person in a real situation," he explained. "It sounds simple. It's the hardest thing to do in acting."

title: Mark Wahlberg, Martha Stewart and others mark 25 years since 9/11 with emotional tributes
summary: Mark Wahlberg, Martha Stewart and Hugh Jackman lead Hollywood's emotional tributes marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks.
story: Actor and comedian Rob Riggle discusses fan outrage over sports on streaming services; his new Fox Nation special on baseball’s impact on New Yorkers after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks; and more on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’
Hollywood is pausing to remember.
As America marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the nation is coming together for ceremonies and moments of silence honoring the 2,977 people killed.
Across Hollywood, celebrities are sharing personal reflections, tributes and messages of remembrance on the anniversary of the day that forever changed America.
PETE DAVIDSON SAYS BECOMING A DAD CHANGED HOW HE VIEWS FATHER'S DEATH ON 9/11
Mark Wahlberg and Martha Stewart led celebrity tributes honoring the victims of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. (Steve Granitz/Filmmagic; Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

Mark Wahlberg shared a video on Instagram showing an American flag raised on a flagpole and waving in the wind, captioning his post, "This anniversary is always a gut punch of emotions…words just can’t say it all. #neverforget911 #freedomisntfree "
Martha Stewart offered a particularly personal remembrance, recalling where she was when she watched the attacks unfold on television while in Tokyo.

"In 2001 I was in Tokyo when we saw on television live footage of the destruction of the WorldTrade Center towers. Of course we could not reach the United States for hours and could not find out the fate of our family members and friends.

"We stayed glued to the television for news and we tried to figure out how we could get back to the United States. We decided to take the train to Kyoto where we knew we could find peace and beauty amidst the horror of the day."
ROB RIGGLE RECALLS 'APOCALYPTIC' SCENE AT GROUND ZERO WHILE SEARCHING FOR SURVIVORS AFTER 9/11

"She was stranded in Paris but urged us to go to the temple at Miho for solace and rest. It had been designed by the very same Minoru Yamasaki who was the architect of the World Trade Center !!!

"As we entered the deserted temple (it was closed that day) the organ played America the Beautiful for us. All of us in my small group stood in awe and disbelief and we all cried for the people lost that day in the attack that changed America forever!"

title: Rob Riggle recalls 'apocalyptic' scene at Ground Zero while searching for survivors after 9/11
summary: Rob Riggle recalls the "apocalyptic" scene at Ground Zero as part of the bucket brigade, describing burned fire trucks and skyscrapers gutted by debris.
story: 9/11 anniversary reflections from Ground Zero: Chaplain Father Brian Jordan and Dana Perino capture the emotional gravity of the historic day 25 years later. Father Jordan shares his firsthand memories of serving as a chaplain at Saint Francis of Assisi Church during the terrorist attacks. He emphasizes the critical responsibility of teaching younger generations the truth about 9/11.
Rob Riggle is looking back at 9/11 and the "apocalyptic" scene he witnessed while assisting at Ground Zero.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the actor and retired U.S. Marine officer recalled the scene at Ground Zero following the terror attacks on the World Trade Center in New York, calling it a "surreal" thing to process.

"It was so unreal that it was surreal," he said. "I was looking at skyscrapers that had the front of the building clawed out from the falling of the towers. They had gouged out other buildings. They had knocked other buildings over. They had weakened buildings to such a state that they would collapse."

He remembered seeing the Brooks Brothers store across the street from the towers, saying "it looked like Godzilla had scratched out the front" of the building, as it "was all gutted out from where falling debris had smashed into" it.
SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE
Riggle referred to the scene at Ground Zero as being "apocalyptic." (Robby Klein/Getty Images for IMDb)

"Then you had burned-out fire trucks and police cars and there were pictures and paper debris, and it was just, it was surreal," he explained. "It was surreal to see that much of Manhattan laying in some sort of apocalyptic ruin. It was shocking, and it was hard to process for sure."

Riggle was on site working as a member of the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve based in Manhattan. He was among firefighters, police officers, military personnel, construction workers and volunteers who lined up and cleared debris by hand in buckets.
They avoided using machinery to remove the rubble, in order to avoid hurting potential survivors trapped underneath.

"Everybody was spread out, so when we stopped, you didn't always know necessarily what was going on," he shared. "Were we dropping a listening device into the rubble? Did they find someone? Did they find someone alive or did they find remains? You just never really knew what it was, and so when they blew the whistle to stop moving and stop working, you would pray, you would just put your head down, and you would hope that it was somebody who was still alive."
Riggle was a member of the "bucket brigade," working to clear debris and search for survivors at Ground Zero. (Preston Keres/US Navy/Getty Images)

He added that if they discovered remains, he and the others would say a prayer for them and "that their family would get closure," in addition to praying for themselves, so that they would "have strength to keep going, and hopefully find someone soon."
One thing that stood out to Riggle about the days following the terror attacks was the unity among all Americans, saying it was "a unification that I hadn't seen maybe in my entire life."
He went on to explain that it didn't matter to anyone what anyone's political beliefs were, and that "it didn't feel like there was anything separating us."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I remember seeing the Senate and the House of Representatives out on the steps of the Capitol singing ‘God Bless America’ together," he said. "I remember, nobody asked any questions, no one looked at each other and judged down at Ground Zero. Everybody worked. And we were unified in trying to figure out what happened and then figuring out a way to help."
Riggle said he would rather focus on the heroism of the firefighters rather than the terrorists. (Andy Wenstrand/SXSW Conference & Festivals via Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Twenty-five years after the attacks, Riggle says the first thing that comes to his mind when he thinks about being at Ground Zero are "the firemen that went in that came from all over the city," calling them "heroes," and noting, "that's the thing I like to focus on, rather than the terrorists."

Riggle explained that, for many, 9/11 was "very sobering," because it came with the realization that, "there's people out there that are willing to commit evil acts and do harmful things," but what he likes to focus on is that "for every one terrorist, there were literally thousands of people out there trying to do the right thing."
For him, when people say "never forget", it means remembering the innocent lives that were lost, and that "there are more good people than bad people."

"It means don't forget those innocent people who died. It means, don't forget that there are people in this world that are committed to hurting us. It means we have to be vigilant always. We can never just take a break," he said.

Riggle says it is important not to forget the innocent lives lost, the acts of heroism that day and that there will always be more good people than bad. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

He added, "It reminds me to remember that we have men and women in uniform, whether it's a police uniform or a firefighter's uniform or an EMT or a Marine or a soldier or a sailor or airman or a Coast Guard man. I mean, these are all these people that are wearing those uniforms. They do it so that we can not have more 9/11s. So that just reminds me that we have to be vigilant. We can't be naive. And it also reminds me, don't ever forget that there are more good people than bad people."

title: Denis Leary says firefighters’ darkest days after 9/11 helped bring hit show ‘Rescue Me’ to life
summary: Denis Leary watched FDNY firefighters shift from crushing grief to laughter in minutes, a raw moment that shaped "Rescue Me" into a landmark drama.
story: Grey Bull Rescue founder Brian Stern discusses surviving the September 11 attacks, working at Ground Zero and founding an organization to evacuate Americans from overseas crisis zones.
Denis Leary saw grief and laughter collide inside FDNY firehouses in the devastating aftermath of 9/11 – an emotional whiplash that ultimately helped inspire "Rescue Me."

That collision of heartbreak and humor would become central to "Rescue Me," with Leary drawing from the firefighters he knew and the raw moments he witnessed inside their firehouses in the months after 9/11.

"A lot of the guys I knew that had survived, I was spending time with them and in their firehouses as they were digging through The Pile in the fall right after 9/11," he told the New York Post. "We were witnessing the grief that they were going through."
TWENTY-FIVE YEARS LATER, HOLLYWOOD IS GIVING 9/11 THE SILENT TREATMENT, AND IT’S MAKING US LESS SAFE
Denis Leary revealed that witnessing FDNY firefighters move from devastating grief to laughter after 9/11 helped inspire "Rescue Me." (Bobby Bank/WireImage)
The original idea Leary was working on with writer Peter Tolan was about a firefighter killed in the line of duty, but one moment changed his mind completely.

"It was literally in the blink of an eye," he explained. "We went from watching a guy come up from downtown from ‘the pile’ – they had found a friend, a piece of a friend, and so he was just overwhelmed with grief. I mean, he could barely talk."
"Watching him trying to fight to talk in that firehouse kitchen was a very tough experience to watch," Leary recalled. "Maybe 20 minutes later… all of us were laughing about something."
That moment – moving from crushing grief to laughter in a matter of minutes – helped Leary envision what "Rescue Me" could become.
MICHAEL KEATON SAYS 9/11 FILM ‘WORTH’ IS ABOUT EMPATHY
Denis Leary drew on real-life firehouse stories and the experiences of firefighters who searched through the debris at Ground Zero. (Bobby Bank/WireImage)

"We’re going to make a show where people are on the edge of their seat watching an action sequence involving fire," Leary told the outlet. "And then the next minute they’re crying because they’re so sad, and then the minute after that, they’re laughing their a--es off."

"Rescue Me" stars Leary as Tommy Gavin, a veteran New York City firefighter struggling with alcoholism, family turmoil and survivor’s guilt in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. The supporting cast includes Andrea Roth, Michael Lombardi, Steven Pasquale, Daniel Sunjata, John Scurti and Jack McGee.
Leary and Tolan didn't have to hunt for information. FDNY members and firefighting consultants gave the show's creators plenty of real-life firehouse stories to draw from.

"We went from watching a guy come up from downtown from ‘the pile’ – they had found a friend, a piece of a friend, and so he was just overwhelmed with grief. I mean, he could barely talk. Watching him trying to fight to talk in that firehouse kitchen was a very tough experience to watch. Maybe 20 minutes later… all of us were laughing about something."
"We had so much information on a daily basis, not just comedically, I’m talking about dramatically," Leary said. "All the ideas for our fires came basically from experiences those guys had."
Feedback from younger firefighters was overwhelmingly positive before the show's launch, according to Leary. "They said, ‘You got it. You totally nailed it.'"

Denis Leary said the series aimed to blend intense fire scenes, heartbreaking loss and dark humor. (Tim Grant/WireImage)
Leary had been playing a game of pick-up ice hockey on the fateful day 25 years ago.
He watched an "endless flow" of dust-covered corporate workers fleeing uptown New York City for hours from the West Side Highway.
"They turned the rink into a morgue, and they lined up all the ambulances," he recalled.
Leary added, "The sound of the buildings … it’s almost like it goes into your bones."

Leary had experienced the bond between firefighters firsthand years earlier, after his cousin and close friend Jeremiah Lucey was killed alongside five other Worcester firefighters in a 1999 warehouse fire. He recalled FDNY friends traveling to Massachusetts to help search the ruins.
The actor launched the Leary Firefighters Foundation in 2000, shortly before the 9/11 attacks took the lives of many FDNY firefighters and friends of Leary.

"I knew I was going to hear about firefighter friends of mine from the FDNY that didn’t make it," Leary recalled. "But the next day, to hear that 'Ace' Bailey had died in the thing as well, we were just like, ‘That is crazy.’ I mean, it’s insanity."
The acclaimed firefighter drama premiered on FX on July 21, 2004, and ran for seven seasons, ending in September 2011.

The show's blend of tragedy and dark humor may have resonated with audiences, but Leary recalled that not everyone in Hollywood believed comedy had a place in a post-9/11 world.

"I remember a network executive saying to me at the time or a movie executive saying this is going to alter the way people feel about comedies," Leary said during an appearance on Joy Behar's show in 2011. "And I was like, 'What are you talking about? They're going to need to laugh more than ever. If anything, they are going to be looking to laugh.' And he was full of fear."

Reflecting on the series alongside Leary at the 9/11 Memorial & Museum in 2024, Tolan – co-creator of the show – acknowledged the weight of building a television series around a tragedy that remained deeply personal for so many.

"When you know that, you always have to sort of be vigilant to how far am I going and is it too soon to do this? And I'm not going to say that we were hugely careful because there are elements of the show that are raucous – that are just inappropriately funny," Tolan said. "But that's the human experience."

title: Aaron Rodgers makes bombshell claims about Shailene Woodley split
summary: Aaron Rodgers claims Shailene Woodley left him for another man, directly disputing her narrative that he ruined her life during their 2022 split.

On an episode of "Not Just Football with Cam Heyward," Rodgers explained that he didn't "ruin" the actress' life during their 2022 split.
"I proposed to Shailene and she said yes. Now, she maybe felt like she was forced to make a decision. She could have said no," Rodgers began.

Aaron Rodgers made shocking claims about his 2022 split from Shailene Woodley. (Getty Images)
SHAILENE WOODLEY IMPLIES AARON RODGERS ‘UNAVAILABILITY’ WAS REASON FOR SPLIT

"There wasn’t even a relationship in 2022 to break off. She literally told me, 'I don’t want to be with you' after we tried some reconciliation in 2021. There’s just a lot of narrative out there that isn’t true," Rodgers clarified.
The Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback addressed Woodley directly on the podcast.
"I’m actually a good partner. I don’t wish you any harm … and Shai, you left me, you took the ring off. What are we talking about regarding me ruining your life?" Rodgers asked.
Aaron Rodgers accused Shailene Woodley of calling off their engagement for another man. (WWD via Getty Images)
A representative for Woodley did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Woodley and Rodgers first sparked dating rumors in July 2020, but the two kept their relationship under wraps until going public a few days before they announced their engagement in February 2021. In February 2022, the former couple called off their engagement but briefly reconciled before splitting again that April.
During a 2024 interview with Outside magazine, Woodley shared that she went through a traumatic event in 2022, the same year she and Rodgers split for good.

"I had a really awful, traumatic thing happen in early 2022," she said, without naming anything specific. "I felt like I lost my soul, myself, my happiness, my joy. I really understood depression and anxiety and, like, complete soul detachment."
Aaron Rodgers is the quarterback for the Pittsburgh Steelers. (Getty Images)

Without naming the person, Woodley said that "empathy kind of kept me in this loop of feeling everything for everyone."
"There’s just a lot of narrative out there that isn’t true."
During the same interview, the 34-year-old actress admitted that she hasn't "shared much" about her former romance with the 42-year-old NFL star "because it always makes me cry."
"It was not right. But it was beautiful," the "Big Little Lies" star told the outlet after her "eyes welled up."
Shailene Woodley has addressed her relationship with Aaron Rodgers in previous interviews. (GC Images)

title: Popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to potentially deadly brain disorder
summary: A study linked 15 cases of Wernicke encephalopathy to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro, raising concerns about vitamin B1 deficiency risks.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss a recent University of California San Diego study regarding the effects of GLP-1 weight loss medication on the biological aging process. Siegel outlines the potential cardiovascular and neurological benefits of the drug while noting side effects related to digestion and thyroid function.
Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications.

A new study, published in Clinical Nutrition, identified 15 reported cases of Wernicke encephalopathy, a neurological disorder caused by severe vitamin B1 deficiency, in people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Most of the reported cases involved semaglutide, sold under the brand names Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound.
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS
Researchers found 15 cases through the FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), published medical literature and their own medical center.
Most patients reported gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition, the study noted.
Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications. (iStock)

Reports of the disorder appeared more often among people taking GLP-1 medications than among those taking other drugs, the researchers found. They emphasized, however, that the study cannot prove the medications caused the condition.

Vitamin B1 plays an important role in brain function, the researchers said. Severe deficiencies can cause confusion, trouble walking, balance problems and vision changes. If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent neurological damage or death.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Karthik Achari, a Chicago-based clinician and founder of PepMD who was not involved in the study, said the findings should be viewed in perspective.

"Researchers went through adverse event reports and the medical literature and found a small number of cases, 15, of Wernicke encephalopathy in people taking GLP-1 drugs," Achari told Fox News Digital. "That's out of millions of people on these medications. So this is rare."
Researchers identified 15 cases, finding that most patients experienced gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition. (iStock)
"But it's real, it's serious, and the mechanism makes sense," he added.
GLP-1 medications can reduce appetite while also causing nausea and vomiting, making it easier for some people to become deficient in vitamin B1, Achari said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The drug shrinks your appetite. It doesn't shrink your body's requirements," he said. "You can now eat very little without feeling it, which is the point of the medication, but your need for protein, vitamins, and fluids didn't go anywhere."

People with persistent nausea and vomiting, those losing weight very quickly while eating little, people with a history of bariatric surgery and those who use alcohol heavily may face a higher risk, Achari said.
The medications suppress appetite, experts say, but the body's requirements for nutrients and hydration remain the same. (iStock)
Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," said proper nutrition and hydration should be considered part of treatment while taking GLP-1 medications.

"GLP-1 medications can dramatically reduce appetite, but that also means people may unintentionally under-eat the very things their bodies need most, especially protein, fiber and fluids," she told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Palinski-Wade said ongoing vomiting or diarrhea can increase the risk of dehydration and kidney problems. She urged patients to seek medical guidance if those symptoms continue for roughly 24 hours.
"Don't assume every side effect is just part of being on a GLP-1," Palinski-Wade said. "Severe or persistent symptoms deserve attention."

The researchers acknowledged that the study relied largely on reports submitted to the FDA and cannot prove GLP-1 medications caused the condition. They called for additional research, and experts said patients should not stop taking prescribed GLP-1 medications based on these findings alone.

title: ‘Food divorce’ trend among couples could drive them apart, experts warn
summary: The "food divorce" trend has some couples eating separately, but experts warn the growing trend erodes relationship quality and emotional well-being over time.
story: Regularly splitting apart for meals may contribute to isolation and disconnection, according to dietitian Tanya Freirich. Sharing flexible, modular meals can make it easier for people with different needs or schedules to eat together.

Between differing diet plans, food intolerances and conflicting work schedules, some couples are choosing "food divorce," a term circulating on social media for partners who intentionally cook, order and eat their meals separately.
While taking separate paths at mealtime might solve logistical headaches, experts warn that splitting up at the dinner table can come at a cost to the relationship.
Shared family meals can help people reconnect, build stronger emotional bonds and reduce stress, according to health institutions like Mayo Clinic.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT
For couples, experts say regularly eating apart could become a concern if it reflects broader emotional distance or reduces opportunities to spend meaningful time together.
Nutrition experts emphasize the issue is often less about the food itself and more about the lost opportunity for a built-in daily checkpoint.
"Food divorce" refers to the growing trend of couples intentionally cooking, ordering and eating meals separately due to conflicting schedules or specialized diets. (iStock)
"I think it reflects many people's very busy schedules," Tanya Freirich, a North Carolina-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital.

"Mealtime can be a time to unite, to communicate, to build social relationships and foster a connection," she said. "If we're eating completely alone or at different times than important people in our lives, it may foster a little bit of disconnection."
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Eating separately can contribute to a "roommate dynamic," experts note. Without regular time to reconnect and discuss the day, couples may have fewer opportunities for communication.
The practice can also contribute to isolation, according to Freirich.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes," she said.
"If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for mental health or well-being."

Eating alone can contribute to isolation, an expert warned. "If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for our mental health or well-being." (iStock)
There can also be practical drawbacks because preparing separate meals or ordering from different restaurants may increase grocery costs, preparation time and kitchen cleanup.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, eating solo can affect individual dietary habits. Studies show people dining alone are more likely to eat quickly, mindlessly scroll on their phones or settle for heavily processed convenience foods compared to when they share meals with others.
"Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes."
Couples can accommodate different dietary needs without preparing entirely separate meals.
For those navigating specific calorie targets, plant-based diets or medical restrictions, Freirich recommended building "modular" or "choose your own adventure" meals as a more efficient method.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Something like a deconstructed taco night, grain bowls, a pasta or noodle night or even a sheet pan meal where you're creating each food on its own," the expert said.
"So the protein, the carb, the veggies are being cooked separately. And then you get to decide your portions and make your own meal from those ingredients that can meet everyone's needs."
Research highlights that nearly one in four Americans eats every meal alone on any given day, increasing the risk of isolation. (iStock)
When conflicting schedules or caregiving duties make daily dinners impossible, experts recommend prioritizing quality over frequency.
Even sharing a quick weekend breakfast or setting aside one designated night a week can help maintain connection.

"Be very intentional to connect when you can," Freirich suggested.
"Make that a really special meal. Be intentional with your connection. Put the phone away, and actually enjoy the other person's company."
