title: What does ‘Never Forget’ mean for a generation with no memory of 9/11?
summary: Pentagon 9/11 Memorial leader says new education center aims to connect generations with no memory of 9/11 to the facts and gravity of the attacks.
story: Pentagon Memorial Fund Executive Director Joseph Kornhoff discusses plans for the new 9/11 Visitor Education Center.
Twenty-five years after a generation promised to "Never Forget," that pledge now relies on education for the more than 100 million Americans with no memory of 9/11.

The Pentagon is preparing to help address that challenge by breaking ground this weekend on a long-awaited Visitor Education Center at the only one of the three 9/11 attack sites still without a dedicated museum or education center.

The new center is intended to fill the gap that has grown more pronounced with each passing year by helping Americans who never experienced the attacks understand not only what happened on Sept. 11, 2001, but why it continues to matter.

Joseph Kornhoff, executive director of the Pentagon Memorial Fund, told Fox News Digital that nearly one-third of the country was either not alive that day or has no recollection of it and therefore lacks the "personal connection" shared by those who watched the attacks unfold.
NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS
An American flag is unfurled on the side of the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2026, in Arlington, Virginia. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"That's what we're trying to provide with the visitor education center experience," Kornhoff said in an interview with Fox News Digital, explaining that the goal is to give visitors a personal connection that allows them to "start to understand the gravity of that day."

Flowers lay on a bench at the National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial, adjacent to the Pentagon, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks, in Arlington, Virginia, on Sept. 9, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
Nearly 230 miles north, the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York is confronting the same generational divide.

Beth Hillman, president and CEO of the museum, said the passage of time has only made the annual vow to "Never Forget" more important as the number of Americans with firsthand memories of the attacks declines.

"Many in my generation remember exactly where we were on that horrific day," Hillman said during an Aug. 31 press preview outlining the museum's plans for the 25th anniversary. "Yet, 100 million Americans were not even born or are too young to remember that day for themselves today."
BROOKLYN TEACHERS WHO WITNESSED 9/11 AS CHILDREN REVEAL WHAT THEY WANT THE NEXT GENERATION TO REMEMBER

Noah Rauch, the museum’s senior vice president for education and public programs, said he has watched that transition unfold firsthand through the museum’s work with students and teachers. "I've seen this line creeping up between memory and history, between those who remembered the attacks and those who didn't," Rauch said during the Aug. 31 press event.

The United States is marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, when a group of al Qaeda hijackers flew airplanes into the World Trade Center, Shanksville, Pennsylvania, and the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people. (Jeenah Moon/Pool/Getty Images)

That transition from memory to history also raises a more modern challenge. Americans too young to remember the attacks are increasingly learning about an event they never experienced firsthand, while conspiracy theories and false narratives about 9/11 run rampant online.

Kornhoff said that makes factual education increasingly important, pointing specifically to conspiracy theories surrounding the attack on the Pentagon and narratives suggesting that America "deserved 9/11."

"That's the need for the education center," Kornhoff told Fox News Digital. "As a nation, we need to really take a step back, look at how we're educating our young children to make sure that we're providing them with the facts of the situation... and not these conspiracy theories and entertaining wild ideas that just simply are not true."
REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS
Flowers and American flags rest beside inscribed names at a reflecting pool at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum on Sept. 11, 2026, in New York City. (Jeenah Moon/Pool/Getty Images)

The Pentagon center will include 10 exhibits telling the human stories of the attack, including the 184 people killed at the Pentagon and aboard American Airlines Flight 77, the first responders who rushed to the scene and the military and civilian personnel who aided the wounded.
"We are going to address the facts of the day," Kornhoff said. "We are going to address the entire Pentagon story."

The renewed focus on 9/11 education has also reached Capitol Hill. Reps. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y., and Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., introduced bipartisan legislation ahead of the 25-year anniversary, which aims to direct the Department of Education to examine how 9/11 is taught in schools nationwide and identify gaps in instruction.

Kornhoff praised the effort during his interview with Fox News Digital, saying the legislation reflects a growing recognition of the need to educate generations with no firsthand connection to the attacks.
Stainless-steel benches dedicated to victims are seen at the National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial on Sept. 10, 2026. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images))
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Pentagon 9/11 Memorial Visitor Education Center is expected to open by the end of 2029 near the existing Pentagon 9/11 Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia.

The project received $12 million in federal funding this year, along with $1 million from Virginia and additional private donations raised by the Pentagon Memorial Fund. Once completed, the center is expected to include interactive exhibits, historic artifacts and firsthand accounts from survivors and victims' families while providing visitors with additional context about the attack and its aftermath.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Trump says he would 'love' to see Ireland unified as one nation
summary: Speaking to reporters, President Donald Trump said he hopes to see Ireland become one country in the future, predicting reunification will happen over time.
story: President Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love to see" a unified Ireland, predicting that unification will "happen eventually."
President Donald Trump said Saturday during a trip to Ireland that he would love to see the country unified.
The Republic of Ireland gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1922, while Northern Ireland, established in 1921, has remained part of the U.K.

"I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified. I have friends on both sides, great people. They're Irish people. How can they be bad, right?" Trump said in Dublin while on stage with Ireland's prime minister, Micheál Martin. "I'd like to see a unified country. I think it would be a great feather in everybody's cap if that happened. It's going to happen eventually."
He added that the U.K. "will have something to say about it obviously," but reiterated that unification would be a "great thing."
TRUMP SAYS IRAN CONFLICT COULD END AFTER MIDTERMS
President Donald Trump meets with Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House in Phoenix Park in Dublin on Sept. 12, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
In response to Trump's comments, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement that the U.K. government's stance on reunification remains unchanged.
"I am not aware ​that there is majority public support for ‌another ⁠referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one," Burnham told reporters in Parliament, according to Reuters.
Later Saturday, Trump addressed a crowd at the Deerfield Residence, the official home of the U.S. ambassador to Ireland.
U.S. Ambassador Edward S. Walsh introduced the president, who took the stage to the sound of Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the USA."
Early in his remarks, Trump revisited the question a reporter had asked during his meeting with Martin about the prospect of Irish reunification.
"That's one of those questions where no matter what you say, no matter how well you say it, there's no good answer, right?" he said, before saying reunification would be a "cool thing."
President Donald Trump delivers remarks to U.S. Embassy personnel and business leaders at Deerfield Residence on Sept. 12, 2026, in Dublin, Ireland. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
IRISH AUTHORITIES SEEK EXTRADITION WARRANT FOR SUSPECT IN MURDER OF AMERICAN MOM JAMEY CARNEY: REPORT
The debate over whether Ireland should be one country has been one of the island's most divisive political issues for decades.
At times, it was far more than a war of words. From the late 1960s through the late 1990s, Northern Ireland was gripped by decades of sectarian violence known as "the Troubles."
Irish nationalists and republicans — drawn largely from Northern Ireland's Catholic minority — sought to reunite the island under a single Irish state.
Unionists and loyalists, who mostly belonged to the Protestant majority, wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the U.K.
Throughout the conflict, more than 3,500 people were killed in violence involving Irish republican and loyalist paramilitary groups, as well as British security forces.
A photographer captures a scene of soldiers in front of a building in May 1981 in Northern Ireland. (Joe McNally/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The fighting largely ceased with a peace deal in 1998, but in the decades since, tensions remain between Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland.
A 2024 U.K. Parliament report found that 90% of students in Northern Ireland attend schools that "are effectively segregated along religious lines."
The peace deal signed in 1998 — known as the Good Friday Agreement or the Belfast Agreement — set up a new government that had representation for both nationalists and unionists.
It also established that Northern Ireland will remain part of the U.K. unless a majority of citizens vote to leave through a referendum.

Brexit reignited debate over Ireland's future, with Northern Ireland voting to remain in the European Union even as the U.K. as a whole voted to leave. Still, no referendum has been proposed or scheduled on whether Northern Ireland should leave the United Kingdom.
Reuters contributed to this report.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Pennsylvania lawmaker suggests Trump should rename Lake Erie to 'Lake Pennsylvania'
summary: Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney wants President Donald Trump to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania," following recent name changes to other bodies of water.
story: Rep. Jimmy Patronis, R-Fla., is pushing legislation to rename "Lake America" permanently, after President Donald Trump changed Lake Ontario's name amid a trade war with Canada.
Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney, a Republican, is asking President Donald Trump to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania" following similar renaming efforts by the president.

Maloney is preparing a resolution calling on Trump, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and lawmakers on Capitol Hill to take steps to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania," arguing that the change is needed to reflect the lake’s modern identity.

"This is Pennsylvania’s only Great Lake. Its modern economy and identity are increasingly tied to the boaters, anglers, families and tourists who come to enjoy it," Maloney said in a statement. "Ohio has plenty of shoreline. New York already has two Great Lakes. Canada has four others."
NEW YORK GOV HOCHUL REJECTS TRUMP'S 'LAKE AMERICA' RENAMING WITH BLUNT MESSAGE
Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney, a Republican, is asking President Donald Trump to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania." (Getty Images)
"Pennsylvania has one. Let’s call it Lake Pennsylvania!" he added.

Lake Erie is the smallest of the Great Lakes by volume as well as the shallowest, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. The lake has about 12 million people in its watershed, with 10.5 million people in the U.S. and 1.9 million people in Canada.
This comes after Trump signed an executive order last month to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," a rebranding that Canada does not recognize and has firmly rejected.

"We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement.
SOUTH PARK CREATORS MOCK TRUMP'S LAKE ONTARIO RENAME AND COMPANY COMPLIANCE IN MOCK STATEMENT
President Donald Trump signed an executive order last month to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America." (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)

The renaming only applies to the U.S. federal government, meaning Canada, other international bodies and U.S. states are not forced to acknowledge the change. But both Apple Maps and Google Maps changed the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" for U.S. users following Trump's executive order.

The president has also suggested renaming New Mexico to "New America," prompting several of the state’s Democratic lawmakers to call on Apple and Google to publicly commit to keeping the state's current name on their respective maps applications.
Trump has also floated the idea of renaming the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans.
Canada does not recognize President Donald Trump's executive order last month to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America." (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

On his first day back in office in January 2025, Trump signed an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America," but, similar to the Lake Ontario rebranding, the order only applies to the U.S. federal government and does not bind Mexico, other international bodies or private entities.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Apple Maps and Google Maps also adopted this change for users in the U.S., implementing the update using a region-based approach tailored to the location of the user's device.

title: El-Sayed ignites firestorm after sharing 9/11 message on social media: 'Piece of s---'
summary: Abdul El-Sayed's 9/11 video message drew fierce online backlash over his association with Hasan Piker, who notoriously claimed America deserved 9/11.
story: GOP political strategist Erin Maguire and former GOP national spokesperson Elizabeth Pipko discuss U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's relationship with far-left streamer Hasan Piker, examining the political fallout and how the controversy could shape Michigan's closely-watched Senate race on 'Fox News @ Night.'
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, sparked social media backlash after posting his 9/11 message on his X account.
"They didn’t just attack America that day they attacked the idea of America," El-Sayed said.

"The notion of a nation brought together by ideals — a place where freedom and commitment to justice bind us, even if, at times, we struggle to fully realize it," the controversial far-left candidate continued.
"Today on 9/11 we remember the lives that were taken from us in a terrible act of terrorism."
CBS NEWS TAKES HEAT OVER REPORT ON DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED'S NOW-DELETED 9/11 POSTS

Hasan Piker, left, listens as Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks in a green room before a campaign rally April 7, 2026, at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Mich. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)
Online viewers quickly reminded El-Sayed of his friendship with Hasan Piker, the progressive streamer who has gone viral multiple times for previously claiming that the U.S. "deserved 9/11."
"Shut up, you FRAUD," the Libs of TikTok, a conservative X account that focuses on key social and cultural issues, said in a post Friday.
Steve Guest, a frequent political commentator and a former staffer for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, echoed the criticism in a post of his own, posting a picture of Piker and El-Sayed standing together.
"This you?" Guest wrote.
He also included a caption on the photo with another one of Piker’s quotes.
"‘I hate America… at least I say it with my f---ing chest,’" the picture’s caption read.
"Campaigning with a guy who said we deserved 9/11… his brazen dishonesty makes him all the bigger piece of s---," GOP consultant Ryan Girdusky posted on X.

"You’re a disgrace. You remain unwilling to disavow your chief spokesman who said "America deserved 9/11," National Republican Senatorial Committee communications director Joanna Rodriguez posted on X.
"You belittled the American lives lost year after year while giving excuses and showing sympathy for terrorists."
"Good job reading from that script buddy," GOP digital strategist Mike Hahn wrote on X.
Joey Mannarino, the co-founder of the Overton Institute, a right-wing media group, expressed surprise that El-Sayed had gained any kind of momentum in his campaign for Senate.
EL-SAYED TORCHED ONLINE AFTER BRUSHING OFF QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER CAMPAIGN TIES: ‘WHAT A PAL’
Hasan Piker during an interview at a New Jersey protest. (Michael Dorgan)

"How in God’s name is Abdul El-Sayed even close to winning this race? The man campaigns with people who say America deserved 9/11. He is a radical Islamist extremist if I’ve ever seen one. And this is who Michigan wants to put in the Senate?" Mannarino wrote.
In the past, El-Sayed has made statements noting he doesn’t share all of Piker's views.
"But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokesperson," El-Sayed said after Piker called Israel a "Jewish ISIS."

"And while politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools and healthcare. Because that’s what Michiganders keep asking about."

Chuck Ross, an investigative reporter with The Washington Free Beacon, noted that El-Sayed’s post didn’t focus on the wars that followed 9/11, a topic El-Sayed has frequently invoked when speaking about the terror attack.

"El-Sayed, reading off a teleprompter, gives a statement about 9/11. This time he sticks to just 9/11 and not the ‘War on Terror’ aftermath that he usually mentions in his 9/11 anniversary posts," Ross wrote.
In the past, El-Sayed has held up the war on terror as an example of military aggression, using it as Israel prepared to strike Gaza back in October 2023.
ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK

Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks during a primary election night event Aug. 5, 2026, at the Majestic Theatre in Detroit. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

"The President’s visit to Israel as it plans a major escalation & invasion of Gaza is already being held up as an endorsement of the violence being unleashed on innocent Palestinians. I can’t help but hear echoes of 9/11. When do we learn that more violence doesn’t fix violence?" El-Sayed wrote.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment on why he had not made more efforts to disavow Piker.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Pence group knocks Vance plan to pay stay-at-home parents up to $9K per child
summary: Advancing American Freedom warns JD Vance's childcare subsidy for stay-at-home parents could invite government intrusion and create work disincentives.
story: Advancing American Freedom praised the Trump administration's focus on supporting families but warned that Vice President JD Vance's draft plan to subsidize stay-at-home parents relies on flawed implementation mechanics that punish career growth.

A proposal backed by Vice President JD Vance to subsidize stay-at-home parents with up to $9,000 per child annually would invite government intrusion and undermine the initiative's original purpose of encouraging work and independence, according to a group founded by former Vice President Mike Pence.

In a one-page document, Advancing American Freedom (AAF) urged conservatives to oppose the plan, which it said would "expose the sanctity of the family to government intrusion, punish work, and create new avenues for fraud."
Vance is pushing for the expansion of the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), which was created during the Clinton administration to help low-income and working-class families pay for childcare.
The program provides about $9,000 per child annually, with funds typically paid directly to childcare providers.

FILE - Vice President JD Vance and second lady Usha Vance with their children, including newborn baby Alec. Vance has backed the proposal, which would subsidize stay-at-home parents. (Second Lady Usha Vance @SLOTUS on X)
CONSERVATIVES CAN FIGHT THE RISE OF SOCIALISM BY DEFENDING THE AMERICAN FAMILY

Under Vance's draft plan, families with a stay-at-home parent earning below state income limits could receive up to $9,000 per child annually. To qualify, a married couple must feature one spouse who stays at home while the other works at least 35 hours a week.
Unmarried couples and non-working single parents would not be eligible.
"Parenting is the most difficult job in the world. Vice President Vance is right to focus on the family," AAF President Tim Chapman told Fox News Digital.

"Unfortunately, as sympathetic groups around the movement have noted, this particular proposal would do more harm than good, opening up the family to government audits, benefit cliffs, dependency and new disincentives to work."
AAF looks forward to the continued debate about family policy and the future of the conservative movement, Chapman added.
EXCLUSIVE: VIDEO SHOWS MICHIGAN LAWMAKER TOURING DAYCARE IN $1.1M TAXPAYER FUNDING PROBE
Vice President JD Vance is pushing a plan to allow a stay-at-home spouse to collect as much as $9,000 per child each year. (iStock)

Roughly 870,000 families — 80% of whom are single parents, predominantly mothers — receive up to $9,000 a year per child, the AAF said. Expanding eligibility to stay-at-home parents, the group warned, could create more competition for already limited resources. The CCDF is already stretched thin, with nearly one-third of states having waitlists, according to AAF.
Vance's plan would require an auditable "childcare service," the group said, and could open the door to fraud if not properly monitored.

"We generally like these kinds of different creative proposals. There's no job that's more difficult than raising kids," John Shelton, the vice president of policy at AAF, told Fox News Digital. "And, so, that's a laudable thing, but the devil's in the details.

"What should be this opportunity for celebration and excitement could actually end up being this huge setback where you get a $1,000, $5,000 bonus, and suddenly you lose out on access to north of $10,000 depending on how many kids you have," he added.
"That's a disincentive to work to kind of grow and get promoted. That is not the kind of conservative ideal for how these programs should work."

The offices Advancing American Freedom, the policy and advocacy organization founded by former Vice President Mike Pence, in Washington, D.C., March 18, 2026. The group opposes the vice president's draft plan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
NEWT GINGRICH: WANT TO REFORM MEDICAID? ACCOUNTABILITY IS THE WAY FORWARD
Furthermore, stay-at-home spouses would be penalized for taking on remote, part-time or gig work, and families could take a financial hit for receiving a raise or promotion at work.
"Welfare’s goal is to get people into work and off of welfare," the AAF said. "This proposal would do the opposite."
PHYLLIS SCHLAFLY WAS RIGHT: AMERICA MUST PUT BABIES AND MOTHERS FIRST
Supporters argue stay-at-home parents should receive financial support on par with families that use subsidized childcare services.

"Parents who hand their kids to commercial day care get subsidy payments, while parents who bear the toil, expense, and opportunity cost of raising their kids at home currently get ZERO," Roger Severino, vice president of the Heritage Foundation, wrote on X. "It’s illogical and unjust and this proposal would level the playing field."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Shelton praised the Trump administration’s intent but argued the policy's execution falls short.
"I give the administration [an] A for effort, but a C or a D for implementation of what we've seen so far," he said.
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Vance's office for comment.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Clinton, Bush received multiple warnings on bin Laden hijack plots before 9/11, declassified files show
summary: Bill Clinton and George W. Bush received repeated CIA warnings that Usama bin Laden's network planned to hijack jets and attack U.S. cities.
story: Javed Ali, a former US counterterrorism official who served at DHS and with the FBI, says America is safer from a 9/11-style attack, but today’s threats are harder to detect.

Former presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush were given multiple warnings that 9/11 organizer Usama bin Laden and his terror network were planning to hijack large commercial jets in an effort to attack the United States, according to a batch of files released by the Trump administration Friday.

The reports, contained in previously classified documents from presidential daily briefs (PDBs) and high-level CIA intelligence memorandums, noted that operatives had already evaded security checks during a trial run at an unidentified New York airport three years before members of al Qaeda took down the World Trade Center.
The plotters aimed to leverage hijacked flights to demand the release of imprisoned extremists, including Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman and Ramzi Yousef.
USS COLE COMMANDER RECALLS CHILLING 9/11 WARNING AT CIA JUST 20 MINUTES BEFORE FIRST PLANE HIT

Former President Bill Clinton greets former presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama during a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks at the National 9/11 Memorial & Museum in New York City on Sept. 11, 2026. Newly declassified files reveal that intelligence warnings about a potential terror attack spanned across presidential administrations. (Getty Images)

"Some members of the bin Ladin network have received hijack training, according to various sources, but no group directly tied to bin Ladin's al-Qa'ida organization has ever carried out an aircraft hijacking," a Dec. 4, 1998 presidential daily briefing states. "Bin Ladin could be weighing other types of operations against US aircraft."

Months before the December 1998 briefing, a Sept. 10, 1998, PDB memorandum noted that bin Laden’s preferred option was to strike on U.S. soil in Washington, D.C. That report warned that the terror network responsible for the East Africa embassy bombings could possibly fly a plane packed with explosives into an American city.
AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11; THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

Throughout 1998, U.S. intelligence agencies tracked bin Laden's movements and support system, while identifying associates and sympathizers operating across several states, including New York, California, Texas, Michigan and Florida, the documents state.

The warnings spanned two presidential administrations. An Aug. 6, 2001, PDB delivered to Bush informed him that the FBI uncovered patterns of suspicious activity inside the U.S. consistent with preparations for hijackings or other attacks, as well as recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York.
KASH PATEL REVEALS THE CHILLING HOLIDAY TERROR PLOTS FBI FEDERAL AGENTS QUIETLY STOPPED

"Al-Qa’ida members — including some who are US citizens — have resided in or traveled to the US for years, and the group apparently maintains a support structure that could aid attacks," that document states.
"After US missile strikes on his base in Afghanistan in 1998, bin Laden told followers he wanted to retaliate in Washington."
AT GROUND ZERO, 9/11 FAMILIES TURN TO TRUMP AS OBAMA’S OLD DECISION RESURFACES

Flowers and American flags rest beside inscribed names at a reflecting pool at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum Sept. 11, 2026, in New York City as the nation commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. (Jeenah Moon/Pool/Getty Images)
Weeks before the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, a daily brief for Bush said the FBI was conducting around 70 field investigations throughout the U.S. that it believed were related to bin Laden.
The documents were released as part of a broader push by the Trump administration to shed light on what intelligence agencies knew before the attacks.

"Today I authorized the release of 71 Presidential Daily Briefs to honor the lives of those killed on 9/11, along with CIA officers who subsequently gave their lives to the fight," CIA Director John Ratcliffe said in a statement posted on X.

Matt Dunleavy and his daughter Ellie Dunleavy attend to the reflecting pools at the 9/11 Memorial for the ceremony to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11th terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center at the National 9/11 Memorial & Museum Sept. 11, 2026, in New York City.  (Jeenah Moon/Pool/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In his second administration, Trump has also released classified files on the assassinations of President John F. Kennedy, his brother Robert F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: First use of Alien Terrorist Removal Court sends Afghan woman back after Election Day ISIS plot: DOJ
summary: Nazira Haji Zada admitted she was an "alien terrorist" in the first-ever use of a specialized federal court created 30 years ago by Congress after an ISIS Election Day plot.
story: U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche discusses the Justice Department's Alien Terrorist Removal Court and how he is working to prevent tragedies like 9/11 on 'America Reports.'

An Afghan woman accused of supporting an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day 2024 has been deported to her home country in the first successful use of a specialized federal court established by Congress — the U.S. Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC) — 30 years ago to determine whether a non-citizen is an "alien terrorist."
Nazira Haji Zada, 47, was sent back to Afghanistan after recently admitting to the ATRC that she was an "alien terrorist" and waving an appeal, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ).

"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

"Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the [DOJ] will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."
TRUMP TURNS TO 'ZOMBIE' COURT AFTER BOASBERG POINTED TO IT IN DEPORTATION FIGHT
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche calls the successful use of the U.S. Alien Terrorist Removal Court to remove an "alien terrorist" a landmark case. (Getty Images, File)

Zada’s son and son-in-law, Abdullah Haji Zada and Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, were previously convicted for their part in the alleged plot. The men were arrested in October 2024 after allegedly buying guns and ammunition from an undercover FBI agent.

They later admitted to buying AK-47 rifles to carry out a mass shooting on behalf of the Islamic State. Zada's son was sentenced to 15 years in prison, and Tawhedi is awaiting sentencing, according to the DOJ.
Zada, who had been living as a permanent resident in Fort Worth, Texas, is not allowed back in the U.S. again. The court had issued an order of removal for Zada on Aug. 20.
EXCLUSIVE: 25 YEARS AFTER 9/11, ICE SAYS MORE THAN 2K KNOWN OR SUSPECTED TERRORISTS HAVE BEEN DEPORTED

The Department of Justice used a specialized federal court approved by Congress 30 years ago to deport an Afghan national who admitted to being an "alien terrorist." (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo, File)
FBI Director Kash Patel called Zada’s deportation a "historic and vitally important step in our work to protect the U.S. homeland from terrorism."

He added, "An individual who supported a plot by ISIS-sympathizing family members to commit an attack in America has paid the price for that. She came to our country, betrayed it, and has now lost the right to live here and enjoy our democratic freedoms. This FBI and our Justice Department partners will protect the American people from the threat of terrorism, using all means necessary."
The family allegedly began selling their possessions to raise money for the attack, and the family bought one-way tickets to Kabul, except for her son and Tawhedi.
FBI ARRESTS 3 MEN WHO ALLEGEDLY PLEDGED ALLEGIANCE TO ISIS, FUNDED DRONE ATTACKS TARGETING US TROOPS OVERSEAS
FBI Director Kash Patel called Zada’s deportation a "historic and vitally important step in our work to protect the U.S. homeland from terrorism." (Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)
Haji Zada’s attorneys said her decision to consent to removal "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy."

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process," defense lawyers said in a statement Friday.
"We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue."
The court’s authority was given by Congress in 1996, but Zada’s deportation is the first time it's been used.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Open sore’: Families face agonizing wait as 9/11 mastermind's trial pushed nearly 27 years after attacks
summary: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed's 9/11 trial is set for 2028, but a ruling barring key FBI statements raises doubts families will ever see a verdict.
story: Families of those killed in the Sept. 11 attacks reflect on a case still unresolved 25 years later, as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three co-defendants await a 2028 trial.

Twenty-five years after nearly 3,000 people were killed on Sept. 11, families waiting to see the accused plotters brought to justice are confronting another extraordinary possibility: They may still never see a verdict.

A military judge has scheduled alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three co-defendants to go on trial June 5, 2028, nearly 27 years after the attacks. But the date remains tentative, and a recent ruling barring prosecutors from using statements Mohammed made to FBI agents has underscored the legal obstacles still threatening the case.

"It’s like an open sore, and that sore gets even more hurtful when we get to anniversaries," John Ryan, former chief of department with the Port Authority Police who spent nine months working on the recovery operation at Ground Zero, told Fox News Digital.
JUDGE THROWS OUT KHALID SHEIKH MOHAMMED'S 9/11 CONFESSION IN ALREADY LONG WAIT FOR TRIAL

Ryan is among the victims’ families and first responders who have watched the prosecution drag through years of litigation over evidence obtained after the defendants were subjected to torture in CIA custody, a collapsed plea agreement, repeated changes in military judges and a mountain of unresolved pretrial motions.

"It’s like an open sore, and that sore gets even more hurtful when we get to anniversaries," John Ryan, former chief of department with the Port Authority Police who spent nine months working on the recovery operation at Ground Zero, told Fox News Digital. (Fox News Digital)

"Here we are 25 years later, and I’m still involved in this aspect of that here because we still have not convicted or taken to justice the five people that are being held at Guantánamo Bay," Ryan, who later became a commander with the FBI-led Joint Terrorism Task Force, said. "The planners, KSM and the others that are in custody, are awaiting trial."

Mohammed and three other defendants have been held by the U.S. for years without facing trial for their alleged roles in the plot that killed nearly 3,000 people. A fifth defendant, Ramzi bin al-Shibh, is being handled separately after being found mentally incompetent to stand trial.
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, has been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2003. (AP)

A military judge recently barred prosecutors from using statements Mohammed made to FBI agents in 2007, finding that the statements were tainted by the coercive treatment he had experienced in U.S. custody. The government chose not to appeal the ruling, saying an appeal could jeopardize the June 5, 2028, trial date.

The judge set the trial 18 months after the prosecution’s proposed January 2027 start to give the defense and government time to work through a long list of unresolved legal disputes. He is the fifth military judge to oversee the case since the defendants were arraigned in 2012.
For families who lost loved ones on Sept. 11, the years of delay have become another part of the trauma.
I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11; PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES
Sean Passananti, whose father was killed on the 100th floor of the North Tower, said the passage of time has made the case feel increasingly detached from the scale of the crime.

"It feels really like a twilight zone and unbelievable that we have to fight for justice for the worst terrorist attack that ever happened on our soil," Passananti said. "It doesn’t feel real. It’s unexplainable."
SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’
Passananti said he has attended the memorial ceremony every year but one since the attacks.
"I wish I wasn’t here, obviously, but I feel like I have to be here every year," he said.
Sean Passananti, whose father was killed on the 100th floor of the North Tower, said the passage of time has made the case feel increasingly detached from the scale of the crime. (Fox News Digital)
Dennis McGinley, whose older brother Danny worked on the 89th floor of the South Tower, said the delays have kept his family from closing a painful chapter.

"President Trump has a unique, historic opportunity here to be a hero, be our champion, finally close the books on this American nightmare, which is now becoming an American embarrassment," McGinley said.
McGinley described the families’ grief as an injury that keeps reopening.
"It is like the wound never healed, and every year we get salt poured back into that wound," he said.

Ryan said he lost 37 police officers he had worked with during his career, along with civilian colleagues at the Port Authority. After the recovery operation, he moved into counterterrorism work. He said he expected the 9/11 case to remain part of his professional life, but not for this long.
"The fact is that they’ve all admitted their involvement. It’s not a question of guilt. It’s just a question of the process and the fact that the process has taken 25 years," Ryan said.
The case has been moving through the military commissions since the defendants were arraigned in 2012. By then, Mohammed had already spent nearly a decade in U.S. custody.
He was captured in Pakistan in 2003 and held for years at CIA "black sites," where he was subjected to harsh interrogation techniques, including repeated waterboarding.
Mohammed and the other defendants were transferred to Guantánamo in 2006.
The treatment of the defendants in CIA custody has become one of the central obstacles in the prosecution.

Defense attorneys have argued that statements obtained after the defendants were tortured cannot be considered voluntary. Prosecutors have argued that later statements made to FBI agents by a "clean team" should be admissible.

The recent ruling excluding Mohammed’s 2007 FBI statements dealt another blow to that effort and highlighted a problem that has followed the case for years: whether prosecutors can separate evidence gathered later from the coercive interrogations that came before it.
The case has also been disrupted by changes in judges, the coronavirus pandemic and a failed plea agreement.

In 2024, the defendants reached plea agreements that would have required them to plead guilty in exchange for life sentences rather than face the death penalty. Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin withdrew the agreements, prompting another round of litigation. A federal appeals court later blocked the defendants from entering guilty pleas under the withdrawn deals.
Years earlier, the Obama administration had tried another route.

In 2009, the administration announced that Mohammed and four other defendants would be prosecuted in federal court in Manhattan. That plan was abandoned after fierce opposition from New York officials and lawmakers who raised security and logistical concerns.
The case was moved back to the military commissions at Guantánamo, where it has remained.
The delays have left the accused plotters aging at a detention complex that has cost taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars while producing no verdict in the 9/11 case.
Dennis McGinley, whose older brother Danny worked on the 89th floor of the South Tower, said the delays have kept his family from closing a painful chapter. (Fox News Digital)

The criminal prosecution is separate from the civil lawsuit that 9/11 families have brought against Saudi Arabia, although the two proceedings intersect in the families’ broader search for a full accounting of the attacks.

The military commission is focused on whether Mohammed and the other defendants planned and carried out the terrorist operation. The civil case examines whether Saudi government employees or agents helped two hijackers establish themselves in the United States.

A trial in the civil case could force testimony and the release of evidence that families believe may clarify how the plot was supported before the attacks. The Saudi-related allegations, however, are not the charges at issue in the Guantánamo prosecution.

Ryan said the passage of time means the case now spans two generations of victims’ families: people who were children when the attacks happened and are now adults and older parents and grandparents who fear they may never live to see a verdict.
If the current schedule holds, the proceedings would begin June 5, 2028, almost 27 years after the attacks and 16 years after the defendants were arraigned.

"Our justice system isn’t designed to work that late," Ryan said. "It’s designed to produce justice in a fair time. And the emphasis needs to be on the victims as opposed to the five enemy combatants."

title: Inside Trump’s intimate meeting with nation’s bravest soldiers during whirlwind Texas trip
summary: Trump toured the new National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, then signed legislation for a new monument near the Lincoln Memorial.
story: U.S. Army Lt. Col. William Swenson said the upcoming Medal of Honor monument will be a 'symbol to the future to inspire Americans' and praised President Donald Trump's visit to the new National Medal of Honor Museum.

ARLINGTON, Texas — During his whirlwind trip to Texas to rally Republican voters ahead of November’s elections, President Donald Trump on Thursday made a pit stop to honor America’s bravest warriors the day before the anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
The intimate gathering was held at the National Medal of Honor Museum, where Trump also met privately with the Medal of Honor recipients who were present.

Trump also signed legislation clearing the way for a new monument honoring the award's recipients on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., before addressing roughly 100 guests, including 16 of the nation’s 65 living Medal of Honor recipients.
REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG

President Donald Trump signs the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act during an event at the National Medal of Honor Museum Sept. 10, 2026, in Arlington, Texas.  (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"It’s very special for all of us," Trump said. "It's special for me to be here, and it's an American treasure devoted to the best and bravest warriors of our country. And, frankly, it's really the best they've ever produced."
The event was a stark contrast to the tens of thousands to whom Trump had addressed about 13 hours prior at the GOP midterm convention, a half hour away in Dallas.
DAVID MARCUS: IN DALLAS, GOP SEEKS UNITY ON 9/11, KIRK ANNIVERSARIES

Charlotte Jones, daughter of Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, is the chairman of the museum’s board of directors and served as the event’s emcee. Her father beamed with pride as he sat front and center, which Trump noted from the stage.
High-ranking Republican politicians, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, were among the high-profile guests who huddled in the room for the event.
Both Jones and Troy Bertram, the CEO of the new center, stressed that the National Medal of Honor Museum (NMOH) is not just a war museum.
"We are not a military history museum," Bertram told Fox News Digital. "We are storytelling around the humans, about their courage, their sacrifice. Who they were before what they became."
Trump’s speech struck a tone of admiration for the men and women honored by the museum.
MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH'
A band performs outside the National Medal of Honor Museum. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

"They stormed into hellfire and crushed America's enemies," the president said. "They had bravery like few people could even think of having. They carried the wounded out of battle and on their own backs and carried them back and forth. … They stood in the way of bullets, purposely just standing just like this and taking bullets, and it's amazing."
One of those warriors was Army Lt. Col. William Swenson, a man of steely resolve who serves on the museum’s board.
DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL

His heroic 2009 actions in Afghanistan, where he fought during Operation Enduring Freedom, earned him the highest military decoration awarded by the U.S. government in 2013, presented by then-President Barack Obama.

Pinned down by the enemy during a seven-hour battle in the Ganjgal Valley of the country’s Kunar Province, Swenson saved lives by making multiple trips into active combat zones, pulling wounded soldiers to safety and loading them onto helicopters for evacuation.

"The president and our commander-in-chief has been a strong supporter of this project," Swenson told Fox News Digital. "He continues to be a strong supporter of this project, and having him as involved as he is going to be a great contribution to get the monument done to standard, on time and to start signaling the messaging to the American people what’s important about service."

The 47th president is working with private donors to build the new monument in Washington, D.C., near the Lincoln Memorial, in honor of recipients of the nation’s highest military award for heroism in battle. He previously signed the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act, officially clearing the path for its construction.

President Donald Trump holds up the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act after signing it during an event at the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, Sept. 10, 2026.  (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
WWII VET GIVES DIRECT MESSAGE TO YOUNG PEOPLE TODAY: 'WE GAVE UP OUR YESTERDAYS FOR YOUR TOMORROWS'

"When he died, Woody was the last surviving recipient from World War II. [He] had one of the most dangerous jobs of war, and that’s operating a flamethrower," Trump said, speaking of the man for whom the bill was named.

"In the Battle of Iwo Jima, he carved a path to American victory — literally carved a path so soldiers could get in and win through a deadly gauntlet of enemy strongholds. And back and forth he went. He just kept going back and forth."

Williams was one of about 300 flamethrowers in Iwo Jima, a famed and defining battle in the war’s Pacific theater. The late soldier’s family members were in the audience and were fondly acknowledged by the president.

"America will never, ever forget what they did and what they risked and how much they risked [and] what they meant to their families and what they've meant to our country," Trump concluded. "I want to thank you all once again."
Swenson described the importance of remembrance.

"What we do to ensure that we have common history, common beliefs, is we have monuments, and we have museums. We have our mythology that tells us who we are as Americans and what we will continue to be in the future," he said. "Without this mythology, we don’t have that narrative.
President Donald Trump signs legislation for a Medal of Honor monument in Washington during a visit to the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)
The fact that the event was held the day before the 25th anniversary of 9/11 wasn’t lost on him, either.
He described the tragedy as a "seminal event" for him, which happened just as he was finishing college, that shaped his entire future. Swenson spent 22 years in the Army after the attack.

"The United States is forged in fire," he said. "We’ve had revolutions, we’ve had civil wars, we’ve had global conflicts, we’ve had civil strife. There will always be challenges to our freedom and to our country, and it’s up to us to move forward from those events and create that more perfect union.

"That said, we must always learn from these events to help better prevent them and also to honor the sacrifice of the service members who fought in these conflicts, and also understand how we as citizens can create a better country that does not have these problems — that does not have these challenges. It’s our responsibility to future generations to prevent that."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Thousands of hacked sites trick you into installing malware
summary: Over 5,400 legitimate websites now serve fake CAPTCHA scams that trick users into pasting malware commands into Windows Run via ClickFix attacks.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
You land on the real website of a local business and a CAPTCHA appears. It looks routine until the page tells you to open Windows Run and paste a command. That should stop you cold.
Security researchers say thousands of legitimate small-business websites have been compromised to spread this malware trap. Here's what to know before a familiar website catches you off guard.

FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC
A routine visit to a legitimate website can turn risky if a fake CAPTCHA tricks you into running commands on your computer. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
More than 5,400 websites have been compromised

This campaign is much bigger than a handful of infected pages. Netskope Threat Labs says it identified more than 5,400 compromised websites across more than 2,200 organizations worldwide over the past few months.
The sites have little in common beyond many belonging to small businesses. Researchers found clinics, plumbing companies, online stores and other businesses among the victims.
Where Netskope examined individual sites, they most often ran WordPress and sometimes PrestaShop. Researchers still do not know how attackers initially compromised them.
That is important because you could visit the legitimate website of a business you recognize and still encounter a malicious prompt.
Netskope says several hundred compromised sites can be active on a given day. It has recently seen more than 300 sites contacting the malicious infrastructure each weekday.
How the fake CAPTCHA malware trick works

The attack starts with malicious code hidden inside a compromised website. When you visit the site, that code can load another script. Then the page may blur and show what looks like an ordinary CAPTCHA.
Instead of simply asking you to prove you are human, the page tells you to open the Windows Run dialog and paste a command. That command can download and launch the attacker's malware.
Here is the warning sign I want you to remember: A legitimate CAPTCHA should never tell you to open Windows Run or paste a command into your computer.

We have seen fake CAPTCHA scams use this same trick before. The page looks familiar, so you may assume the instructions are part of a normal security check. They are not. The criminal is trying to get you to launch the attack yourself.
CLICKLOCK MAC MALWARE LOCKS APPS UNTIL YOU GIVE IN
Researchers found compromised websites using fake verification prompts that tell Windows users to open the Windows Run dialog and paste a command that can launch malware. (Netskope)
Why ClickFix can fool careful people
This technique is known as ClickFix. The clever part has less to do with some exotic computer hack and more to do with psychology.

You are already used to CAPTCHAs. Websites ask you to click a box or prove you are human all the time. So, when a convincing verification screen appears on a legitimate website, your guard may be down. Then the instructions make the dangerous action look like one more step in the verification process.

Cybercriminals have used similar ClickFix tricks with fake Windows update screens. The appearance changes, but the warning remains the same. A webpage should not be telling you to run computer commands.
Why hackers are hiding part of the attack on a blockchain
This is where the campaign gets more unusual. The attackers are using the BNB Smart Chain test network to store instructions used by the compromised websites.

You do not need to understand cryptocurrency to understand why criminals like this setup. Normally, attackers might keep malicious code on a regular web server. Once investigators find that server, a hosting provider may be able to shut it down.

A blockchain works differently. In this campaign, the attackers store code inside something called a smart contract. Think of it as a place where the hacked websites can check for their next set of instructions.
Netskope says the attackers are using the test version of BNB Smart Chain. Developers normally use this network to experiment without spending real cryptocurrency.
That gives the criminals inexpensive infrastructure that can also be harder to take down through traditional methods. There is another advantage.

The attacker can change what the smart contract delivers. The compromised websites can then pick up those new instructions without criminals having to modify every hacked site individually. That helps explain why this infrastructure is so useful to them.

Netskope researchers say attackers are also abusing WebRTC to create a direct connection from a victim’s browser to an attacker-controlled server and deliver additional malicious code. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The campaign is already changing tactics

Netskope also found a newer version of the attack that skips the fake CAPTCHA. This version uses technology called WebRTC. Your browser normally uses WebRTC for things such as video calls and real-time communications. The attackers found another use for it.

Their code can create an encrypted data connection with the attacker and receive additional malicious code through the browser. Netskope says the code can then run without first being saved as a traditional file on the computer.
For you, the technical details are less important than the larger point. The criminals can change how the attack works while continuing to use the same network of compromised websites.
6 ways to protect yourself from fake CAPTCHA malware
A few simple habits can help you avoid handing control of your computer to an attacker.
If a website tells you to open Windows Run, PowerShell or Command Prompt, stop. Do not paste anything it gives you. Close the page instead.

A normal CAPTCHA may ask you to click a checkbox or identify pictures. It should not require you to change settings or run commands on your PC. If the instructions suddenly leave the browser, close the page.

Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious scripts and malware if something slips past you. Keep it updated and enable real-time protection. If you accidentally follow suspicious instructions, run a full system scan. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Install security updates when they become available. However, update Windows through Windows Update. Update your browser through its built-in settings or official source. Do not trust an unexpected webpage that says you must download an update.

If you followed the instructions from a suspicious CAPTCHA, disconnect the computer from the internet. Run a full antivirus scan. Then use another trusted device to change passwords for sensitive accounts you accessed on that computer. Start with your main email account. Also review active login sessions and enable multifactor authentication wherever you can.

Website owners should take this campaign seriously too. Netskope recommends checking the integrity of your content management system files. Researchers found malicious code added to legitimate JavaScript files or hidden inside fake plugin directories. Keep WordPress, PrestaShop and any plugins you use updated. Remove plugins you no longer need. Keep in mind that Netskope has not identified how attackers initially broke into the websites in this campaign. Those steps are good security practices, but researchers have not tied a specific WordPress or PrestaShop vulnerability to these compromises.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets me about this attack is how ordinary everything can look at first. You could be visiting the real website of a neighborhood business you have used before. Then a familiar CAPTCHA appears. That sense of trust is exactly what can make the next instruction dangerous. The blockchain technology behind the campaign makes life harder for security teams trying to shut it down. For the rest of us, though, the best defense is refreshingly simple. A website should never need you to open Windows Run or paste a command to prove you are human. If you see that request, close the page. That one warning sign could save you from installing malware yourself.

Would you recognize a fake CAPTCHA if it appeared on the website of a business you already trusted, or would the familiar site make you more likely to follow the instructions? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI robot for seniors can alert family after a call for help
summary: Tuya Smart's Doova AI home robot rolls to seniors who call for help and connects family via live video, but key privacy questions remain unanswered.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have a parent or grandparent who wants to stay in their own home, you probably know the question that can sit quietly in the back of your mind: What happens if they fall and nobody realizes they need help? Tuya Smart thinks its small artificial intelligence robot could become part of the answer.

The company unveiled Doova at IFA 2026 in Berlin. This wheeled AI home companion is designed for seniors who live independently. It can move through the home, respond when someone calls for help and connect family members through live video when an emergency appears to be unfolding.

That gets my attention because Doova goes beyond sitting on a table waiting for someone to press a button or call out from across the room. It can actually come to you. And that raises a bigger question: How much could a robot like this really help someone live safely and independently at home?
THE BEST TIME TO TALK TO YOUR PARENTS ABOUT SENIOR CARE — BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE
NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Health Care With AI

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your healthcare. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed.
Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com
Doova is an AI home companion designed to help seniors with safety, daily routines and staying connected with family. (Tuya Smart)
How Doova responds when a senior calls for help
Doova uses LDS LiDAR to navigate around the home. A four-microphone system helps it figure out where a voice is coming from. Meanwhile, AI vision analyzes a person's skeletal posture.

If someone falls or needs assistance, that person can say, "Hey Tuya, help." Doova then locates the person and rolls over to assess what is happening. Tuya says that if the user does not respond within 60 seconds, Doova starts an emergency response workflow. Family members receive an alert with a two-way live video call so they can see what is happening and arrange assistance.

For now, Tuya has not said that Doova automatically detects falls without the user first calling for help or that it directly contacts 911 or a professional monitoring service. So, I would treat it as an added layer of support rather than a replacement for a dedicated medical alert system.
Doova wants to be an AI companion too

Emergency help is only part of what Tuya has built into Doova. The robot uses a multimodal large language model so people can talk with it in a more natural way instead of memorizing rigid voice commands.

For someone spending long stretches at home alone, Doova can carry on a conversation or play entertainment. It can also help make sense of a confusing bill or letter. Another feature caught my eye. Tuya says Doova can identify potential scam risks.
YOUR SENIOR PARENTS ARE EASIER TO IMPERSONATE THAN YOU ARE

That could be useful for older adults who receive a suspicious message and want a second opinion before responding. However, I would never want someone relying solely on an AI robot to decide whether a bill, email or financial request is legitimate.

AI can make mistakes. If Doova flags something suspicious, the safest next move would still be to verify it independently or share it with someone you trust. We've seen how much personal information scammers can gather about older adults, particularly after major life changes such as moving into a retirement community.
A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME
Attendees watch Doova in action at IFA 2026, where Tuya showed how the robot can move through the home and respond when someone needs help. (Tuya Smart)
It can help with everyday routines around the home

Doova can remind you to take medication, keep track of your schedule and give you weather updates. Tuya says it can also learn your preferences over time, which could make its suggestions feel more useful day to day.

The company plans to add a feature that helps find misplaced items around the house. If that works well, I can see the appeal. Plenty of us have spent far too long looking for glasses, keys or a remote that was nearby the whole time.
WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY?
Doova can patrol your home while you are away

Doova also doubles as a mobile home-monitoring device. Rather than continuously hugging the walls as some patrol robots do, Tuya says Doova travels to selected locations near the center of rooms. From there, it can perform a 360-degree scan.
The robot then creates a safety report that can be sent to the user's phone. When the battery runs low, Doova can return to its charging dock on its own.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
That gives the robot another possible use when someone travels or spends part of the day away from home. However, this capability also leads straight into the biggest question I have about Doova.
What about privacy with Doova?

Doova has microphones, AI vision and live video inside the home. It can also learn a user's preferences over time. That can make the robot more helpful, but it also means giving it access to a lot of personal information.

We raised similar questions when we looked at another AI home robot that can recognize family members and build personalized memories. With Doova, I would want to know where video and audio are processed, what gets stored, who can see it and whether users can permanently delete what the robot has learned.

Tuya's launch announcement does not spell out those Doova-specific privacy controls. Until it does, that is something I would look closely at before bringing a camera-equipped AI robot into a loved one's home. You can also review our guide to limiting the information popular AI services collect about you.
Tuya showcased its connected-home technology at IFA 2026 in Berlin, including Doova, as part of its growing AI-powered smart home ecosystem. (Tuya Smart)
Doova can control your smart home

Tuya also designed Doova to work as a central smart home controller. A senior could use voice commands to adjust connected lights or curtains. Doova can also interact with compatible kitchen and bathroom devices.

I like the thinking here. Smart homes can become complicated very quickly, especially when every device has its own app. If Doova can put those controls into a simple conversation, that could make smart home technology far easier to use.
The robot has a 10.1-inch HD display with animated facial expressions. Its rounded design also looks more like a friendly household companion than an industrial machine.
What we still do not know about Doova

There are still some important blanks to fill in. Tuya has not announced a retail price or when consumers will actually be able to buy Doova. I also want to see how it handles a real home. Rugs, cords and tight spaces can trip up mobile robots. Stairs are another obvious challenge for something that moves around on wheels.

The bigger question is how dependable Doova would be during an actual emergency. Someone may be frightened, speaking softly or lying somewhere the robot cannot easily reach. That is where real world testing will tell us much more than a demonstration on the show floor.
We reached out to Tuya Smart with questions about Doova's emergency response, privacy protections, connectivity and availability but did not hear back before our deadline.
What this means to you

If you are helping a parent or loved one age in place, Doova gives us a pretty good look at where home technology is heading. Instead of relying only on stationary smart speakers or cameras, future AI assistants may move around the house and respond to what is happening nearby.

That could give families another way to stay connected while allowing older adults to maintain more independence. However, I would look closely at the emergency process before relying on any product like this. Find out who gets contacted and what happens when the internet fails. You should also understand exactly what the cameras and microphones collect.
Finally, think about the person who will actually use it. The best technology in the world offers little value if someone finds it confusing, intrusive or uncomfortable.
Kurt's key takeaways

What interests me most about Doova is the move from passive smart devices toward AI that can physically come to you. For an older adult who wants to remain independent, having a robot respond to a call for help and bring family into the situation quickly could offer real peace of mind.

Still, I would want much more information before trusting Doova with someone I love. Safety technology has to prove itself outside the controlled environment of a trade show. I want to know how reliably it reaches someone during an emergency and how much personal information it collects along the way.

The privacy side deserves just as much attention. A moving camera and microphone that learns your routines can become incredibly helpful. It can also become one of the most intimate connected devices in your home. Doova has an interesting idea at its core. Now Tuya needs to show the technology can earn the level of trust its role requires.

Would you put an AI robot with cameras and microphones in an aging parent's home if it could help family respond faster during an emergency, or would that feel like too much surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Man films himself taking down Flock cameras, gets arrested
summary: Jevon Martinez livestreamed himself removing 10 Flock Safety cameras in Bernalillo County, but authorities say eight belonged to neighborhood associations.
story: Flock Safety founder and CEO Garrett Langley joins host Kayleigh McEnany on 'Saturday in America' to address the growing backlash against AI license plate reader cameras. While critics like Senator Bernie Sanders raise mass surveillance and privacy concerns, Langley defends the technology by highlighting its role in solving over one million crimes and locating 10,000 missing persons across America.
You might expect someone taking down surveillance cameras to avoid being filmed. Jevon Martinez did the opposite.

The 44-year-old Rio Rancho, New Mexico, man recorded himself removing Flock Safety camera equipment around Bernalillo County on Sept. 2. He loaded the equipment into his pickup truck while explaining his reasoning to people watching online. The timing gave Martinez his opening.

Days earlier, Bernalillo County Sheriff John Allen had moved to end the department's three contracts with Flock Safety. Allen cited concerns about privacy, data sharing and his confidence in the company. However, he still supports automated license plate reader technology and plans to look at other vendors.

Martinez apparently saw the remaining cameras as unfinished business. What happened next shows how quickly a fight over surveillance can turn into a criminal case once someone starts removing hardware they do not own.
