title: Man accused in brutal motel stabbing sought as person of interest in 4 deaths, child attack
summary: Kaegan Jude Solet is sought as a person of interest after four people were found stabbed to death and a child critically wounded in Houma, Louisiana.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Louisiana man previously accused of repeatedly stabbing a woman and locking her inside a motel room is now being sought by law enforcement after four people were found stabbed to death and a child was critically wounded.

Terrebonne Parish Sheriff Tim Soignet said detectives identified 47-year-old Houma resident Kaegan Jude Solet as a person of interest in the apparent series of stabbing incidents in the Ashland Drive area of Houma.
Deputies were initially called to the 200 block of Ashland Drive, where they discovered the wounded child, according to the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office.
NORTH CAROLINA MAN BROKE INTO EX'S HOME, FATALLY STABBED HIS 5-YEAR-OLD SON BEFORE GOING TO TACO BELL: POLICE

The Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office identified Kaegan Jude Solet as a person of interest. Anyone with information about his whereabouts is urged to contact detectives. (Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's Office)

The child was flown to an out-of-area hospital and remained in critical but stable condition after suffering "extremely significant" injuries, Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office Lt. Blake Tabor told Fox News Digital.
"That’s not something that you want to see ever," Tabor said.
TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING'
Deputies found four people dead inside homes near Ashland Drive after responding to a critically wounded child, authorities said. (Google Maps)
As deputies searched the surrounding area, they made a grim discovery inside nearby homes.

At least four victims were found dead, according to the sheriff’s office. Authorities have not released their identities or disclosed what relationship, if any, they had to one another, the injured child or Solet.
SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER MOM, PREGNANT TEEN, 12-YEAR-OLD FOUND BOUND AND MURDERED
Investigators also have not said what may have sparked the violence or whether the victims were attacked inside more than one home.
Solet has not been arrested or charged in the latest deaths. The sheriff’s office stressed that identifying him as a person of interest does not mean he has been accused of a crime.
DEPUTY US MARSHAL FATALLY SHOT WHILE SERVING ARREST WARRANT IN LOUISIANA
Authorities believe Solet is likely still in the area but said they are not ruling out other possibilities.
"We’re using every investigative tool that we have," Tabor said. "Our hope is that we plan to get him in custody very quickly."
Tabor said investigators do not have information indicating Solet intends to leave the state or "go on the run" but added that authorities are "exploring all options."
Solet had not been located as of the latest update.
REPEAT OFFENDER RELEASED EARLY FROM JAIL NOW CHARGED WITH CAPITAL MURDER OF PREGNANT WOMAN
Authorities are searching for Kaegan Jude Solet, 47, after identifying him as a person of interest in a series of deadly stabbing incidents. (Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's Office)
The latest investigation is not the first time Solet’s name has surfaced in violent crime allegations.
Solet was arrested in December 2019 after allegedly stabbing a woman repeatedly and leaving her locked inside a Houma motel room, according to a police news release from the time.
Houma police responded to the Red Carpet Inn shortly after midnight on Christmas Eve 2019 and found a 59-year-old woman lying on the floor of her room with numerous stab wounds.
The Red Carpet Inn in Houma, La., where Kaegan Solet allegedly stabbed a woman in 2019. (Google Maps)
The woman was taken by ambulance to a medical facility with injuries considered life-threatening, police said.
Witnesses told investigators they heard someone yelling for help from inside the room. When they entered, they found the woman on the floor and unable to move.
Investigators identified Solet, then 40, as the suspect and said he had been invited into the woman’s room before the two became involved in an argument.

Police alleged the confrontation turned physical, and Solet repeatedly stabbed the woman in her head and upper body. He then allegedly fled and locked the motel room door behind him, leaving the critically wounded woman inside.
MANIAC WHO STABBED BOY OUTSIDE WALMART WAS PREVIOUSLY FREED AFTER ATTACKING DAD, CHURCH RAMPAGE: REPORT
Kaegan Jude Solet had not been arrested or charged in the latest deaths as authorities continued searching for him. (Houma Police Department)
Officers located Solet approximately 18 hours later and took him into custody without incident.
He was transported to the Terrebonne Parish Criminal Justice Complex and booked on one count of attempted second-degree murder, according to Houma police.
Terrebonne Parish detectives had also obtained a warrant for Solet’s arrest on a charge of second-degree murder in January 2019, according to a separate sheriff’s office news release.

The warrant was obtained during the investigation into the Jan. 9, 2019, killing of Kemple Paul Scott Lovell. Then-Sheriff Jerry Larpenter said detectives were searching for Solet, who had last been seen in the Houma area.
The final dispositions of both 2019 cases were not immediately available.
ILLINOIS NO-CASH BAIL LAW 'UTTERLY MANIPULATED' BY VIOLENT OFFENDERS, DEM ALDERMAN SAYS AFTER COP'S KILLING
Asked why Solet was no longer in custody, Tabor said authorities were also searching for answers.
"I can’t tell you. Certainly, that’s the hot question, right? Why is he out?" Tabor said. "We’re probably just as stunned as everyone else is."

Tabor emphasized that the sheriff’s office has a strong working relationship with the Terrebonne Parish District Attorney’s Office but said questions remain about how Solet’s previous cases were handled.
"How this slipped through, I certainly don’t know, but it’s a question that probably needs to be answered," Tabor said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the district attorney’s office seeking the circumstances surrounding Solet’s release and whether he remained under any court-ordered supervision but did not immediately receive a response.
Detectives are continuing to gather evidence and develop information surrounding the latest deadly incidents as the search for Solet continues.

The sheriff’s office urged anyone with information about his whereabouts to contact Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office detectives at 985-876-2500.
The investigation remains active and in its preliminary stages. Authorities said additional details will be released as they become available.

title: Florida woman accused of setting stranger on fire at gas station, leaving horrific burns
summary: Video captured Eleanor Crawford allegedly igniting gasoline while a stranger pumped fuel at a St. Petersburg Mobil gas station, police said.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A Florida woman pumping gas was engulfed in a fireball after a stranger allegedly walked up and deliberately ignited the fuel with a lighter in a seemingly random attack, police said.

The 41-year-old victim, identified in court records as Christine Sherbuk, was filling her Volvo SUV at a Mobil gas station in St. Petersburg on Thursday night when Eleanor Crawford approached her, according to police and an arrest affidavit.
Crawford, 41, allegedly lit the gasoline at about 8 p.m., setting the SUV ablaze and leaving Sherbuk with second-degree burns to her arms and back.
GEORGIA MOTHER FIGHTS OFF ALLEGED CHILD SNATCHER WITH GAS PUMP IN SURVEILLANCE VIDEO
Eleanor Crawford allegedly ignited gasoline while a woman fueled her SUV at a St. Petersburg Mobil station, leaving the victim seriously burned, police said. (St. Petersburg Police Department)
She was rushed to the trauma center at Tampa General Hospital in serious condition. Police said she was stabilized and is expected to survive.
Scotty Gramling told Fox 13 Tampa Bay he was parked nearby when the violence erupted and raced to help Sherbuk as flames swallowed her vehicle.
MAN ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY THROWING MOLOTOV COCKTAIL AT PERSON IN WHEELCHAIR NEAR OKC POLICE HEADQUARTERS
Police said a woman suffered second-degree burns after a stranger allegedly ignited gasoline as she fueled her SUV at this St. Petersburg Mobil station. (Fox 13 Tampa Bay)
Gramling helped the injured woman into his truck and called 911. He described what he witnessed as a "fireball."

Moments earlier, Gramling said, he had called the police non-emergency line after seeing Crawford involved in some kind of altercation across the street. It appeared someone was trying to pull her out of the roadway before a fight broke out, he told the outlet.
Officers were already heading to that disturbance when the gas station attack unfolded, according to the outlet.
Police caught Crawford a couple of blocks away within about 20 minutes. The arrest affidavit says multiple witnesses saw her ignite the gasoline and that the incident was captured on video.
SUSPECT NAMED IN NEW YORK CITY ALLEGED INCENDIARY DEVICE ATTACK, HAD 'ANTI-ICE STUFF' ON HIM
St. Petersburg police arrested Eleanor Crawford shortly after a woman was seriously burned in an alleged gas station arson attack. (St. Petersburg Police Department)
Crawford and Sherbuk did not know each other, investigators said. Authorities have not identified a motive.

"I don't know if alcohol and drugs were involved, but indicative of her history, there might've been something that diminished capacity there," Assistant Police Chief Mike Kovacsev told Fox 13. "Why would she even do something like this?"
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH ABUSING HER KIDS, SETTING FIRE IN HOUSE WHILE MAKING MENTAL HEALTH DEFENSE
Police said Crawford has an extensive record that includes several drug- and alcohol-related charges. Authorities have not said whether she was under the influence at the time of the alleged attack.

"It's kind of a unique case because you don't see anything like this, especially something that results in such horrific burns," Kovacsev said. "But they went out there, they worked with the fire department and, luckily, they were able to get her stabilized, and she's going to make it."
ARMY VETERAN FACES ARSON CHARGE AFTER ATTACK OUTSIDE NYC FEDERAL BUILDING: 'CAME ARMED WITH BAD INTENTIONS'
Police units respond to an emergency. (Getty Images)
Crawford was charged with attempted felony murder and two counts of arson. She is being held on $350,000 bond while awaiting trial.
A judge ordered her to be fitted with a GPS monitor by the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office before her release from jail, court records show.

title: Son of notorious Somali dictator reportedly living in Ohio, decades after brutal regime's collapse
summary: Ayanle Siad Barre, son of Somalia's former dictator, has been living in Ohio's large Somali community, prompting calls for a U.S. investigation.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The son of former Somali dictator Mohamed Siad Barre, whose brutal regime was accused of widespread atrocities during his more than two decades in power, has been living in Ohio for years, according to a new report.
Ayanle Siad Barre, 61, lives in the Columbus area, home to a large Somali community, the New York Post reported. The outlet also identified his sister, Deka Mohamed Siad, as living in Ohio.

Their father ruled Somalia from 1969, until his government was overthrown in 1991. His regime has been accused of mass killings that left as many as 200,000 people dead, torture and other human rights abuses, including atrocities against the Isaaq clan. Mohamed Siad Barre died in 1995.

Historian and Oxford University doctoral researcher Mohamed Haji Ingiriis described Ayanle as his father's "right-hand man" and alleged that he wielded significant power within the government, according to the Post. Fox News Digital has not independently verified those allegations.
TRUMP DOJ ESCALATES CITIZENSHIP CRACKDOWN ON GROUP ACCUSED OF HIDING TERROR TIES, VIOLENT CRIMES
Mohamed Siad Barre, president of Somalia, on Nov. 18, 1981 (UPI/Bettmann Archive/Getty Images, File)
Fox News Digital previously reported that another figure from the Barre era, former Somali military commander Yusuf Abdi Ali, had lived in the U.S. before being deported.

An immigration judge determined in 2024 that Ali personally engaged in torture while serving in the Somali National Army and ordered soldiers under his command to detain and torture civilians and assist in extrajudicial killings, according to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Ali, who had been living as a permanent resident in Virginia, was deported to Somalia in December 2024.
"The United States will not be a safe haven for those who commit human rights violations," ICE official Russell Hott said at the time.
EX-PHILIPPINE PRESIDENT DUTERTE TO FACE TRIAL ON CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY CHARGES
Somalia President Mohamad Siad Barre in 1981. (Kevin Fleming/Corbis via Getty Images, File)
The Post also reported that Ayanle established a translation services company called Somal Global Services.
His sister, Deka, and her late husband operated Vanguard Home Health Care, which received more than $1.8 million in Medicare funding, according to documents reviewed by the publication.
The Post reported that the company appeared to have operated legitimately and filed the appropriate paperwork.
Some survivors of the Barre regime are now calling for U.S. authorities to investigate members of the former dictator's family.
Human rights activist Suleiman Bolaleh called for an investigation to determine what Barre family members knew or did during the dictatorship, according to the Post.
DOJ CHARGES 19 DEFENDANTS IN ALLEGED $4M PHILADELPHIA MEDICARE AND MEDICAID FRAUD

Mohamed Siad Barre, left, president of the Somali Democratic Republic from 1969 to 1991, stands with military officers and senior regime officials in Mogadishu in 1969. (Pictures from History/Universal, File)
The calls for an investigation do not establish wrongdoing by Ayanle or other family members.
Fox News Digital reached out to Ayanle Siad Barre for comment, but attempts to reach him through publicly listed contact information were unsuccessful.

ICE, the Department of Justice and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Officers with the Green Bay Police Department responded to a disturbance at a food truck at about 2:15 a.m. local time Saturday and were attempting to take some people into custody when a car drove toward bystanders and officers, prompting one officer to open fire.
The suspect then fled, which led to a short police chase that ended when officers did a PIT maneuver, a tactical move used by police to stop drivers.

title: Ex-mayor found liable for alleged sexual assaults of 7 women, ordered to pay $13M
summary: Dominic Foppoli, former Windsor, California, mayor, faces a punitive damages phase after a jury awarded seven women $13 million in sexual assault case.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
The former mayor of a small town in northern California was found civilly liable Friday for allegedly sexually assaulting seven women.
Dominic Foppoli, who led the town of Windsor from late 2018 to 2021, was ordered to pay a combined $13 million in compensatory damages.
The payouts to the women, whose allegations span from 2001 to 2020, will range from $6,000 to $4,650,938 each, KTVU FOX 2 reported.
He could also have to pay punitive damages to the women. That phase of the civil trial will begin on Tuesday.

Foppoli has consistently denied all wrongdoing and has never been criminally charged in connection to the allegations. He stepped down as mayor in May 2021 after four women came forward to the San Francisco Chronicle to accuse him of sexual assault.
FORMER NJ DEM MAYOR ALLEGEDLY DRUGGED, SEXUALLY ASSAULTED CHILD HE MET ONLINE

Dominic Foppoli appears in court during opening statements in the trial held against him at Sonoma County Civil and Family Law Courthouse in Santa Rosa, Calif., on July 15, 2026. (Jessica Christian/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)

The lawsuit, filed in April 2022, detailed allegations from seven Jane Does. Several women alleged Foppoli drugged their drinks before assaulting them, while Jane Doe 1 claimed he raped her dozens of times, including one alleged incident in which she said he handcuffed her to a bed.
According to the San Francisco Chronicle, a total of 13 women have accused Foppoli of sexual assault or misconduct.

In 2024, the state attorney general’s office suspended its criminal investigation into Foppoli, saying prosecutors did not have enough evidence to warrant filing charges on the cases not barred by the statute of limitations at that time.
Foppoli testified during the civil trial, which began in July, again denying the allegations against him.

"I've been a terrible boyfriend and partner, cheating, selfish and egotistical, but I've never done any of those things I'm being sued for," Foppoli said on the stand, according to KGO Eyewitness News.

The jury also found the Santa Rosa chapter of Active 20-30, an all-male charitable social club where Foppoli was a member, liable for Jane Doe 4's alleged assault and awarded her an additional $2 million, the Chronicle reported.

Dominic Foppoli appears in court with his lawyer Andrew Watters at Sonoma County Civil and Family Law Courthouse in Santa Rosa, Calif., on July 15, 2026. (Jessica Christian/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)
FBI AGENTS CONFRONT SWALWELL AT AIRPORT IN NEW FOOTAGE AS VIEWERS ZERO IN AND PILE ON

According to the lawsuit, the woman alleged Foppoli sexually assaulted her during the national Active 20-30 convention in Reno, Nevada, in June 2012. She also accused the organization of failing to investigate complaints she made to its leaders.

Traci Carrillo, an attorney for the plaintiffs, told Fox News Digital that the initial San Francisco Chronicle story "gave some of our clients a voice that no local news agency wanted to touch because it accused a powerful and connected local politician of crimes and sexual misconduct."

"It took over 5 years to get them justice, which was always about accountability. Their trauma was real, and they were believed, not shamed or silenced in the courtroom," Carrillo added. "They feel vindicated and will now focus on the much-needed healing the jury has provided for them."

Foppoli's attorney, Andrew Watters, said in a statement to Fox News Digital that he would seek a mistrial over claims that the court improperly excluded key witnesses for the defense. If that fails, Watters said he would pursue an appeal.

Farrah Abraham arrives for an event at The Sunset Room on June 22, 2019, in Hollywood, California. Abraham accused Dominic Foppoli of raping her in March 2021 at a house party in Palm Beach, Florida. (Gregg DeGuire/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"What happened with the verdict was that the jury sent a message based on questionable self-reported evidence and junk science, and that’s not appropriate. It appears the passions of the jury were inflamed by the evidence, and they hated my client, so they made a very large award to punish and make an example of him," Watters said in a statement.

Foppoli, speaking at a press conference outside the courthouse Friday, said his accusers "are trying to crucify me for a cause I'm not responsible for," adding that they were motivated by the $13 million payout.

Foppoli still faces a separate lawsuit from Farrah Abraham, a social media influencer and former reality television personality who claims the ex-politician raped her in March 2021 at a house party in Florida. That civil case is expected to go to trial next year, according to court records.
The Chronicle reported that Christopher Creek Winery, which Foppoli owns, settled a separate lawsuit filed by a Montana woman who alleged Foppoli raped her multiple times in 2020 when she was 18.

story: New York lawmakers are looking at a bill that would make it easier to take city-issued press passes away from people who abuse them, including "fangirls" of Luigi Mangione, according to City Council Speaker Julie Menin. (Courtesy of FOX 5 New York)
The New York City Council is considering a bill that would make it easier to strip official press passes away from people who abuse them or use them for non-journalistic purposes.

"We are introducing a bill today, sponsored by Councilmember Banks that will make reforms to press credentials to solve the problem of the Luigi Mangione fangirl, if you will," City Council Speaker Julie Menin told FOX 5 New York's "Good Day New York" Thursday morning. "These fangirls, who are not journalists, are showing up at the trial with press credentials that the City of New York is giving to them."

title: Lindsay Clancy DA rarely does plea deals, but her case could be the 'exception,' veteran attorney says
summary: Lindsay Clancy's mistrial sparks plea deal speculation as a veteran attorney says the Plymouth County DA's office may break its no-deal norm.
story: Veteran Boston defense attorney Peter Elikann told Fox News Digital the Plymouth County DA is known for rarely cutting plea deals, but Lindsay Clancy's case, after an 11-1 deadlock, could be the "exception."
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
The Plymouth County district attorney prosecuting Lindsay Clancy is known for rarely cutting deals, but a veteran defense attorney who has worked alongside him says her case may be the "exception."
Clancy, 36, faced three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan, all under age 6 — who were found strangled at the family's home in January 2023.
LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN
Lindsay Clancy looks on as jurors enter the courtroom during her murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Sept. 4, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

The future of Clancy's murder case is unclear after Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial on Friday, Sept. 4, after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict, ending in an alleged 11-1 divide.

Boston-based criminal defense attorney Peter Elikann, who has experience working against the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office, told Fox News Digital that the office is known for its reluctance to negotiate.
SOCIAL MEDIA IS LINDSAY CLANCY WILD CARD THAT COULD TILT POTENTIAL RETRIAL TO THE DEFENSE, RETIRED JUDGE SAYS
Lyndsay Clancy's defense lawyer, Kevin J. Reddington, arrives at Plymouth Superior Court on Sept. 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

"Normally, the reputation of the Plymouth County DA's office is that they don't like to do deals as much as other district attorney's offices do, that they will push a case to trial even if it's not their strongest case," Elikann said. "This very well could be an exception."
Elikann said it has become "conventional wisdom" that it's "unlikely that you'll ever get 12 jurors to agree that she committed first-degree murder."
PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

"It would make sense that as a win-win situation that the DA's office puts their head together with the defense counsel and they try to work out some sort of compromise that they can both live with," he added.
Elikann said Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz likely realizes it's going to be an uphill battle to secure a murder conviction at a potential retrial.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"Different juries can differ. But that might be an indication that it's going to be really rough to get 12 people to find her guilty of first-degree murder. Therefore, it would be something that they would mull over. Why have another trial if the likelihood of getting a conviction would be considered so minimal by a lot of people?" Elikann said.
Nick Dargie, one of the jurors, told ABC News the holdout juror refused to explain how witness testimony helped prove his stance.

"There was several times I would ask him to show us evidence or, you know, describe a witness testimony that helped to prove what he was saying, and... he couldn't," Dargie said. "There wasn't a single piece of evidence or witness testimony that he used to prove why he was thinking the way he was, which is why we ultimately sent in that note."
Cruz, who has not decided whether to retry Clancy, said after the mistrial: "There will be no decisions made today regarding that."

District Attorney Timothy Cruz leaves Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Sept. 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
"I'm going to be meeting with our team, and we will address this case further at the appropriate time and in the context of an official court proceeding," Cruz said.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, said he hoped the two sides can "work something out" when asked about a possible plea agreement on Tuesday during a "Good Morning America" interview.

Reddington filed a motion on Wednesday asking Sullivan to enter a finding of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility on each charge. He wants the motion to be heard at a hearing on Sept. 29.
"A hung jury is not a verdict; jeopardy does not terminate on a hung jury, and a mistrial ordinarily permits retrial," Reddington conceded in the filing.

He argued that 11 of the 12 jurors "applied the reasonable doubt standard," concluding that the prosecutors hadn't proven that Clancy was criminally responsible. The lone holdout on the jury, according to the motion and other jurors, allegedly ignored doubts he had and wanted a guilty verdict.
Lindsay Clancy holds her son, Callan. (Plymouth Superior Court)

"I‘m willing to listen to Tim. I‘ve known Tim for 30 years. He‘s a very hard charging prosecutor," Reddington said, referring to Cruz. "I hope, however, after sitting through this trial and seeing the evidence that was presented from the government as well as from the defense, that he would revisit that issue and hopefully would be able to work something out that would be acceptable to both sides."
TRUMP WEIGHS IN ON LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL DUBBED 'KANGAROO COURT' BY GOP LEADERS
WATCH: Retired Mass. judge doubts prosecutors will deal in Lindsay Clancy case, despite calling it a 'good idea'
Retired Massachusetts Superior Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital while he thinks a plea deal is a "good idea" and would be in the public's "interest," he doesn't think prosecutors would agree.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I predict that the prosecutor's office will approach this the same way, at least as the charges are concerned, as they did for trial number one, seeking a conviction of first-degree murder. There is some possibility that they'll reduce the charges, and that would, that could happen, but I wouldn't be predicting that," Lu said.

Kevin Reddington, an attorney for Lindsay Clancy, speaks to reporters outside Plymouth Superior Court on Sept. 1, 2026. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)
"I think it's the honest philosophical point of view of the prosecutor in this case that this individual should be convicted of first-degree murder," he added.

Clancy is due back in court on Sept. 29 for a status hearing, where more information about the future of her case may be revealed.

story: A firefighter confronts an agitator who was protesting near the 9/11 Memorial on the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks Friday. (X/@FrontlinesTPUSA and X/@choeshow)

title: Texas man remembered by Fox News hosts after repeat offender arrested in savage park bench slaying
summary: Surveillance video captured the fatal Round Rock, Texas, stabbing of Andrew James Wimsatt on a park bench moments after visiting his mother nearby.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A 62-year-old Texas engineer with ties to multiple Fox News hosts was stabbed to death from behind in what authorities have described as a random attack on a park bench in Round Rock, Texas, and deputies have arrested a repeat offender who spent months in the local jail earlier this year.
Andrew James Wimsatt, of Austin, was killed on Sept. 7 — minutes after he sat down in the park after visiting his mother at a nursing home nearby, according to authorities.
Williamson County deputies have arrested a 26-year-old local man named Benedict Chinedu Ogbodiegwu on murder and theft charges.
GOT A TIP?
Andrew Wimsatt in a selfie taken last year after he received a package from Fox News contributor Kat Timpf. (Courtesy of Kat Timpf)
The murder was recorded on surveillance video, according to the Williamson County Sheriff's Office.

A man identified as Wimsatt sat down on a park bench at around 11 a.m., authorities said. A few minutes later, another man, alleged to be Ogbodiegwu, grabbed him from behind and repeatedly drove a knife into his neck.

The victim struggled but was unable to push his attacker away as the stabbing continued, according to a probable cause affidavit obtained by Fox 7 Austin. The suspect then wiped the blood off on his shirt and walked out of view.
REPEAT OFFENDER BUSTED AGAIN LESS THAN 24 HOURS AFTER RELEASE IN BRAZEN JEWELRY STORE THEFT CASE: POLICE

The suspect, identified by the Williamson County Sheriff's Office as Benedict Ogbodiegwu, 26, is pictured in surveillance video near the scene. He is being held on $1 million bond. (Williamson County Sheriff's Office)

Wimsatt, who had a Ph.D. in civil engineering, is credited on IMDB as an executive producer of the Penn Jillette horror/comedy "Director's Cut." He worked for the Texas A&M Transportation Institute, staying on part-time even after retiring, and had an Instagram account filled with photos of wildlife, vintage storefronts and city landscapes.
He also had ties to several Fox News personalities.
"The crime, to me, is so heinous and shocking that I’m still trying to comprehend it," Greg Gutfeld said Friday. "I may never."
They first met when Wimsatt became a fan of a former show, "Red Eye," Gutfeld said. The engineer would clip segments from the show and attend his live events.

"At first, I was suspicious, because I always assume people do things because they want things," he told Fox News Digital. "I was wrong with Andrew. He did stuff for people — lots of people — because he enjoyed being of service, and promoting stuff that he genuinely enjoys and believes in."

Kat Timpf called him a "fan who became a friend" — a friend not only to her, but also to her family. They had lunch in Fort Worth in June, and she said she was expecting to see him at a show in Nevada later this month.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Andrew Wimsatt, 62, had a Ph.D. in civil engineering and worked for the Texas A&M Transportation Institute. (Texas A&M Transportation Institute)

"He was so kind and generous it almost seems impossible," she told Fox News Digital Friday. "He always supported me... whether that was sending me clips I wanted to post or offering truly helpful words of encouragement during the times throughout my career that the internet was piling on me."
They spoke regularly — once a week or more for years — and he became known for sending TV clips to members of the "Gutfeld!" cast.
"Whenever the rest of the internet was making me feel hopeless about the state of the world, I could always count on a message from Andrew to remind me of the good that's out there, too," Timpf said.
Wimsatt attended Tyrus' standup shows as well.

"[He] took care of his mother… always positive… he was kind man, 62 years old fragile looking but had a monster laugh," Tyrus said in a statement. "I was honored to know him I was honored he cared so much and honored that my jokes and thoughts brought him joy."

On Labor Day, a witness called 911 after finding Wimsatt on the ground in the park, and paramedics pronounced him dead at the scene, according to authorities.

Investigators were able to retrace the suspect's steps and allegedly recovered prints and other evidence, including bloody clothes and the suspected murder weapon, according to the affidavit. When confronted with video evidence, Ogbodiegwu allegedly claimed he had a twin brother but could not provide his name.

Booking photos of Benedict Ogbodiegwu from his arrest on Sept. 7 in connection with the murder of 62-year-old civil engineer Andrew Wimsatt. He is being held on $1 million bond in what authorities have described as a random attack. (Williamson County Sheriff's Office)

Ogbodiegwu has a criminal record in Williamson County going back to at least 2017, when he was charged with stealing. He had two prior arrests this year, on charges involving theft and carrying fake identification.
Prior to his arrest in connection with Wimsatt's murder, he was most recently released from the county jail on June 9. He had also been incarcerated between January and April.

He's being held on $1 million bond. His next court date is on Oct. 8 at 1:30 p.m., for a pre-indictment docket call.

"He was a kind, generous man, nearly beheaded in a park on a sunny morning, for no reason, just because," Gutfeld said. "I believe everyone who allowed the person who killed him to roam free like that, deserve severe accountability."

title: Family of off-duty FDNY firefighter retraces steps as Tunnel to Towers mission continues on 9/11 anniversary
summary: Tunnel to Towers Foundation chairman and CEO Frank Siller and relatives retraced the steps of his late brother Stephen Siller, a firefighter who died responding to the 9/11 attack.
story: Tunnel to Towers CEO Frank Siller and his nephew Stephen Siller Jr. discuss bringing a World Trade Center steel beam back to Ground Zero to honor September 11 heroes. They retrace firefighter Stephen Siller's final journey through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel.

Tunnel to Towers Foundation Chairman and CEO Frank Siller and family members honored his late brother Stephen Siller — a heroic 34-year-old husband, father, and firefighter who, after hearing about the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attack, loaded himself down with gear, and traversed through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel on foot heading to the Twin Towers, and ultimately giving his life — by retracing the man's steps on Friday as Americans marked the grim 25th anniversary of the heinous attacks.
"Together, they carried Stephen’s memory, his legacy, and the promise that his sacrifice – like so many others – would Never Be Forgotten," Tunnel to Towers noted in a press release.

The charity transported a steel beam from one of the Twin Towers around the U.S. for several months, with their "Steel Across America" tour finally culminating with the Siller family's trek through the tunnel today.
AMERICA MARKS 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS
Stephen Siller Jr. (left) and Tunnel to Towers Foundation Chairman and CEO Frank Siller (right) on "Fox & Friends." (Fox News Channel)

"This morning’s walk through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel was part of the conclusion of Steel Across America, a journey that began four-and-a-half months ago and carried a 21-foot, 16,900-pound World Trade Center steel beam more than 10,500 miles through nearly 40 stops across the country and back, stopping in more than 21 states," the organization noted. "For over four months, the steel has been a gathering place for communities to remember the events of September 11th, to honor first responders and veterans, and to ensure that a new generation understands the significance of what happened 25 years ago."

Stephen Siller Jr., who was just 9 months old when his father died, according to Frank Siller, said during a Friday morning appearance on "Fox & Friends," "The Tunnel to Towers foundation has given my family so much, through the loss of my father, through the work we're doing to keep his memory alive. Every day we have events across the country. Every day we're helping somebody in his name. That is such a beautiful, beautiful gift," he noted.
FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE
Stephen Siller went to help respond to the 9/11 attacks after having already worked an overnight shift with the New York City Fire Department, according to Tunnel to Towers.

"On the morning of September 11, 2001, Stephen had just completed his overnight shift as an FDNY firefighter and was going to play golf with his brothers when he heard about the attacks on the World Trade Center on his personal scanner. He turned his car around and headed toward Manhattan to help. When he found that his unit had already responded and that the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel closed to traffic, he strapped 60 pounds of firefighting gear to his back and ran through the tunnel on foot toward the Twin Towers. Stephen, like so many others that day, never came home," the organization noted.
FAMILY OF 9/11 HERO TO RETRACE HIS STEPS IN FINAL TUNNEL TO TOWERS STOP
The Tunnel to Towers Foundation was started in honor of FDNY firefighter Stephen Siller, who died responding to the 9/11 attacks. (Tunnel to Towers Foundation)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Born from the tragedy of 9/11, the Tunnel to Towers Foundation carries out its mission to "do good" by providing mortgage-free homes to Gold Star and fallen first responder families with young children and by building specially adapted smart homes for catastrophically injured veterans and first responders," according to the press release. "Children of the Foundation’s home recipients are offered full scholarships for undergraduate degrees and accredited trade school programs, helping secure their futures. The Foundation is also committed to eradicating veteran homelessness and helping America Never Forget September 11, 2001."
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

She also addressed Vice President JD Vance, the most senior Trump administration official to attend the ceremony in Lower Manhattan.
President Donald Trump spoke at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.

"It has been one betrayal after another. President Trump can still change that. Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this," Strada said. "Vice President Vance, thank you for being here today. Please carry that message back. Stand with the families. Stand with the survivors. Stand with Americans."
Strada's husband, Tom Strada, was on the 104th floor of the North Tower when it was struck by American Airlines Flight 11, Strada told WPTV in an interview on the 20th anniversary of 9/11.

Tom Strada, 41, worked at Cantor Fitzgerald and days before the attacks, he and his wife had brought their third child home from the hospital. After the impact of the plane, he called her and said he was heading toward the stairwell.

During her speech, Terry Strada urged Vice President JD Vance to take her message of pursuing accountability for Saudi Arabia to President Donald Trump. Vance was in the audience at the Ground Zero memorial on Sept. 11, 2026. (Hiroko Masuike - Pool/Getty Images)
9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY

Since her husband's death, along with the deaths of nearly 3,000 others at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and aboard the hijacked planes, Strada has become a leading advocate for accountability and transparency surrounding the Sept. 11 attacks.

Strada is among thousands of Sept. 11 family members and survivors who sued Saudi Arabia, alleging the kingdom provided material support to the al Qaeda hijackers. Saudi Arabia has repeatedly denied the allegations.

During her remarks Friday, Strada reminded the crowd that a federal judge ruled last August there was "reasonable evidence" that two Saudi government employees supported two future al Qaeda hijackers who came to the United States in early 2000 and took flight lessons.
The judge, George B. Daniels, allowed the lawsuit to go forward, denying Saudi Arabia's attempt to dismiss it.

Terry Strada poses near her husband's name on the memorial on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11th terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center at the National 9/11 Memorial & Museum on Sept. 11, 2026, in New York City. (Adam Gray - Pool/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For more than a decade after the Sept. 11 attacks, victims' families were barred from pursuing a lawsuit against a foreign government because of sovereign immunity protections.

That changed in September 2016, when Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), allowing Americans to sue foreign governments accused of providing material support for terrorist attacks on U.S. soil.
In her speech, Strada criticized President Barack Obama for vetoing JASTA.

At the time, he argued the legislation went too far by threatening "to strip all foreign governments of immunity from judicial process in the United States based solely upon allegations by private litigants."
Congress overrode his veto days later, making JASTA law and paving the way for the lawsuit against Saudi Arabia to be filed in March 2017. The case remains pending in federal court.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Lindsay Clancy's attorney challenges Jonathan Turley over holdout juror criticism
summary: Kevin Reddington says Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley was "wrong" for criticizing his comments about the Lindsay Clancy holdout juror and says he'd welcome a debate.
story: Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley criticizes a ‘remarkably dangerous’ move from Lindsay Clancy’s criminal defense attorney Kevin Reddington on ‘The Story.’

Lindsay Clancy defense attorney Kevin Reddington fired back at Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley on Thursday, saying the legal analyst "was wrong" for criticizing his public comments about the lone holdout juror in Clancy's murder trial and saying he'd welcome the chance to debate him.

"I'd like to meet with him sometime and maybe debate a few things," Reddington told Fox News correspondent Bryan Llenas when asked about Turley, a Fox News contributor and George Washington University law professor.
Llenas referenced Turley's earlier criticism of Reddington's public comments about the lone juror who prevented a unanimous murder verdict.

"Professor Turley said your attack on the juror was quote, ‘utterly reprehensible, a breathtaking abandonment of restraint and decency. He effectively put a target on the back of a juror who committed the unpardonable sin of not being convinced by his arguments,’" Llenas said.
LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS
Lindsay Clancy's defense lawyer, Kevin J. Reddington, addresses the media outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Wednesday, August 26, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
Reddington rejected that assessment.

"Well, I guess Jonathan Turley was wrong, wasn't he? Based on what we now know as far as the reason why this jury did not vote in accordance with the law," Reddington said. "Maybe Jonathan Turley should check out the record before he makes his accusations. I kind of think his comments were reprehensible."
Llenas pushed back, noting the public still does not know the holdout juror's version of events.
"We don't know what this one juror actually means or have said," Llenas said.
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT
"Probably a matter of time before he's getting interviewed somewhere, and you can find out," Reddington replied.

The exchange is the latest chapter in a public disagreement that erupted after Clancy's trial, when Reddington publicly criticized the lone holdout juror who prevented a unanimous verdict on murder charges. Turley responded at the time by accusing the veteran defense attorney of abandoning the professional restraint lawyers should exercise toward jurors after a trial.
Turley responded again Thursday after Reddington's Fox News interview was published.

"I was surprised to learn this morning that Kevin Reddington challenged me to a debate in an interview with Fox News reporter Bryan Llenas over my criticism of his attack on the holdout juror in the Clancy trial," Turley wrote on X.
LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE
Kevin J. Reddington addresses the media as he arrives at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026.  (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
"I am curious as to what is debatable in his view: the professional duty of lawyers not to fuel the rage against a holdout juror or his apparent self-exemption from that duty," he added.

Turley has argued that lawyers have an ethical obligation not to inflame public anger against jurors who exercise independent judgment during deliberations. Reddington has maintained that the holdout juror failed to follow the judge's instructions and that subsequent information supports his criticism.

Clancy's trial ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked on whether she was criminally responsible for the deaths of her three young children. Prosecutors have said they plan to retry her on the murder charges.

title: ‘I’m coming home’: Last words haunt a 9/11 daughter 25 years later as she builds a legacy in his honor
summary: Kayla Fallon Smith lost her father in the 9/11 World Trade Center attacks at age 8 and now runs a nonprofit offering equine therapy to veterans.
story: 25 years after losing her father at Cantor Fitzgerald, Kayla Smith opens up about her final morning phone call with him and the equine-assisted therapy program she built to help others heal from trauma.
"I'm getting out. I'm coming home."
Those were the final words of William Lawrence Fallon Jr. before he was killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center 25 years ago.
He worked as an IT manager for Cantor Fitzgerald and was just 38 years old when he was killed.
I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES
Kayla Smith was eight years old when her father, William Lawrence Fallon Jr., 38, was killed in the 9/11 terror attacks. She clutches a photo of him. (Photograph by: Peter Turnley)
His daughter, Kayla Fallon Smith, was 8 years old when she learned her father would not be coming home.
Before the attacks, Smith, now 33, said her father – who always commuted to work early – would call the house phone in the morning to wish her and her sister well before they would head to school.

📸 Instagram: kelsiecairns_tv
🎥 Facebook: Kelsie Cairns
An old photo shows Kayla Smith and her sister posing with their father, William Lawrence Fallon Jr. (Kayla Smith)
He went in early so he could leave earlier in the afternoons to take her to dancing school after her school day.

"That was the kind of man he was. I remember he would get up and work out in the morning before even going to work, so you'd hear the weights dropping in the house. I do remember that as a kid," Smith said.
Those quick and light-hearted morning phone calls to his daughters set the tone for the day.
Kayla Smith and her late father pose for a photo on the beach. (Kayla Smith)
"He would tell us what the skyline looked like. Sometimes it would be cloudy below him, and he couldn't even see the street, but it'd be sunny up there," she said.
FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE
Smith remembers hearing her father's voice for the last time on Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001.
Kayla Smith and her father pose for a lakeside photo on a boat. (Kayla Smith)
"I spoke to him on the house phone that day, as I always did," she said, to which he said on the phone, "Have a good morning," she said.
"I'm sure I said something like, 'I love you, have a great day'," Smith said.
Her dad called again that fateful morning – sometime after the first tower was hit.
SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE
This time, her mother answered the phone.
"He said something to the degree of, 'I'm getting out, I'm coming home,' and that was it," she said.
Smith's mother replied and said, "What are you talking about?" He responded and said, "Turn on the news."
After that, he hung up.
9/11 DEATH TOLL KEEPS GROWING DECADES LATER AS TOXIC EXPOSURE HAUNTS SURVIVORS
His family never heard from him again.
William Lawrence Fallon Jr., 38, was an employee at Cantor Fitzgerald when he was killed. (Getty Images: MediaNews Group; Kayla Smith)
"Those words haunt me a little bit," Smith said. "Every year, grief is different. It doesn't go away. It's a myth when people say that time heals all wounds; it doesn't."
In the last 25 years of growing up without her father, Smith has turned her pain and grief into purpose. She's devoted her life to helping others living with grief and mental struggles.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Smith is a licensed mental health counselor who founded Trails of Purpose – a nonprofit organization that provides free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members, veterans, first responders and their families.
"As I was getting my graduate degree, I started to experience equine-assisted therapy, and I really — it just clicked for me," she said.
William Lawrence Fallon Jr. holds his daughter Kayla Smith. (Kayla Smith)
She went on to say, "I never experienced that as a kid, and I had a lot of trauma therapy growing up. The resources were abundant for 9/11 victims, and I never experienced equine therapy."

She started her organization in 2019.

"I needed a place to just be when my brain always felt on fire. I think I've created that, and it's seeming to resonate with other people."
William Lawrence Fallon Jr. is one of the thousands of names engraved at the National September 11th Memorial reflecting pools. (Kayla Smith)

"The horses, and the connection that they have when words don't seem to come, the horses can just be with you," she said.

"I created the thing that I think I needed: community and understanding, and a place that's safe and quiet, and a respite," she said.

title: Could Africa be the next AI frontier as US and Europe hit limits?
summary: U.S. companies are winning massive data center and AI deals across Africa, including a $6.2 billion project in Lesotho for hydropower and computing.
story: China expert Gordon Chang discusses why he believes Beijing is looking to exploit U.S. opposition to new data centers as China works to narrow America’s lead in AI infrastructure.
FIRST ON FOX: Africa could become the next major frontier for data centers and artificial intelligence, experts say.
The Trump administration is backing and promoting American companies to make AI development, in their words, "the gold standard."
The U.S. is trying increasingly to grab business opportunities in Africa as backlash and environmental restrictions hit data center development in the U.S. and Africa.

"Africa is emerging as a significant potential location for building AI infrastructure, especially as many mature markets face increasing environmental and power constraints," Abhishek Goyal, consultant at specialist research group Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, told Fox News Digital.
US COMPANIES WIN BILLIONS IN AFRICAN DATA CENTER DEALS IN DIRECT COMPETITION WITH CHINA

A rendering of U.S. company Cybastion’s projected data center in the Ivory Coast, West Africa. The U.S. Embassy in Abidjan helped facilitate a $170 million contract with the government of the Ivory Coast, which includes the provision of the data center.  (Cybastion)

"The continent could become the next major frontier for AI infrastructure development. As the U.S. and Europe encounter challenges such as power scarcity, grid congestion, permitting issues and environmental regulations, Africa's underdeveloped infrastructure presents an opportunity rather than a disadvantage."

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "We are committed to ensuring that American AI, including enabling infrastructure like data centers, continues to be the gold standard worldwide and that we remain the partner of choice for foreign governments and businesses who are seeking to upgrade their telecommunications networks and AI capabilities."
Amongst other deals, this year with U.S. help, an American company has won a $6.2 billion deal in Lesotho in Southern Africa for a data center and hydropower plant.

In the central African country of Gabon, the U.S. Embassy helped win $600 million in business for American companies in 2025. And this year, the embassy in this central African country has assisted in securing a $100 million contract to supply two data centers and a gas-to-power plant in the face of strong competition from China.
TRUMP GETS MAJOR WIN AGAINST CHINA IN AFRICAN RARE EARTH MINERALS RACE

A rendering of the Kobong, Lesotho, Pumped Hydro project, which is to be constructed in Lesotho by U.S. company Convalt Energy as part of a $6.2 billion deal with the government of Lesotho facilitated with the assistance of the U.S. government. (Convalt Energy)

Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia previously told Fox News Digital, "Under President Trump’s leadership, the United States is assisting U.S. companies to find new markets and flourish in Africa."

"Africa is experiencing a data center boom, but it begins from a very small base," Arthur Goldstuck told Fox News Digital. Goldstuck is CEO of South African technology research group World Wide Worx and author of "The Hitchhiker’s Guide to AI – The African Edge."
MASSIVE AI BOOM PUTS ONE OF AMERICA’S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS ON PATH TO DOUBLE IN SIZE, CEO SAYS

Goldstuck said that because of a lack of capacity, "Africa will not replace either market as any kind of center of global computing. Rather, its attraction lies in serving a rapidly growing African cloud market and processing African data closer to the people and businesses that generate it.

He continued, "Africa also gives U.S. companies access to a cloud and AI market that remains severely underserved. The opportunities extend from operating data centers to supplying AI chips, cooling systems, cybersecurity and power infrastructure.

"In some countries, a data center can also become the guaranteed customer that makes a new renewable energy project financially viable. American companies can therefore develop computing capacity and electricity generation together, in partnership with African companies and governments."

A recent site visit to the construction zone for a new data center in the Ivory Coast, which is part of a $170 million contract facilitated by the U.S. Embassy for development by the U.S. company Cybastion.  (Clement Djakey for Cybastion)
But Goldstuck said data center growth is fueled by local needs on the continent.

"It is a boom by African standards," he said. "Africa remains far behind the U.S. and Europe in installed capacity, and weak electricity grids make construction and operation more difficult. Demand is growing rapidly as governments, banks and other large companies seek local cloud and AI services. They increasingly want sensitive information stored within their own countries, which adds momentum to the expansion."
Arizton’s Goyal added that "countries such as South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, Morocco and Egypt are attracting large-scale (AI) projects.

"The U.S. government aims to offer credible solutions that leverage public and private financing in priority areas, such as emerging technology, which demand that global telecoms networks remain secure for U.S. citizens and business," a State Department spokesperson said.
"For example, undersea cable networks are being constructed across the Atlantic, providing more opportunity and connectivity to Africa than ever before."
THE BIGGEST THREAT IN AMERICA'S RACE WITH CHINA ISN'T BEIJING, TECH EXECUTIVE WARNS

The Isando Campus, home to the Teraco Data Environments JB1 East & West, JB3 and JB5 data centers, in Johannesburg, South Africa, Sept. 28, 2025. Outside South Africa, computing resources on the continent are often expensive and scarce.  (Leon Sadiki/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
U.S. companies using undersea AI cables to connect with African data centers is a possibility, Goldstuck said, but there are limitations.

"Distance creates a slight delay, so African facilities would be less attractive for U.S. services requiring an instant response from American users" Goldstuck said. "They could work well for backups, disaster recovery and some intensive AI processing, provided that the cost, security and legal jurisdiction made sense."

Analysts say much of Africa lacks regulation and is creating the risk of a Wild West approach to business. The South African government recently claimed the country hosts 70% of the continent's total data center capacity.

But Pitso Tsibolane, senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Cape Town, told Fox News Digital that, in South Africa, "there is currently no public register of data center facilities, no requirement that operators disclose how much water, electricity and land they will use and no binding commitments against which performance can be measured.
The Isando Campus, home to the Teraco Data Environments JB1 East & West, JB3 and JB5 data centers, in Johannesburg, South Africa, Sept. 28, 2025.  ( Leon Sadiki/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"That gap serves nobody. Communities cannot see what is being traded on their behalf, and responsible operators cannot distinguish themselves from the rest because nobody’s numbers are on the table.

"South Africa hosts the majority of Africa’s data center capacity and has a real opportunity to become the jurisdiction that gets this right early: transparent disclosure, an independent factual baseline and predictable approvals. That combination is good for households, good for the grid and good for every investor who intends to be here for the long term."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Arizton’s Goyal says the future for Africa could be bright.

"Several African countries present a unique opportunity due to their abundant renewable energy potential — such as solar, wind, hydro and geothermal sources — as well as available land, lower development costs and fast-growing digital economies," Goyal said.
Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: Sweden votes as migration, crime and economy dominate high-stakes election
summary: Gun violence, asylum policy and welfare reform dominate Sweden's election as Ulf Kristersson's coalition battles Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats.
story: ‘Saturday in America’ host Kayleigh McEnany discusses President Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland, warnings to Europe over its immigration policies and more on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’

Swedes head to the polls Sunday with Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s center-right party slightly behind the center-left Social Democratic Party led by Sweden's former prime minister, Magdalena Andersson, and the election dominated by fears of mass migration, crime and the economy.

"Years of gang violence, Islamist extremism, persistent unemployment and pressure on public services have intensified the debate over whether integration has kept pace with immigration," foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz, told Fox News Digital.

Sweden Democrats party leader Jimmie Åkesson addresses an election campaign event at Sjodalsparken in Huddinge near Stockholm Aug. 18, 2026, as part of his party's national campaign tour ahead of Sweden's upcoming general election in September.  (Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via GettyImages)
After Germany's AfD victory in a state election last week, Sweden's hard-right Sweden Democrats are in a position to enter government if Kristersson's party wins again.
DENMARK'S LEFT-WING PM WARNS: 'BIG ENEMY HAS STARTED TO GROW FROM WITHIN' AS EUROPE FACES MIGRANT RECKONING

The Associated Press reported that the anti-immigration party has shifted toward the political mainstream and is likely to get cabinet posts. It has so far supported the Kristersson government from the outside.

The Associated Press reported that the Sweden Democrats were founded by activists in far-right-wing extremist groups, including neo-Nazis. But since then, under its leader, Jimmie Åkesson, it toned down that rhetoric and kicked out racist members. Åkesson, who has led them since 2005, is said to be responsible for the success of a once marginal party.
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson trails in polls as Sweden holds its general election Sept. 13 to elect members of its parliament, the Riksdag. (Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto)
Sweden, once a model of the Western social welfare state, has been under economic strain as governments from both the left and the right were forced to restructure their welfare system.
While social benefits continue to be extensive, Sweden’s welfare state has changed amid rising crime rates, but the expectations for public benefits remain.

"Sweden went from being described as a ‘humanitarian superpower’ to a 'humanitarian basket case.’ Discontent with migration policies extends to both foreign-born and native-born residents. Shootings have declined sharply, but fewer shootings do not mean the integration problems are solved," Schatz, who is Swedish, added.
Gang violence has rocked parts of Sweden over the last few years. (Oscar Olsson/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images)

Prime Minister Kristersson’s government took power in 2022, when the nation was experiencing a dramatic rise in gun-related violence, with the country witnessing 391 shootings resulting in 62 deaths, according to The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention, a government agency under the Ministry of Justice.
SWEDEN JAMS SUSPECTED RUSSIAN DRONE NEAR FRENCH CARRIER AS NATO WAR FEARS RISE
The homicide rate in Sweden has been on the rise since 2013, when gun homicides contributed to a general increase in Sweden’s total homicide rate.
The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention notes that Sweden’s homicide rate ranks high compared with other European countries, at approximately four deaths per million inhabitants per year.
The average for Europe is approximately 1.6 deaths per million inhabitants.
Swedes go to the polls on Sunday in a closely watched election race. (Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images/Sweden OUT)

The issue of immigration is another major issue that dovetails with voters’ concerns over crime and gun violence. Like much of Europe, Sweden experienced a wave of immigration in 2015 coming from those fleeing the Syrian civil war as well as the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Sweden took in over 160,000 asylum seekers in 2015, or 12% of all those who sought protection in the EU, according to Sweden’s Migration Agency.

"After the 2015 influx of asylum seekers from Syria and other war-torn countries strained its reception system, Sweden began tightening its borders. The current government has taken that shift much further," Schatz said.
ANTI-MIGRANT AFD SEEKS TO BREAK GERMANY’S POLITICAL ‘FIREWALL’ IN HISTORIC STATE ELECTION

Election campaign posters featuring Swedish Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson are displayed in central Stockholm, Sweden, on Sept. 7, 2026. (Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images)
Prime Minister Kristersson’s parliamentary ally, the right-wing Sweden Democrats, filled the void in the anti-immigration position in parliament.

Nicholas Aylott, professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, told Fox News Digital the link between the increase in immigration and the rise in crime changed Swedish politics.
Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats leads the polls against the incumbent Prime Minister, Ulf Kristersson. (Anders Wiklund/various sources/AFP via Getty Images/Sweden OUT)
"Migration and law and order became much higher electoral priorities," Aylott said.

"The Sweden Democrats based their pitch on them. The other parties, rather belatedly, adapted their positions. The Sweden Democrats had at first been completely ostracized by the other parties, but they were gradually accepted as a legitimate partner by three of the other parties of the right between 2018 and 2022," he said.
As anti-immigration backlash rose and the Sweden Democrats were more included in the policymaking process, Sweden cracked down on immigration and made it harder to seek asylum.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While asylum claims dropped and gun violence was dramatically reduced as well, with only 158 shootings and 44 fatalities to date, the government still might suffer a defeat at the hands of Andersson’s center-left coalition.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

summary: The Virgo Transport 8 vanished crossing the Java Sea with 240 people aboard en route from Surabaya to Banjarmasin, triggering an urgent search.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A passenger ship carrying 240 people vanished from contact in the Java Sea on Sunday, triggering an urgent search as Indonesian crews raced to locate the vessel.

The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Surabaya, East Java, to Banjarmasin on the island of Borneo when communications with the ship were lost, The Associated Press reported, citing Indonesia’s Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office.
Authorities said the vessel was last tracked roughly 92 miles from a pier in Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province.
MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING
Authorities are searching for the Virgo Transport 8 after the passenger ship lost contact while traveling from East Java to South Kalimantan. (EyesWideOpen/Getty Images)
Search-and-rescue teams launched an operation after receiving a report that the ship had lost communications capability during the voyage, according to the AP.
Officials had not reported any deaths or injuries as of Sunday, and it was not immediately clear what caused the vessel to lose contact or whether weather conditions were affecting the search.
MULTIPLE RESCUED FROM PONTOON BOAT NEAR ALCATRAZ AS SEARCH CONTINUES FOR MISSING PERSONS
The Virgo Transport 8 lost contact while traveling from Surabaya to Banjarmasin, according to officials. (EyesWideOpen/Getty Images)
The Virgo Transport 8 departed Surabaya, Indonesia’s second-largest city, before losing contact while crossing the Java Sea toward South Kalimantan.
The search remains underway.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Saudi Arabia tells Trump now is the time for military action as Iran-backed Houthis advance
summary: Houthi forces seized Perim island and key positions along Yemen's Bab al-Mandab Strait as Saudi Arabia urged Trump to take direct military action.
story: Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen joins Brian Kilmeade to discuss reports of Yemen's Houthis seizing a strategic Red Sea port. Thiessen warns of the ongoing threat from a nuclear-armed Iran and analyzes President Trump's past decisions on airstrikes. The conversation focuses on national security concerns and the broader geopolitical conflict in the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia is urging Washington to take direct military action against Iran-backed Houthis, Fox News Digital learned after the terrorist group seized key positions along Yemen’s Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday.

The dramatic strengthening of Houthi's positioning along the coastline of Yemen is in one of the world's most important shipping choke points — a narrow passage that links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, which has been used as a bypass as the Iran war continues to severely disrupt shipping, especially of oil, through the Strait of Hormuz.

The rapid advance on Friday triggered urgent discussions at the highest levels in Riyadh and Washington, and a source familiar with the matter tells Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis.
NEW RISK FOR U.S. CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT
Houthi supporters demonstrate in solidarity with Iran, amid a two-week ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran, in Sanaa, Yemen, April 10, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)

The Houthis reached the strategic island of Mayyun, also known as Perim, after Yemeni government forces withdrew and also took the mainland coastal town of Dhubab, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Friday.

Fox News Digital independently confirmed key elements of an Axios report with a source familiar with the matter, who said the crown prince spoke with Trump a few times over the past 24 hours about the escalating situation in Yemen.
The U.S. does not want to take direct military action for now, but Trump told bin Salman that Washington would assist Saudi Arabia with intelligence and targeting support, according to the source.
The source also confirmed that U.S. Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper traveled to Saudi Arabia for coordination talks.
The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on the calls or whether additional U.S. military action is under consideration.

A Saudi official told Fox News Digital on background that the kingdom "will continue to support the internationally recognized government in Yemen in its effort to promote peace, unity and stability across the country and is working closely with its partners, including the United States, to ensure freedom of navigation in the Arabian Gulf and Red Sea."
"The Kingdom will also take every necessary measure to ensure that its own citizens and residents are safe and its borders are secure," the official added.
IRAN'S BIGGEST WEAPON AGAINST THE U.S. MAY BE SLIPPING AWAY, EXPERTS SAY

U.S. President Donald Trump walks with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during an official state arrival ceremony at the Saudi Royal Court on May 13, 2025, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

The convergence raises the prospect of simultaneous pressure on two of the world’s most consequential maritime arteries: Iran disrupting traffic through Hormuz while its Houthi allies strengthen their position around Bab al-Mandab.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the shift reflects Tehran’s effort to recover leverage as pressure around Hormuz changes.

"Trump’s success in pushing back on Iran’s maritime threat in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf has made the regime lose the maritime leverage it had, and now it is looking to double down on the Houthis who have proven to be able to impact Red Sea shipping and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the past," Ben Taleblu said.
"As Tehran loses leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, it is trying to wield a knife and a handshake at once: diplomacy with Arab states and a knife in the back via the Houthi offensive," he added.
IRAN CALLS ON HOUTHIS TO PREPARE TO CUT OFF RED SEA GATEWAY — CAN THE TERROR GROUP DO IT?

Satellite imagery shows Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key shipping waterway and the gateway to the Red Sea, as Iran threatens using Yemen's Houthi allies to shut the Bab al-Mandab gateway to the Red Sea, in this handout picture dated July 12, 2026. (Nasa Worldview/Handout via Reuters)
The latest advance follows the Houthis’ capture Thursday of the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, which was previously held by forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

Former U.S. special envoy for Yemen Timothy Lenderking said Friday that the Houthis had spent the years since the 2022 U.N.-brokered truce rebuilding their military strength and are now exploiting the broader Iran conflict to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia.

Speaking during an on-the-record Middle East Institute virtual briefing, Lenderking said the April 2022 truce largely put Yemen’s civil war on pause but also "did allow the Houthis to regroup, retrain, refit, restock."

"They’re extremely entrepreneurial. They use every opportunity to build their capability, to test their capabilities, such that they are now the most lethal non-state actor in the entire Middle East," Lenderking said.

Lenderking traced the latest round of escalation in part to Iranian Mahan Air flights into Sanaa earlier this summer, which he said brought personnel and equipment intended to support the Houthi war effort, adding that the personnel were from Iran and were "probably IRGC members."
IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI THREAT IN RED SEA COULD LEAD TO MAJOR U.S. POLICY SHIFT, ANALYSTS SAY

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces fire a tank during what they say to be clashes with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in a location given as near Al-Hazm, Yemen, in this screen grab obtained from a handout video released September 9, 2026. (Media Centre Of The Yemeni Armed Forces/Handout via Reuters)
Lenderking said the Houthis are now taking advantage of the wider conflict with Iran to increase their leverage over Riyadh.
"They’ve seized this opportunity, bringing these various lines of effort together, to put a great deal of pressure on the Yemen government and the Saudis specifically," he said.

On Thursday, a senior Trump administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."
The stakes extend well beyond Yemen.

The Bab al-Mandab is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. About 7% of global oil output passed through the strait in June, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Disruption can force ships to reroute around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope, adding significant time and cost to voyages.

Reuters reported Friday that only seven vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, compared with a prewar daily average of 125, underscoring the pressure already facing the region’s other critical maritime choke point.
EXPERT WARNS OF 'GENERAL ESCALATION' OF FIGHTING IF HOUTHIS RESUME RED SEA CAMPAIGN

A vehicle burns after being attacked by Houthis during fighting with Saudi-backed forces at a location given as Al Jawf, Yemen, in this still image taken from a handout video released September 9, 2026. (Al Masirah/Handout via Reuters)
Ben Taleblu said the speed of the Houthi advance exposed vulnerabilities in the Saudi-led effort to contain the group.

"The U.S. should help the Saudis stymie the Houthi advance," he said. "The inability of the Saudis to prevent the Houthis from taking the strategic port city of Mocha, for example, does not bode well for what may come."

Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the danger extends beyond the territory captured. Retreating government forces, he said, left behind military equipment that could strengthen the Houthis on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."
