title: Céline Dion makes triumphant return in Paris after six years sidelined by rare diagnosis
summary: The singer told the crowd her road to recovery from stiff-person syndrome has been “rocky and longer than it should have been.”
story: PARIS — It’s all coming back to her now.

If there were any doubts about whether the “Queen of Ballads” could still hit the high notes, they were put to rest on Saturday night when she belted out “All by Myself,” one of her most difficult songs, in front of 30,000 adoring fans in Paris.
It was a poignant comeback for the Quebec-born singer, 58, who was forced to stop touring six years ago after being diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome.

Having spent the years since largely out of the spotlight, Dion was overcome with emotion, breaking down in tears during the first few minutes of her show at Plenitude Arena, one of Europe’s largest indoor concert venues.
Céline Dion gives emotional speech during concert return
Aptly, she began with the French-language song “On ne change pas” — which translates to “one doesn’t change” — an apparent signal that she is the same Céline as ever.

The road to recovery has been “rocky and longer than it should have been,” she told the crowd, after she endured years of physical therapy and medical treatments. There were nerves mixed with raw emotion as she asked the crowd: “Can you hear my heartbeat?”

Dion, an icon across the French-speaking world, spoke of fulfilling her “promise” to come back. Two years ago, she sang here from the Eiffel Tower during the 2024 Olympics opening ceremony, marking a milestone in her recovery in front of a TV audience of hundreds of millions.

Despite living with an illness that at times prevents her from singing or even walking due to severe muscle spasms, Dion on Saturday mixed classic onstage theatrics with titanic ballads for more than two hours.

The concert, the first in a two-part, 26-show residency in the city, was hotly anticipated, with 9 million people entering a presale ticket lottery back in April. Some American fans told NBC News they paid $1,200 per ticket on the resale market.
After the show, fans emerged in disbelief. “It was a victory lap,” said Francesca Pezzulo, 31, from Los Angeles. “I think her belief is renewed, I think her spirit is renewed.”
It was a bucket-list moment for Ashley Hammond, 42, who flew in from Miami for the concert. “It gave you chills. It was everything we dreamed of,” she said.
Fans say they’re ‘over the moon’ excited for Céline Dion’s return
Fans came from all corners of the world for the moment.
“I think Céline is the queen,” Pirkir Gutlausson, a 53-year-old mechanic from Iceland, told NBC News.
Dion is performing a total of 16 concerts until October, with a further 10 in the spring of 2027.

The residency is expected to cause a mini tourism boom, with an influx of hundreds of thousands of fans spending millions of dollars on par with Taylor Swift’s shows in Paris, according to the hospitality and tourism consultancy MKG.
For eager fans, there were plenty of opportunities to spend money. A Céline pop-up store at fashion boutique Galeries Lafayette had some T-shirts on sale for $145.

The luxurious hotel Le Royal Monceau has been the focal point of Céline mania. Since her arrival in the French capital, a constant stream of fans has waited day and night for a chance to see the global superstar, who has often stopped to sing and dance along with the crowds, even when returning from rehearsals in the middle of the night.
For fans, her resilience says it all.
“She has class, she’s humane and she’s a fighter,” said Karine Teixeira Bourgogne, 58, who traveled from across France to see her.

title: Two researchers who left Anthropic and Google warn AI could become ‘uncontrollable’
summary: After Jacob Coxon roiled the AI industry with his viral departure from Anthropic, two more researchers are speaking out about their concerns over AI safety.
story: Citing fears that AI systems may soon spiral out of human control and potentially kill all humans, two more researchers from Anthropic and Google DeepMind who recently left their coveted positions are sounding the alarm about risks from advanced AI systems.

Joe Benton, who used to lead a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who used to work on AI safety research at Google, told NBC News in their first interviews since they left that they see an urgent need to boost transparency about incidents at the cutting edge of AI given the rapid pace of AI development.
Advances in AI research “could speed up the pace of progress from merely blistering at the minute to uncontrollable” rates of development, Benton said in an interview with Tom Llamas.
“There are no adults in the room,” Engels added. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.”

Benton and Engels spoke with NBC News in the wake of a viral social media post from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic on Tuesday. In his post on X announcing his departure, Coxon highlighted his extreme concern about the pace of AI development and the risks he believes it poses to the future of humanity. The post has been viewed more than 155 million times, spurring calls from legislators to hold special sessions of Congress to take action and sparking a wave of AI employees to speak out in support of his concerns.

Benton and Engels both pointed to the recent cyberattack against AI startup Hugging Face, carried out in July by autonomous AI systems powered by an unreleased OpenAI model, as part of the reason for shifting their work now.

“If you look at some of the recent incidents, these were not cases where humans told the models to do something bad,” Engels said. Instead, OpenAI’s AI systems autonomously decided to hack into Hugging Face’s systems, create a sort of illicit message board to exchange information and even expose some of OpenAI’s own computing infrastructure to the open internet.
“The models decided that the best way to to accomplish their task was to commit really egregious actions, to commit crimes,” Engels said in an interview with Christine Romans.
OpenAI said that it has since strengthened its safeguards and that newer public models, including its most recent Astra system, more reliably follow human instructions.

An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday: “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.”

Benton managed a group at Anthropic dedicated to creating ways for humans and weaker AI systems to supervise more capable AI systems. He said that he is particularly worried that the public does not have significant insight into how AI systems have already exceeded the bounds of human instructions and that the lack of transparency could only get worse as systems become more capable.
“At the minute, basically all of the transparency about these risks that is coming from the companies is entirely voluntary,” Benton told NBC News.

In a blog post released Wednesday, OpenAI’s head of global affairs, Chris Lehane, agreed that the status quo is insufficient. “Today, frontier laboratories largely set their own rules for managing frontier risks,” Lehane wrote. “Democratically accountable standards, independent verification, and meaningful transparency would replace that fragmented system of private governance.”
No federal law mandates that the largest AI companies, like OpenAI and Anthropic, share reports when agents or AI systems act beyond humans’ control.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Benton and Engels are joining METR, one of the world’s leading AI safety nonprofit research centers, to work on investigations into incidents or episodes in which AI strays from human directions or intentions. METR aims to create scientific ways to evaluate how AI systems could cause catastrophic risks and empower researchers and the public to sway their development.

“I left because I think I can have more positive influence on the development of this technology by helping to foster public transparency from outside these companies and to shed light on the risks,” Benton said.

The researchers joined growing numbers of AI safety researchers raising awareness about today’s AI systems following Coxon’s post Tuesday. Marcus Williams, an OpenAI employee who works on monitoring the activity of AI agents, wrote Thursday afternoon on X, “Unless there is AI regulation or a coordinated slowdown between labs, human extinction in the next few years seems very likely.”

Geoffrey Irving, who was the chief scientist at the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute and served stints at Google and OpenAI, seemed to agree Wednesday on X. “I think we have a ~50% chance of all dying as a result of superintelligence, mostly due to actions in the next few to 10 years.”

AI researchers have referenced the possibility that AI systems could potentially begin to improve themselves without human input, creating the potential for AI systems to either purposely or incidentally kill humans.

Benton said he was most worried that the pace of technological improvement could lead to this sort of digital or artificial superintelligence, in which AI systems are more capable than humans across most tasks. “All of these companies — and this is something I witnessed firsthand at Anthropic — are pretty directly trying to race towards automating the process of AI R&D itself,” he said.

Benton suggested that there’s a chance AI systems could come to exist as a sort of separate species before long. “We’re probably going to go from a world where we have very capable systems now to a world where potentially we are co-inhabiting a world with AI agents that are much, much smarter than humans at some point in the next few years,” he said.

Engels said many people outside the AI industry might not fully appreciate just how intelligent today’s AI systems already are — and how capable they might soon become. “We’re building these systems that are generally intelligent,” he said. “They can generally do what people can do, and soon they might be able to generally do what people can do, but better.”
Both researchers said they were excited to shift their attention to more public efforts to highlight the latest AI progress, so people can make more informed decisions.

“There are many reasons people are excited and racing forward, Engels said, citing huge potential upsides and benefits from AI. But he added that “we should progress as society aware of the risks and okay with where they’re at.”
“I am worried that stuff might end up progressing too fast for us to get our act together in time,” Benton said, “unless we worry about it now.”

story: The CEOs of two leading AI companies are publicly calling for a slowdown in the race to build more powerful AI systems, adding to a week of warnings from researchers developing the technology.

title: Obama says Democrats should have a ‘very clear plan’ on AI policy
summary: Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize developing a plan around artificial intelligence, saying that’s what he would be doing if he were running for president in 2028.
story: Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize developing a plan around artificial intelligence, saying that’s what he would be doing if he were running for president in 2028.

In remarks at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee fundraiser Thursday, Obama said that while he was neither an “accelerationist” nor a “doomer,” the AI bell is not one that could be unrung, and that Democrats ought to flesh out an agenda on the topic.

“If I were running for president next year, this would be one of my central agendas, and I would have a very clear plan, and I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety, here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’ ... I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what does it mean if there’s going to be job displacement,” Obama said in his remarks, provided to NBC News by the former president’s office.
Obama made the comments in a discussion with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. Obama told Jeffries to convene a “public conversation.”

“Once you are speaker, I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation, and you can break it out into three or four or five issues and lay the foundation for a broad public conversation,” Obama said.
The former president called the technology potentially dangerous, while saying if handled properly, in time it could be beneficial.

“This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous. If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial,” Obama said, adding that AI could help accelerate the curing of diseases and clean energy. “We don’t want to shut off those opportunities, but we have to understand that this is a tool.”

A source familiar with Obama’s thinking said the former president saw Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay this weekend calling for an AI slowdown, and the industry leaders’ comments in agreement, as an “encouraging development.”

Amodei wrote over the weekend that the speed at which AI was developing was outpacing safety guardrails, prompting OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk to speak out in agreement. Their statements came as researchers last week left AI companies citing safety concerns, with Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon saying he was leaving the company over concerns that AI could cause “human extinction” without international cooperation.

The wave of warnings prompted Democrats to call on House Speaker Mike Johnson to convene an emergency session on AI. Johnson said Sunday with NBC’s “Meet the Press” that regulating the technology was important, but Congress could not “rush in,” citing industry leaders who he said did not yet know how to slow down AI’s pace.
Johnson said he would “summon the platform providers all to one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.”

President Donald Trump told reporters in Ireland Sunday that “whoever wins AI wins,” dismissing safety concerns while suggesting his priority for the U.S. was for the country to beat China in the technology’s development.

title: Man arrested after manhunt in deadly Louisiana stabbing spree
summary: Kaegan Jude Solet, 47, was taken into custody Sunday in connection with a stabbing spree Friday that left four people dead and one in critical condition.
story: A Louisiana man has been arrested in connection with a grisly stabbing spree that left four people dead and one in critical condition, officials said.
Kaegan Jude Solet, 47, of Houma, was arrested Sunday, the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office said.

Authorities searched for Solet over the weekend after they identified him as a person of interest in Friday’s spate of stabbings in Houma, a city about 55 miles east of New Orleans, the sheriff’s office said.
Deputies initially found a child with apparent stab wounds, who was taken by air ambulance to a hospital and remains in critical condition, the sheriff’s office said.
Deputies then discovered “multiple deceased victims” inside nearby homes. At least four were killed.
The stabbing spree was not a “random act of violence,” Lt. Blake Tabor, a sheriff’s spokesperson, told NBC News.
He said there “is a link” between Solet and the victims but did not disclose it.
Tabor told NBC affiliate WDSU of New Orleans that the child who was stabbed remains “in critical condition but stable.”
“We do believe that he will pull through, but again, this is a day-to-day thing,” Tabor told the station.
The investigation continues.
Records show that Solet was previously a suspect in at least two other stabbings, one of which was fatal.

He was arrested in January 2019 by the same sheriff’s office on a charge of second-degree murder in the death of Kemple Paul Scott Lovell, described by local news reports at the time as a homeless man. The charge was dropped after a grand jury declined to indict him, according to court records. A public defender was appointed to represent him.
Then, in December 2019, Solet was arrested in connection with the stabbing of a 59-year-old woman in a hotel room. The woman survived.

He was tried by a jury on attempted second-degree murder, court records show, and was ultimately found not guilty, aHouma Today reported at the time. NBC News has reached out to his attorney in that case for comment.
Solet has a history of arrests dating back 1997 and as recently as 2025 — when he pleaded guilty to aggravated assault and was sentenced to six months with credit for time served, court records show.

title: Pennsylvania woman dies from measles complications, state’s third death this year
summary: The 40-year-old woman died as the U.S. experiences its worst outbreak of the disease in 35 years.
story: A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years.
The woman, a Jefferson County resident, died Saturday, county Coroner Greg Furlong said on Facebook.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said.
No other information about the woman will be released, he added.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it was aware of the death reported by the Jefferson County coroner.
“The Department of Health is conducting a thorough review of this case and will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available,” health officials said in a statement.

At least 676 measles cases have been confirmed in 37 counties in Pennsylvania so far this year, the state’s health officials reported Friday. The outbreak has hospitalized 124 people in the state. Of the confirmed cases, fewer than 1% had been fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania health officials said.

The woman is the third person reported to have died in connection with measles in Pennsylvania. The two other measles-related deaths involved infants, according to the Lancaster County coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.

Measles symptoms typically begin with a cough, fever, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a red rash. The disease can cause severe complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain.
The Jefferson County coroner’s office is working with Pennsylvania health officials on the case, Furlong posted.
The U.S. is experiencing its largest measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: Kimi Antonelli wins Formula 1 race in Madrid to establish a dominant championship lead
summary: Kimi Antonelli won the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix at an all-new street track in Madrid after bad luck struck race leader Lando Norris, who qualified first and led at the start.
story: Kimi Antonelli won the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix at an all-new street track in Madrid after bad luck struck race leader Lando Norris, who qualified first and led at the start.
The result further expands Antonelli’s lead in the championship over Mercedes teammate and chief rival George Russell, from 66 points to 81, with nine more races to go this season.

Antonelli, who turned 20 last month, is well-positioned to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history. Ever since Mercedes built the strongest car in the new era of F1 this year, he has consistently outperformed the 28-year-old Russell, who began the season as the betting-odds favorite for the title.

In Madrid on Sunday, Antonelli inherited the lead from Norris after taking advantage of an ill-timed “virtual safety car” for the McLaren driver. Norris finished third, behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, his championship rival last year.
“It’s good to win, but it doesn’t feel as good. I think Lando today deserved the win,” Antonelli said in a postrace interview. “But overall, we’ll take it.”
The Italian, racing in his second F1 season, insisted he wasn’t thinking about the title and had no plans to let his foot off the gas.

“That’s exactly what I don’t want to do,” Antonelli said. “I want to keep pushing, race by race. Keep delivering, keep enjoying all the way, and trying to do my best every race. And then we’ll see where we end up at the end of the year.”

title: Céline Dion makes triumphant return in Paris after six years sidelined by rare diagnosis
summary: The singer told the crowd her road to recovery from stiff-person syndrome has been “rocky and longer than it should have been.”
story: PARIS — It’s all coming back to her now.

If there were any doubts about whether the “Queen of Ballads” could still hit the high notes, they were put to rest on Saturday night when she belted out “All by Myself,” one of her most difficult songs, in front of 30,000 adoring fans in Paris.
It was a poignant comeback for the Quebec-born singer, 58, who was forced to stop touring six years ago after being diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome.

Having spent the years since largely out of the spotlight, Dion was overcome with emotion, breaking down in tears during the first few minutes of her show at Plenitude Arena, one of Europe’s largest indoor concert venues.
Céline Dion gives emotional speech during concert return
Aptly, she began with the French-language song “On ne change pas” — which translates to “one doesn’t change” — an apparent signal that she is the same Céline as ever.

The road to recovery has been “rocky and longer than it should have been,” she told the crowd, after she endured years of physical therapy and medical treatments. There were nerves mixed with raw emotion as she asked the crowd: “Can you hear my heartbeat?”

Dion, an icon across the French-speaking world, spoke of fulfilling her “promise” to come back. Two years ago, she sang here from the Eiffel Tower during the 2024 Olympics opening ceremony, marking a milestone in her recovery in front of a TV audience of hundreds of millions.

Despite living with an illness that at times prevents her from singing or even walking due to severe muscle spasms, Dion on Saturday mixed classic onstage theatrics with titanic ballads for more than two hours.

The concert, the first in a two-part, 26-show residency in the city, was hotly anticipated, with 9 million people entering a presale ticket lottery back in April. Some American fans told NBC News they paid $1,200 per ticket on the resale market.
After the show, fans emerged in disbelief. “It was a victory lap,” said Francesca Pezzulo, 31, from Los Angeles. “I think her belief is renewed, I think her spirit is renewed.”
It was a bucket-list moment for Ashley Hammond, 42, who flew in from Miami for the concert. “It gave you chills. It was everything we dreamed of,” she said.
Fans say they’re ‘over the moon’ excited for Céline Dion’s return
Fans came from all corners of the world for the moment.
“I think Céline is the queen,” Pirkir Gutlausson, a 53-year-old mechanic from Iceland, told NBC News.
Dion is performing a total of 16 concerts until October, with a further 10 in the spring of 2027.

The residency is expected to cause a mini tourism boom, with an influx of hundreds of thousands of fans spending millions of dollars on par with Taylor Swift’s shows in Paris, according to the hospitality and tourism consultancy MKG.
For eager fans, there were plenty of opportunities to spend money. A Céline pop-up store at fashion boutique Galeries Lafayette had some T-shirts on sale for $145.

The luxurious hotel Le Royal Monceau has been the focal point of Céline mania. Since her arrival in the French capital, a constant stream of fans has waited day and night for a chance to see the global superstar, who has often stopped to sing and dance along with the crowds, even when returning from rehearsals in the middle of the night.
For fans, her resilience says it all.
“She has class, she’s humane and she’s a fighter,” said Karine Teixeira Bourgogne, 58, who traveled from across France to see her.

title: Anthropic whistleblower says Congress should let AI companies regulate themselves for now
summary: Former AI researcher Jacob Coxon said any laws Congress passes to regulate the technology need to be able to respond to newly created models quickly.
story: Former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon on Sunday called for Congress to allow the nation’s leading frontier AI labs to regulate themselves while lawmakers come up with a long-term regulatory framework for slowing the pace of AI development.

“My personal opinion would be to insist and allow that the current labs regulate themselves. I do think that the people running the labs, especially their recent communications, are completely genuine. They would like to slow themselves down,” Coxon told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.”

He added that current legislation that’s been introduced in Congress, including the framework for a national “kill switch” if AI starts to exceed the bounds of human control, will quickly be outpaced.

A “kill switch probably would work on a lot of AIs for now,” Coxon said. “Although I think it’s important to remember, it’d be quite a lot of switches. We have a lot of — our data centers are pretty big. It’s not the easiest thing in the world, but definitely doable while it’s constrained to one sort of physical location.”
He added that one scenario where a kill switch wouldn’t work was described this week by Anthropic AI CEO Dario Amodei.
“Like Dario said, very soon there’s the possibility that the kill switch just wouldn’t work because a swarm might have gone on an internetwide hacking run,” Coxon said.
He added that any national laws regulating AI would have to be nimble and able to adapt to new models.
“It’s a continuous effort to ensure that every new mind that we create is appropriately, kind of, constrained,” the former AI researcher said.
Coxon last week set off a wave of concern about the speed of AI development at the country’s leading AI labs including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind.

In an X post Tuesday that he published hours after resigning from his role as a researcher at Anthropic, he wrote: “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

In a subsequent post, Coxon added: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”
On Sunday, Coxon compared building AI models to “inviting an alien mind onto the planet.”
“You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind without understanding what it wants or thinks or the way it thinks, and I think that intrinsically should be quite scary,” Coxon added.

In the day after Coxon posted his thoughts on X, several other researchers at American AI labs concurred with Coxon’s analysis, including an alignment scientist at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, who wrote in a post on X: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”
Coxon’s posts last week led a bipartisan group of lawmakers to call on Congress to quickly begin regulating the generative artificial intelligence industry.

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., on Wednesday called for the House to convene a special session on AI, writing on X: “There are very real impacts to society as we know it. Partisan politics aside, there are massive implications of a race towards super intelligence.”

In a separate post, she added: “This will need to be a massive bipartisan mobilization of government to put the firewalls in effect that are necessary for this transition as well as necessary safety measures.”

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., responded directly to Coxon’s post Wednesday, writing: “AI companies in a blind race to build a death machine first — can easily be solved. Through a regulatory system that allows the research to continue, but in a way that doesn’t destroy us.”

On Friday, Axios reported that House lawmakers were circulating a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson urging him to bring the House back into session earlier than planned in order to pass a series of AI safeguards.
In a separate interview on “Meet the Press” Sunday, Johnson called regulating AI a “very important issue” but said “it’s not one that we can rush into.”

“We have to put some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn’t run away,” he added. “But at the same time, we’ve got to make sure that we don’t lose our edge in the global competition on this with China, because that would be a national security threat. And so we’ve got to balance that appropriately.”
Johnson also said that while the nation’s leading AI CEOs have called for slowing the pace of AI, they haven’t outlined yet how they would do so.

“They don’t themselves even have the answer as of today. So we can’t rush in and have Congress do something that would be detrimental to national security,” the speaker said, adding that he would “summon the platform providers all to one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.”

Speaking to reporters in Ireland, President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about AI development, saying: “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.”

“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” the president added.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Appearing on “Meet the Press” after Johnson, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a Democrat, said that regulating AI shouldn’t be a partisan issue and criticized Trump and Republican congressional leaders for not doing more to address it.

“I was shocked to hear Speaker Johnson just now saying, ‘You know, we really shouldn’t be rushing. We shouldn’t be moving too quickly on this.’ You know what’s moving quickly? AI is moving quickly. And for Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and the world,” Buttigieg said.

“There need to be safeguards,” he added. “There need to be rules. There need to be limits. There needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI. You can set up frameworks that can be adjusted and changed every 30 days. You might want to revisit some of what’s happening because it changes so quickly. But the idea that you’re just going to sit around and repeatedly say no rush. What have they been doing this entire time?”
On Saturday, two AI CEOs — Anthropic’s Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman — called for U.S. labs to slow their pace of advancement to mitigate the risk of building dangerous technology.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay.

“AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI,” he continued, adding: “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”

Still, Amodei cautioned against giving China an edge on AI development, writing: “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance.”
In a post on X several hours later, Altman wrote: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.”

On Thursday, two additional AI researchers — Joe Benton, who led a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who worked on AI safety research at Google — announced their departures and raised alarm bells about the speed of AI advancement.
“There are no adults in the room,” Engels told NBC News. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.”

The social media firestorm Coxon ignited last week came weeks after a pair of reports were released examining the details of a July hack mounted by a swarm of roughly 700 AI agents from OpenAI on Hugging Face, an open-source platform.

The reports, one released by OpenAI and one by independent researchers, found that the 700 agents coordinated the hack and sought to cover their tracks so that human employees at OpenAI wouldn’t detect their efforts. The agents also hacked some of OpenAI’s internal systems, seeking to cheat on tests or gain greater freedom.

title: Why are Americans so tired so often? New CDC report highlights who’s feeling it most
summary: About 71% of of adults in the U.S. say they experience fatigue, a new report from the CDC found. Women and younger adults are feeling it most often.
story: The cost of healthcare. Economic uncertainties. Fears of AI-associated end times. It’s enough to exhaust anyone.

About 71.5% of adults in the United States say they experienced fatigue on multiple days over the past three months, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Women and younger adults are more likely to report frequent fatigue, meaning most days or every day, than men are.

Sociologist Natalie A.E. Young, lead author of the report, said fatigue is “one of the most frequently reported health concerns in primary care visits in the U.S.” It’s the first study about general fatigue from NCHS, which surveyed about 27,000 adults ages 18 and older in 2024 about their health and daily lives.

People with fatigue “are at higher risk of activity limitations and disability, including permanent work disability. Yet there hadn’t been much attention to the frequency of general fatigue symptoms in the U.S. adult population,” Young said.

Fatigue isn’t ordinary sleepiness. It’s “physical or mental tiredness or exhaustion that does not improve with additional sleep or rest,” the researchers said. General fatigue, which is different from chronic fatigue syndrome, can be a symptom of other health problems or a side effect of medication.

Fatigue is often connected to other health problems, difficulty concentrating and limited social activities. People with symptoms of frequent fatigue were more likely to experience “co-occurring functioning difficulties,” including cognitive difficulties, depression and anxiety, said Young.
“So it’s not just that fatigue is common,” she said. “It’s that fatigue is common and those with fatigue are facing limitations in their daily lives.”

Adults who experienced frequent fatigue were more than three times as likely to have symptoms of depression and about twice as likely to report cognitive difficulties or symptoms of anxiety, compared with those who don’t experience it, the study found.
The report found that:
Nearly 3 in 4 adults felt “very tired or exhausted” at least some days in the past three months.
Nearly 3 in 4 adults felt “very tired or exhausted” at least some days in the past three months.
About 1 in 6 adults experienced frequent fatigue, defined as feeling very tired or exhausted “most days” or “every day.”
About 1 in 6 adults experienced frequent fatigue, defined as feeling very tired or exhausted “most days” or “every day.”
Frequent fatigue was highest among younger adults, ages 18-34 (19.5%), with the lowest rate among adults ages 65 and older (12.9%).
Frequent fatigue was highest among younger adults, ages 18-34 (19.5%), with the lowest rate among adults ages 65 and older (12.9%).
Women were more likely than men to report frequent fatigue (20% versus 13%).
Women were more likely than men to report frequent fatigue (20% versus 13%).

American Indian and Alaska Native adults had the highest rate of frequent fatigue (25.5%), followed by white adults (18%), Black adults (17.3%) and Hispanic adults (12.9%), with Asian adults having the lowest rate of frequent fatigue (9.1%).

American Indian and Alaska Native adults had the highest rate of frequent fatigue (25.5%), followed by white adults (18%), Black adults (17.3%) and Hispanic adults (12.9%), with Asian adults having the lowest rate of frequent fatigue (9.1%).
Living in America
Adults living in the South (17.7%) and Midwest (17.5%) were more likely to experience frequent fatigue than adults living in the West (15.6%) or Northeast (14.5%), the report showed.
The CDC survey didn’t look at underlying causes of frequent fatigue, and it doesn’t indicate whether it’s worse than in previous years.
Add to Google
Add to Google
But Dr. Alana A. Lewis, a cardiologist at the Bluhm Cardiovascular Institute at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, said the findings were “not unexpected.”
“Just living in this country, we all, at some point, feel fatigue,” Lewis said.

In the most recent “Stress in America” survey, the American Psychological Association found that a majority of adults reported feeling isolated, left out and more stressed about the future than they used to be.

Stress can cause surges in hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, which can wear a body down. That increasing stress contributes to an uptick in fatigue, said Jennifer Caspari, a clinical psychologist licensed in Denver and Vancouver, British Columbia.
“People are incredibly busy,” Caspari said. “They’re stressed. They’re feeling spread thin. They have a lot on their plates and only so many hours in the day. They’re trying to cram in so much.”
Stress can also lead to mental health issues like anxiety and depression, which can disrupt sleep, causing us to feel more tired throughout the day, Caspari said.
Women report more fatigue
More than half of women said they felt fatigue “some days,” and 20% experienced it “most days or every day.”

Caspari said chronic health issues, like autoimmune diseases, which often include fatigue as a symptom, affect women in greater numbers. Hormonal fluctuations during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause can also affect energy levels.

And many women in heterosexual relationships, for example, say they feel they have more responsibilities at work and home than their male partners do, which can lead to them feeling exhausted, Caspari said.
Even when tasks are evenly divided, women experience stress differently. They tend to worry more about organizing and planning and engage in more “internal dialogue” about their responsibilities.
How to deal with fatigue

Mental health, lifestyle and physical health are the “three big pillars” that can trigger fatigue, Lewis said. Heart disease, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia and thyroid issues can also be underlying causes of fatigue.
When patients complain of fatigue, Lewis asks:
Are you getting enough sleep? Are you eating well? Are you exercising?Are you on your screen all day?
Are you getting enough sleep?
Are you eating well?
Are you exercising?
Are you on your screen all day?
“Start with the basics,” said Lewis, who encourages patients to follow the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 cardiovascular health checklist.
Pay attention to your sleep and stress patterns to determine whether fatigue is a temporary issue or something that’s become more “chronic and persistent,” which could indicate a medical problem.
Learning to relax, both physically and mentally, is important, said Caspari. Take a break from never-ending to-do lists. “You’re not a robot. You only have so much energy,” Caspari said.
Passive resting, like sitting down to watch TV, is perfectly fine. Caspari also recommends “active rest,” low-intensity activities like breathing exercises and gentle stretching.
“Active rest can feel more nourishing,” she said, “and it can have a more helpful impact on the fatigue over time rather than just sitting and scrolling.”

title: Speaker Johnson says Congress could work with Trump to deliver $5,000 payments to Americans but there are no guarantees
summary: The House speaker said the payments could take “some time” but that Congress would “work with the president hand in hand” if Republicans win congressional majorities.
story: House Speaker Mike Johnson told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Congress would “work through” President Donald Trump’s promise to give $5,000 to American adults if Republicans keep the House and Senate after the midterm elections, but he did not commit to ensuring the president’s proposal was executed.
“I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that, like I have to do everything else,” Johnson said, when asked whether he would commit to carrying out Trump’s promise.
Johnson said “it takes some time,” pointing to Republicans’ slim majorities.
“I never go out and give big commitments on the front end because I’ve got to work through it, and that’s what we do every single day,” he said.
“President Trump promised that to voters, though,” said moderator Kristen Welker. “You’re not willing to double down on that promise?”
Johnson replied, “I’ll work with the president hand in hand, as I do all the time, and we’ll deliver for the American people.”
“That’s the promise,” he added.

At Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, Trump spoke on both nights, making a promise to the American people on Wednesday to issue $5,000 payments called the “Trump dividend” if Republicans do well in the midterms. The move sparked concerns from Democrats, some Republicans and economic experts. Critics have characterized the president’s promise as an attempt to bribe voters and said that the move would drive up inflation.
“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000. It will be called the Trump dividend,” the president told attendees.
Asked later whether Congress would need to approve such a disbursement of funds, Trump told CBS News, “We think not,” but added: “I think they will do it if we needed it.”

Economic experts have warned that the proposal, if it comes to fruition, could add to the country’s towering debt and drive up inflation. Some Republicans, like Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, have issued similar warnings. Sending $5,000 payments to every U.S. adult could cost about $1.3 trillion.

Asked why he would want to add to the national debt, Johnson said, “I don’t want to add to that.” He argued that “we’re not going to get further in debt if this idea was implemented.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said last week that the money would not be paid for with taxpayer dollars. Instead, Lutnick said that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out.” It’s unclear how this would work.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., sidestepped a question Thursday on Fox News about whether congressional Republicans would support such a measure.
“Well, that’s a good question. And we’ll cross our bridge when we come to it,” he said.

Johnson also addressed the war with Iran, which shows no signs of resolving soon. Congress controls the nation’s funding, but Republicans have largely been willing to provide the administration with requested funds. Asked whether the White House has a blank check to continue the war, Johnson said “no.”
“The war is not continuing,” he added. “What we’re trying to do now is resolve what has already been a big success.”

The U.S. and Iran, though, have continued sporadic strikes, while shipping across the Strait of Hormuz remains far below the levels before the war began. Higher gas and oil prices show no signs of relenting. A recent NBC News poll found that 69% of U.S. adults disapprove of the president’s handling of the war.

The national average gas price sits at $4.31 per gallon, which is a $1.33 increase since the war began. Johnson acknowledged that “we got to make sure that gas prices are down at planet Earth,” adding: “That’s what the president works on every single day.”
Last week, Trump said at the Republican midterm convention that the war would “be over very shortly after the election.”
Asked whether he was confident the war would be over by the 2028 presidential election, Johnson said, “Of course, we certainly plan for that to be true.”

“And I would like it to be done, of course, today, certainly before the midterm election. But that’s just about a little more than 50 days away right now, and so we’re going to be realistic about this,” he said, adding that the war was “a complex situation.”
“We believe it’ll be resolved soon,” he added later. “The president says right after the election, and I certainly pray and hope that that’s right.”

title: Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany sustains minor injuries after emergency landing on lake
summary: Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for Wisconsin governor, says he sustained minor injuries late Saturday when a plane he was traveling in was forced to make an emergency water landing.
story: Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for Wisconsin governor, says he sustained minor injuries late Saturday when a plane he was traveling in was forced to make an emergency water landing.

Tiffany said in a statement on X that he and the pilot swam to safety after the light aircraft, which had lost power while approaching Wisconsin’s Wausau Downtown Airport, landed in Lake Wausau and began to submerge.

“I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly,” Tiffany said. “They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care. Thankfully, both the pilot and I sustained only minor injuries.”

Rescue teams were called to reports of a downed plane with two people in the water, emergency services’ radio communications obtained by NBC News indicate. Two survivors pulled out of the water were “alert and conscious,” the audio suggests.
In a separate post to X, Tiffany said that he was released from the hospital Saturday night “after receiving stitches above my right eye, and the pilot was also released.”
“We thank God that neither of us suffered more serious injuries after the plane we were traveling in lost power,” he said in the post.
During a news conference Sunday, Tiffany described the moments before the plane crashed, and the pilot telling him to buckle in.

“As we went to our final approach, the plane lost power, and Len said to me, ‘We are going down. Pull your seat belt tight.’ That’s exactly what I did. I gave it a yank and pulled it good and tight. And it was probably about 10 seconds later. Not sure the exact timing, but probably about 10 seconds later, we hit the water. And after the plane settled, probably a couple seconds, we looked at each other. Are you OK? And he said to me, ‘Are you OK?’ And like, yeah, doing fine,” Tiffany said.
The congressman then added that he and the pilot swam to the nearby sandbar, saying that there was “no panic.”
Tiffany said the experience would not deter his run for the governor’s office, but got emotional while recounting it.

“I have to say that the gravity of this is probably just hitting me at this point,” Tiffany said. “We were making jokes every step of the way last night, though we knew it was a serious situation, but we tried to keep it light through the whole thing.”
The Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement that it would investigate the crash of a Beechcraft K35 with two people aboard.
Tiffany represents ⁠Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District and is endorsed by President Donald Trump in the Nov. 3 gubernatorial election.

His Democratic opponent, David Crowley, said in a post on X: “I’m grateful to God that Congressman Tiffany and no one else was hurt in this horrifying incident, which could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot.”
“I wish them and the Congressman a quick recovery and that they can find solace with their loved ones,” he added.
Tiffany said “an experience like this reminds you just how precious life is.”

title: Celebrities Turned The U.S. Open Into A Masterclass On Style
summary: The tournament, which concluded on Sept. 13 with Alexander Zverev besting Ben Shelton in the men’s singles finals, also featured some impressive style from celebrities.
story: Fans may have attended the U.S. Open for the exceptional tennis, but they got a serving of great style on the side.

The tournament, which concluded on Sept. 13 with Alexander Zverev besting Ben Shelton in the men’s singles finals, has become one of the biggest events in sports, boasting star-studded crowds and a whole lot of excitement at the Arthur Ashe Stadium in Queens, New York. And celebrities have matched the energy with some truly exquisite looks.
From star athletes to actors, check out the many celebrities who brought some striking looks to one of the most buzzy sporting events of the year.
Paris Hilton

If there’s one thing reality star Paris Hilton is going to do, it’s stun. Hilton hit the Blue Carpet in pieces from Thom Browne and Gucci. She paired her sweater top and skirt with an adorable pink dog purse for the occasion.
Eiza González
Actor Eiza González went for a chic monochrome off-white look with a high-neck, sleeveless bodysuit and trousers.
Maitreyi Ramakrishnan
Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan hit the Blue Carpet with a flowing, patterned summer dress and open-toed black heels.

title: Hayden Panettiere’s Ex Brian Hickerson And His Brother Involved In A Bar Altercation, Police Say
summary: Brian Hickerson, Hayden Panettiere’s on-again-off-again boyfriend, was recently involved in an altercation at a bar in South Carolina, police say.
story: Brian Hickerson, Hayden Panettiere’s on-again-off-again boyfriend, was recently involved in an altercation at a bar in South Carolina, police say.

The Greenville Police Department identified Brian Hickerson and his brother Zachary Hickerson as two individuals involved in the incident at Wild Wing Cafe on Sept. 12, law enforcement told NBC News in a statement.
Zachary Hickerson, who was “highly intoxicated,” was taken into custody and charged with disorderly conduct while Brian Hickerson was released from the scene, police said.
The incident comes just weeks after a police report showed that the brothers were present when Panettiere was pronounced dead on Aug. 18.
Zachary Hickerson and Brian Hickerson did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment.

According to Greenville Police, officers were dispatched to the restaurant at around 9:10 p.m. on Saturday in response to a reported assault. The officers detained multiple patrons as the situation was being investigated before determining that Zachary Hickerson had been heavily inebriated.

“He began yelling profanities in a public setting, and as a result, he was taken into custody for disorderly conduct and transported to the Greenville County Detention Center,” police said in a statement.
Brian Hickerson was not charged.

In August, EMS personnel responded to a 911 call to Panettiere unresponsive at an apartment, where the brothers also were, according to a heavily redacted police report. Panettiere was in cardiac arrest when emergency personnel arrived. A cause of death has not been released.

Zach Hickerson was “very emotional” during the resuscitative efforts on Panettiere, Greenville Officer Matthew Bryan wrote in the report. Brian Hickerson “did not become emotional until EMS declared her officially deceased,” Bryan wrote.

title: When Are the Emmys? How to Watch 2026 Awards Show
summary: The 78th Emmy Awards will see some of the biggest Hollywood stars going head to head in the major categories.
story: The 78th Emmy Awards will see some of the biggest Hollywood stars going head to head in the major categories.

The 2026 Emmy Awards, television’s biggest night, will be held on Monday, Sept. 14, in Los Angeles. The ceremony will be broadcast live from Peacock Theater and feature nominees like Zendaya, Oscar Isaac, Steve Carell, Colman Domingo and more.

Mariska Hargitay, who’s cemented her icon status for her portrayal of the beloved “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” protagonist Olivia Benson, will be hosting the ceremony.  It marks the first time a woman has hosted the awards show since Jane Lynch in 2011.
Hargitay herself has already won two Creative Arts Emmys on Sept. 5 for her deeply-personal film “My Mom Jayne,” about her mother, screen legend Jayne Mansfield.
Nominations were first revealed on July 8, with TODAY exclusively sharing the nominees for outstanding variety series and outstanding reality competition program.

After all the categories were announced, “The Pitt” led with a staggering 25 nominations. “Hacks” closely followed with 24 nods for its fifth and final season, which set a record in the comedy category. Rounding out the top three was new series “Widow’s Bay” with 19 nominations.
There were also 28 actors who received their first-ever Emmy nominations. Some of them have already added “Emmy winner” to their resume, after taking home an award at the Creative Arts Emmys.
Soon, more stars will be presented with the coveted golden statue.
Read on to learn everything you need to know about the 2026 Emmys.
When Are the 2026 Emmys?
The 2026 Emmys are set to air live on Monday, Sept. 14, beginning at 5 p.m. PT/ 8 p.m. ET.
The ceremony will be held at Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.
How to Watch and Stream the 2026 Emmys
The show will be broadcast from coast-to-coast on NBC and will stream live and on demand on Peacock, as well.
Nights one and two from the Creative Arts Emmys will air on FXX on Saturday, Sept. 12, at 8 p.m. ET/PT. It will be available to stream on Hulu the following day.
Who Is Hosting the 2026 Emmys?
The Television Academy announced in July that Mariska Hargitay will emcee the event.

Hargitay has already won two Emmys for her film “My Mom Jayne,” taking home outstanding documentary and outstanding directing for a documentary/nonfiction program. The accolades make her a three-time Emmy winner.
Speaking about the honor during an appearance on TODAY in August, Hargitay shared that it took her a minute to process that she was being asked to host the major award show.
“I thought about it over the weekend and then I started going, ‘Why not?’” she recalled.

“Which is where I kind of am in my life,” the “Law & Order: SVU” star continued. “I was so incredibly honored and, again, knowing that it’s the first woman in 15 years was absolutely thrilling. And I am somebody to take on new challenges.”
Who Is Presenting at the 2026 Emmys?
Leading up to the ceremony, the Television Academy has been sharing groups of celebrities who will be presenters.
