title: Benny Blanco Reveals The Simple Way He Won Over Selena Gomez: ‘I Didn’t Use Black Magic Or Anything’
summary: Record producer Benny Blanco seems to have cracked the code for success in many aspects of life, including romance. He joined Willie Geist for Sunday Sitdown.
story: Record producer Benny Blanco seems to have cracked the code for success in many aspects of life, including romance.
In a conversation with host Willie Geist on TODAY’s Sunday Sitdown, Blanco shared how he won over his wife, actor and singer Selena Gomez.

“Men, listen up. Okay, first of all, I gotta be the poster child for the guy you gotta listen to. Look at me,” Blanco said between laughs. “I have the most beautiful wife in the world. I did it and I didn’t use black magic or anything. I just was nice.”

Blanco expanded on his relationship philosophy and what he’s learned from Gomez, with whom he collaborated with for years on tracks like “Same Old Love” and “Single Soon.” The couple, who confirmed their relationship in 2023, tied the knot in September 2025.

“It’s understanding your partner, and being able to talk about things, and have an open dialogue,” he told Willie. “We’re in a really good spot, and I’m very fortunate. And I think, again, like, not being a d*** and being nice to people put her into my orbit at the right time.”

Blanco, who’s behind some of the biggest hits like Katy Perry’s “California Gurls,” Justin Bieber’s “Love Yourself” and Rihanna’s “Diamonds,” can add another highlight to his list of accomplishments. He spoke to Willie about his upcoming book “F*ck Failure,” which explores his mindset when it comes to turning adverse moments into achievements.

“I think a lot of people probably look at you and they’re like, ‘Huge success professionally. Great personal life. Seems happy, and charismatic, and all the things,’” Willie said. “So, what makes you an expert on failure?”
Blanco responded, describing himself as “the biggest failure in the world.”

“I’ve failed so many times,” Blanco said. “I failed yesterday. I finished a mix from one of my songs. I gave it to the artist. They didn’t like it. They wanted to redo something. And what am I gonna do, like, cry about it? No.”

Blanco said his book tells real stories about times he’s failed and how those experiences have helped him get to where he is today.  He said hopes that readers won’t have to make all the same mistakes he did.

The producer credited his family helping him build his confidence. He also said that Ed Sheeran, who he’s worked with extensively on the singer’s hit album “Divide,” gave him valuable advice about attitude.

“I was talking with Ed Sheeran, and he said, ‘Don’t give people the opportunity to not wanna help you,’” Blanco shared. “Like, if somebody asks you to do something, and it’s seems really small, just do it. It takes so much energy to be a d***.”
Blanco has previously spoken about his relationship with Gomez. In May 2024, he joined TODAY With Hoda & Jenna and shared how his cooking helped steal the heart of his his now-wife.
“F*ck Failure” will be published by Simon & Schuster on Sept. 15.

title: Our 1 Main Question for ‘Practical Magic 2’s’ Xolo Maridueña During Commercial: What’s It Like Being in the Sisterhood?
summary: Xolo Maridueña sits down to talk all things “Practical Magic 2,” including plans for a sequel and how he felt working with Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock
story: Xolo Maridueña is pretty much the nicest person ever. Warm, charming and a smile that reaches his eyes, it’s easy to see why Sandra Bullock was interested in the “Cobra Kai” actor for the Gideon, love interest of Bullock’s on-screen daughter, in “Practical Magic 2.”

If it’s been a minute since you’ve seen the original, the story revolves around Sally (Bullock) and Gillian Owens (Nicole Kidman), a pair of witch sisters and their eccentric aunts Jet (Dianne Wiest) and Franny (Stockard Channing), who grapple with an ancient death curse placed on any man they fall in love with.

The latest installment finds Sally’s two daughters Kylie (Joey King) and Antonio (Maisie Williams) all grown up and in Kylie’s case, head over heels in love. Unaware of her witchy lineage, Kylie professes her love and, you guessed it, Gideon almost instantly becomes yet another casualty of the Owens Curse. The result is a supernatural goose chase across England in hopes of saving him.

On the final stop of the “Practical Magic 2” press tour, Maridueña, sits down with TODAY.com to share his thoughts on the unique sisterhood in “Practical Magic,” the possibility of another film and how one phone call changed his life.
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity.
There is definitely something different when you have a woman writer, women producers, a woman director, a No. 1 on the call sheet, No. 1 through No. 5 on the call sheet, that are women as well.

There is something absolutely palpable that, especially for a story of this nature, I think fit like a glove. To your point, I guess as a male, one of the few men in this movie, I never felt “othered” in a way that I’m sure on the flip side ... movies are a male-dominated field, especially behind the camera.

To have a movie that, not only in front of the camera, is trying to tell the story about matriarchy and the power of women, to talk the talk and walk the walk, I thought was something incredible. I hope it happens more in movies that aren’t necessarily where the main pillar is not sisterhood. This should be allowed to happen everywhere.

The challenge for me, the objective was, we need a handful of scenes to not only make you believe that these two people love each other, but that this is the first person Kylie is going to say “I love you” to.

For me, all of my scenes were make it or break it, because if this relationship isn’t believable, then the whole movie you’re like, “Why is she going on this journey for this guy who’s not even all that and a bag of chips, you know?”

So, in that way, I was very blessed and really have been in my career thus far with getting to play really optimistic, joyous, uplifting characters. It’s been such a help in my own personal life to get to work through scenes with a character who has this mindset and I think “Practical Magic” is no different.

I still am having a hard time wrapping my head around it. It still feels surreal. We just finished. This, literally, this conversation is going to be the exclamation point on this “Practical Magic” journey for me.

From the very first day that I got the call that Sandy was interested in me hopping on board, it instantly feels like a moment where your whole life has been waiting for this opportunity to be let in by the greats and allowed to kind of bear witness to their process.

And that’s not even just Sandy, Nicole, that’s Stockard and Dianne, that’s Maisie and Joey. That’s Susanne (Bier), our director, Denise (Di Novi), our producers. That really goes for everyone. It lived up to all of those expectations.

Of course! I signed onto the second with the third in mind. I really ended up loving what transpired in the second one, how the end does pass the baton, but we get this family, the mother and daughter duo, for the whole movie. I’m super excited about the prospect of figuring out what the story is now.

This movie has done such a great job of being able to keep the themes and the heart of the movie without needing to keep the formula or repeat the same steps. I think if there is a third one, it’ll surely kind of continue with this in that the curse is broken now, but they still have magic. So, I think there’s other areas to explore.
I could be, like, a normal dad who has magic kids (laughs).

title: The Story Behind The Iconic ‘Practical Magic’ House And How It Was Re-Created for the Sequel
summary: All you need to know about the iconic “Practical Magic” house, the history, designers and how it was re-created for the sequel.
story: The Owens sisters are officially back — and so is their gothic, magical Victorian-style house.

Twenty-eight years have passed since fans were introduced to Sally and Gillian Owens in “Practical Magic.” Now, Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman have reunited for the highly anticipated sequel out Sept. 10.

While getting back into character appeared to be quite natural for the two actors — who are now joined by Joey King and Maisie Williams as Sally’s grown-up daughters, Kylie and Antonia Owens, respectively —the Owens’ home was a little bit more difficult to conjure up again. It had to be built from scratch.
“Practical Magic 2” producer Denise Di Novi, who was also involved in the 1998 film, tells TODAY.com the house was re-created across the pond.
“It was a re-creation because the movie is set in London, so we built the house in London,” Di Novi shares. “The original house we had to tear down.”

Though the films are set in a New England town, the original home was built in Washington’s San Juan Island by duo Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of design firm Roman and Williams, according to Architectural Digest.

The pair built the original Owens home based on features described in the 1995 novel by Alice Hoffman. They also drew inspiration from late-19th-century scrollwork, East Coast lighthouses and Victorian homes.
The Owens house in Washington was only used for exterior shots before it was torn down. The interior scenes were filmed on a soundstage in Los Angeles.

This time around, the “Practical Magic 2” house was recreated by production designer Tom Burton on a soundstage at Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden in England. Unlike that of the house in the last movie, the first floor was fully furnished and used for filming, as was the vegetable garden outside. Bullock said that the crew was able to take advantage of the “vast” piece of land on the backlot.

“We were able to build it and make the first floor practical, which meant you can walk inside and outside, in the kitchen, through the solarium, back outside,” Bullock said in the press notes. “And we planted apple trees that then started giving us fruit by the time we shot the film—crew members were eating the fruit.”
Kidman added that as an actor, the actual home gives you “something you can really exist in.”
“I think it’s a beautiful thing to be able to say, ‘That place, that was in existence,’” she said.
The “Practical Magic” home is a character in and of itself, achieving cult status as the perfect space for midnight margaritas.
Di Novi tells TODAY.com that bringing the sequel to life was “a dream come true.”

“It’s one of my favorite movies I’ve produced in my entire long career, and I’ve had the dream for many years to do a sequel,” she says. “This is a unique situation because the fans demanded this movie for the last 10 years.”
And as the Owens sisters and the new generation tackle their treacherous family curse in “Practical Magic 2,” their beloved Victorian abode remains a special place of gathering, family and love.
“That house was emotional; I don’t know how to explain it, it had a soul,” Bullock said. “You can’t have this film without that home.”

title: Celine Dion Breaks Down During Emotional First Concert In 6 Years: ‘I Missed You’
summary: Celine Dion made her return to the stage on Sept. 12 at the Plenitude Arena just outside Paris, France. It was the first concert in six years for the singer, who took a break after she publicly revealed her stiff person syndrome diagnosis.
story: The Queen of Power Ballads is BACK!

Celine Dion made her return to the stage on Sept. 12 at the Plenitude Arena just outside Paris, France. It was the first concert in six years for the singer, who took a break after she publicly revealed her stiff person syndrome diagnosis. And the moment was an emotional one.
Dion, 58, broke down in tears.
“I had promised myself not to cry,” said Dion, whose hits include “My Heart Will Go On” and “Because You Loved Me.” “But I’m so happy to see you all. I missed you.”
She added that she had promised to come back to the stage — a commitment she did, in fact, keep.
“So here I am, singing for you,” Dion said. “Thank you so very much for your support, your patience and if I may say so, I am everything I am because you loved me.”

Dion sang a number of songs in front of the crowd of an estimated 30,000.  For days, people across Paris prepared for her arrival, with fans parked outside her hotel. Dion had even briefly stopped to sing with her admirers, who had long awaited her return.

The concert is part of a 26-date residency in Paris, which she announced back in March on her birthday. In a video posted on social media, Dion had shared that she had started to sing and dance again.

“Over these last few years, every day that’s come by I’ve felt your prayers and support, with kindness and love. You were there for me,” she said in the video. “You’ve helped me in ways that I can’t even describe, and I’m truly so fortunate to have your support.”
She also told fans that she was giving herself “the best gift of my life.”
“I’m getting the chance to see you, to perform for you once again, in Paris, beginning in September this year,” she said.

Dion revealed her diagnosis in 2022, canceling a string of performances at the time to navigate the condition. Stiff person syndrome, a progressive, neurological disorder, causes stiff muscles in the torso, arms and legs, according to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. Many people with the syndrome also experience greater sensitivity to noise, touch and emotional distress which can set off muscle spasms.

“While we’re still learning about this rare condition, we now know this is what’s been causing all of the spasms that I’ve been having,” Dion said in a video shared on her social media accounts. “Unfortunately, these spasms affect every aspect of my daily life, sometimes causing difficulties when I walk and not allowing me to use my vocal chords to sing the way I’m used to.”
Two years later, she sang for the first time at the 2024 Paris Olympics’ Opening Ceremony.

title: What Do The U.S. Open Champions Win?
summary: The ongoing U.S. Open tennis tournament in Flushing Meadows–Corona Park, Queens, which will wrap up on Sunday with the men’s singles final, offers some a total pool of $108 million in prize money.
story: A shiny trophy and a whole lot of glory aren’t the only things that the winners of the U.S. Open get to look forward to.

The ongoing tennis tournament in Flushing Meadows–Corona Park, Queens, which will wrap up on Sunday with the men’s singles final, offers some pretty significant prize money to those who take home the championship. This year, the total pool bumped up to a record $108 million, the largest player compensation package in professional tennis history.
So how does the money break down?

The finals competitions began on Friday, with Taylor Townsend and Katerina Siniakova winning the the Women’s Doubles match against Ashlyn Krueger and Robin Montgomery. The next day, Christian Harrison and Neal Skupski, won the men’s doubles over Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.

Several other finals matches have yet to crown their winners as of the afternoon of Sept. 12, including the Women’s Singles Final, slated for Saturday, in which the current top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka will face off against No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina. The Men’s Singles Final, which will take place on Sunday, is a match between No. 8-seeded Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev, the No. 1 seed.
The winners of the singles finals will each go home with $5,500,000 while the runners-up will get $2,800,000 each.

But players don’t have to make it to the end to take home winnings. All who make it to the qualifying round of 128 get prize money. Semifinalists in the men’s and women’s singles matches each earn $1,450,000 while quarterfinalists bring home $780,000. Those in the round of 128 take home $32,000 per player.
For doubles, the top men’s and women’s teams take home $1,000,000 per team, while the runners-up earn $500,000. Semifinalists get $250,000 while quarterfinalists take home $125,000.

The total compensation pool is up 20% from last year’s $90 million total winnings. Craig Tiley, CEO of United States Tennis Association, previously said that the increases represent a “multi-year investment in athletes.”
“We are proud to deliver record-setting prize money and expanded player benefits as well as providing a new platform to work together with players,” Tiley said in a statement.

title: Our Big Question for Role Model: How’s His Saturn Return Going?
summary: Role Model talks with TODAY.com about his new album “Chuck Timely & the Hourglass” and his upcoming album, which kicked off Sept. 9.
story: When the camera cuts, the interview isn’t over. With “Cut for Time,” TODAY.com asks the questions our anchors couldn’t get to on air.
Role Model has high hopes for “Chuck On Tour,” mainly a desire for fans to experience joy and connection at his concerts.

The 29-year-old singer, whose given name is Tucker Pillsbury, officially kicked off his headlining tour on Sept. 9, supporting his third studio album “Chuck Timely & the Hourglass.” After celebrating its release by crashing Al Roker’s weather segment Aug. 6, he caught up with TODAY.com to tease his plans for tour.

“I’m just excited. Every tour we get to do, we get a little bit bigger of a venue, there’s more space to play with, more room for production and fun things,” Role Model says. “It’s kind of a cliche but I do think this album, more than ‘Kansas Anymore,’ translates better live than it does when you’re listening to it ... This album feels like it’s made for touring, so I’m ready to get to hear it every night and play it.”

Among his goals for the 35-date tour, sponsored by American Airlines and Mastercard which aims at making tickets more accessible to fans, was growing his band to give the audience a bigger musical experience and having the shows be therapeutic. He’s also looking forward to seeing what people will wear to his shows.
“I like when artists set it,” Role Model says, recalling how Chappell Roan had a range of themes and dress codes for different shows. “I think that’s really cool.”
“I had never planned that,” adding that on his last tour “it kind of just naturally happened.”
“Everyone was in cowboy boots or a cowboy hat or both. And then people were fully dressing up as Dorothy from ‘Wizard of Oz,’ and so I love that,” he says. “I didn’t tell anybody to do that.”
The singer is “curious” and excited to see how fans get creative with their concert looks, noting that he’s seen a couple of “outfit inspo” posts online.
“I hope everybody just ends up wearing sunglasses,” he jokes. “The whole crowd just in sunglasses. That’d be so funny. Yeah, whatever they want to do.”

Released on Aug. 7, Role Model created the album’s titular character Chuck Timely to croon about themes of time and feeling stagnant, he says. “But also these very, kind of like, pathetically-desperate parts of myself condensed into this character.”

At 29 years old, one could say Role Model is experiencing his Saturn return, where people are challenged “to grow beyond their lived experiences and evolve into their future selves,” as astrologer Lisa Stardust describes it.
While the singer wasn’t familiar with the term, he says he does “identify with that. Whatever you just said, that hit. So maybe my Saturn has returned.”

“That is kind of what the album was about, and I do think ... there seems to be a shift in my life now, but also for the past like two years,” he continues, adding that with “Chuck Timely & The Hourglass” he identifies “with the confusion, the constant questioning, the loneliness and all that stuff.”

His favorite way of documenting life is through songwriting. Role Model says his latest album “ended up really helping me figure some things out ... that was therapeutic, and it was pretty much journaling in a way, just putting a beat behind it.”
He tries to “camouflage some of the sadness and the feelings” into more uplifting songs, “because I don’t want people to (feel sad) ... I want people to have a moment of joy and connection.”
With that in mind, Role Model is most excited about performing the ballad “Good Thing” and “Stain,” which he initially wasn’t going to add to the set list, “but people ended up liking it.”
The track he’s most nervous to play, he says, is “Honeydew.”
“It’s just a stripped little ballad. I really have to sing in that song, so it’s a little bit scary,” he says.
When it comes to getting up and dancing, he wants to see fans on their feet during “High Hopes 3000” and “Service Receipt.”
As for performing “Sally, When the Wine Runs Out” on tour, which saw a new surprise guest or fan (like Al Roker) join him on stage each night, he’s switching things up.

“I got new things up my sleeve. I’m not doing ‘Sally’ anymore. I publicly decided that a few months ago,” he says, adding that he will still perform the song, “but I think you have to know when to end a bit, so we’ll see if a new bit is born on tour.”
Among the potential “new bits” is possibly having fans sing along to the back-and-forth in “Love I You.” “That’s kind of the plan, I think.”
He also would love to hear the fans belt out “Chuck’s Mantra,” the  opening song on his album that begins with the phrase: “I am deserving of something real/ Something true, someday soon.”

“It’ll be cool for people to hear the mantra at the beginning of the album every night because that’s how we start the show,” he teases. “It would be cool if people sang that to themselves and said that out loud every night because I’m sure that would be good for people to be saying that they are deserving of love and all this stuff.”

title: Our 1 Pressing Question for Joey King, Maisie Williams During Commercial: Is Sandra Bullock a Good Bartender?
summary: Joey King and Maisie Williams open up about working with Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock in “Practical Magic 2” and the sisterhood at the heart of the movie.
story: When the camera cuts, the interview isn’t over. With “Cut for Time,” TODAY.com asks the questions our anchors couldn’t get to on air.

It’s been nearly 30 years since Sally, Gillian, Aunt Franny and Aunt Jet first danced in the kitchen while blending up midnight margaritas in “Practical Magic.” Now the wait for a family reunion is officially over.

“Practical Magic 2,” the sequel to the 1998 cult classic, just dropped in theaters and reunites Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as Sally and Gillian Owens, a pair of witch sisters saddled with a centuries-old curse that prevents them from ever finding true love.
Based on Alice Hoffman’s book series, the latest chapter finds the Owens clan again practicing magic, falling in love and of course, imbibing on their favorite tequila-soaked cocktails.

This time around, the margaritas are brewed in honor of Aunt Jet’s (Dianne Wiest) 78th birthday, and joining the celebration are Sally’s now-grown daughters, Kylie and Antonia, played by Joey King and Maisie Williams, respectively.
It’s the latter two who sit down with TODAY.com in the Orange Room to talk — well, whisper — backstage of Studio 1A on all things magic.

For TODAY’s “Cut for Time,” the on-screen sisters dish on having a legendary sleepover at Bullock’s, the career advice they received from Kidman and the genuine sisterhood at the heart of “Practical Magic 2.”
This interview contains mild spoilers for “Practical Magic 2” and has been lightly edited for clarity.
Joey King: Not really (laughs). It is hard to mess up with negronis.
Maisie Williams: Yeah, they were strong.

JK: They were great ... but how it came to be, we were on a night shoot and then we went back to her place to debrief and have a sleepover. It was five o’clock in the morning and it was the end of our night, even though it was the beginning of the day. We all like gin, we’re all pretty good gin girlies, and that’s what she had. So, we’re like, “Use what she’s got.” It was great.
MW: Yeah, we just chatted about the world.

JK: Yes. I just truly think one thing that I love about this movie and the first film is I do think women are at our best when we’re really seeing the best in each other, and we’re really kind to each other. I do think we’re at our worst when we’re not. This movie is just one of those beautiful reminders of how incredibly powerful we are as females when we are united and seeing the best in one another, being supportive and really feeling like everyone’s just doing their best.

MW: Joey and I have been doing this a long time, and it would be like really perfect and romantic to say that the only criticism that we’ve ever had has been from male journalists, but it’s just not true. So, yes, I think the message of uniting and just really respecting and understanding one another, and having a little grace for one another as women, is so important and not something we talk about enough.

This movie really does propel that, and it’s intergenerational as well. Like, we all have different experiences and we only have our experience in the film industry because of the women who came before us.

Although our experience is different, we’re so grateful for what happened before so that we can have a different time. But that means there are differences between the generations, and in this movie, I think we really get to explore that and how see how that can work alongside one another.

JK: I mean, I got the red hair for the movie and I decided to keep it. But I do feel like every character I play, you oftentimes are faced with, “Do I have anything in common with my character? Do I have nothing in common with my character?” And that’s what makes it so fun and interesting is sometimes you have nothing in common with your character and there’s a real, “OK, I’ve got to conjure up something here.”

I would say Kylie and I are very different. I am not not free-spirited, but I’m definitely not that free-spirited or rebellious or curious. But I think that it always makes me braver when I get to play characters that are a little bit braver than me.

MW: I didn’t do training, but a lot of the supporting artists I was working with worked in medicine. So I got to ask them and they told me what I should be doing at different points, and if someone was really in a coma, what I would be spending my time doing, what the threats are. So, that was really useful because otherwise I was a kind of a fish out of water, really. I’m incredibly squeamish. I think it would be the job that I would be so bad at. So it was really good to be working with people who have done that and could help me.
JK: The garden! The clothing! The library!
MW: Yes, I love the little quaint pub that’s really small. So beautiful. All green-y.

JK: The props, too. I think that one thing that I love so much about the first film is how aesthetically pleasing it was. It really touched on that feeling of falling in love with autumn and feeling the cold air coming. I think this movie gets me so excited for fall and all those little details that you’re talking about. They really add something to the experience of watching the movie. That’s what makes it so lovable. That’s the artistry of all the people that worked on our crew.

MW: Nicole, she just had so much advice about career and that it’s always going to be up and down. But if you’re loving what you’re doing, if you’re loving the work and you want to be present for the work, it will come. It’s never gonna be linear and you can’t plan for the future. It was just like a nice piece of advice about the unpredictability of the world and the career and the industry.

JK: We’ve both been doing this for such a long time already and we’re obviously very grateful to have the careers we have had. And we’re after that longevity of it all. I feel like Nicole really gave those lovely words about what longevity can look like and what it can mean. It’s definitely not a linear path and that’s a beautiful thing.

MW: I definitely wish that I had more questions, but I just felt very concerned about, I don’t know, holding the day up or not being on it. So, I felt like I was trying to be correctly professional when I was on set with Stockard. But there was a few times when she just really put me at ease in a way that I needed so much, which just kind of dropped that barrier between us, which was really, really lovely and really special, and I think about that a lot. If I’m struggling in a scene, sometimes I remember Stockard just being so sweet to me, like, “OK, it’s going to be OK.”
JK: They’re both such legends and they’re both so talented. They’re both so different. Kind of like I would say Sally, Gillian, Antonia and Kylie, you know, Jet and Franny are so different, too.

These actresses are just so incredibly strong at showcasing two brave, strong women, but so differently. I just find their performances and those things so beautiful. They inspired me, and I just find their whole careers to be so inspiring. I felt so lucky to share a space with them.

title: ‘The Carol Burnett Show’ Turns 59. Carol Burnett and Tim Conway Reflect on Their Hilarious Antics in 1995 TODAY Interview
summary: Carol Burnett and Tim Conway stopped by TODAY in 1995 to reminisce about “The Carol Burnett Show.”
story: Welcome to the “TODAY Archives,” where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment highlights “The Carol Burnett Show” and a visit to TODAY from the show’s star and Tim Conway, who reminisced about their classic comedy series on March 3, 1995 .
Nearly six decades after it premiered, “The Carol Burnett Show” still has fans laughing.

The CBS series premiered Sept. 11, 1967, and ran for 11 seasons before concluding its run in 1978. Along with co-stars Tim Conway, Harvey Korman, Vicki Lawrence and Lyle Waggoner, Carol Burnett kept fans in stitches with uproarious skits and parodies.
The show won 25 Emmy Awards and was nominated for 45 more, cementing its place in TV lore.

On March 3, 1995, Burnett and Conway, who died in 2019 at the age of 85, visited TODAY to reminisce about the series with Katie Couric, which gave Burnett the chance to open up about Conway’s flair for making his castmates laugh.
“When Conway was on, he was relentless. He would do things that we never expected, and nobody knew what was going to happen,” she said.
The Cast Had Tons of Fun
Conway felt the cast truly enjoyed themselves making the show, while also praising Burnett.
“I would say that we probably had the best time of a lot of people on television,” he said.

“This lady, not only is she the nicest lady probably you’ll ever meet — it’s so annoying because she never says anything about anybody — and just surrounded herself with those kinds of people,” Conway said. “And it was just a place you wanted to be.”
Who Was Carol Burnett’s Favorite Character?
Burnett played a lot of characters on the show, but when asked who her favorite is, she had no doubt.
“I think it was Eunice,” she said.
Her portrayal of the melodramatic Eunice holds a special place in her heart.

“She started out as such a witch. She was just horrible,” she said. “And then as it developed, you could understand where her rage was coming from. It was this mother feeling trapped, and her dreams of being a movie star, of course, were ridiculous. But she always wanted to be better than what she was.”
What About That Classic ‘Went with the Wind!’ Sketch?

This Season 10 spoof of “Gone with the Wind” featured Burnett as Starlett O’Hara, who wears a dress made out of her window curtain, with the rod going across her back. It’s a classic sketch and one that Burnett said scored more laughs than it may have originally.

“(Costume designer) Bob Mackie said, ‘I have an idea.’ I said, ‘What?’ And he came out with the curtain rod and the dress on it, and I fell on the floor,” she recalled. “I said, ‘This is absolute genius.’”

title: Reverend Shares Lessons From His Mom Who Died in 9/11 After Going Back to Get Her Purse
summary: Elizabeth Holmes, one of thousands who lost their lives on Sept.
story: Elizabeth Holmes, one of thousands who lost their lives on Sept. 11, 2001, originally made it out from the 84th floor of the south tower that day. But after reaching the staircase with her friend and realizing she had forgotten her purse, Holmes ran back inside.
Her son, Reverend Miles Travis Boyd Jr., was just 12 years old when he lost his mother in the terrorist attacks.

On the 25th anniversary of the national tragedy, Boyd, now the senior pastor at Sharon Baptist Church in the Bronx, sat down with TODAY to reflect on his memory of Holmes, what her decision to retrieve her belongings represents and how he is carrying on her legacy.

Boyd, who released a book about the experience ahead of the anniversary, “The Purse She Left Behind: A Son’s Memory, A Mother’s Legacy,” explained why he explored his grief, faith and purpose through his mother’s accessory.

“When I think of this, I think of my mom and what that meant culturally for women, right, you don’t leave your purse just anywhere, your livelihood is in your purse,” Boyd said of the book’s title. “So I decided what way to better tell her legacy by speaking of the truth that she was impacted by at that moment.”

Boyd told TODAY hosts Dylan Dreyer, Craig Melvin and Al Roker that at the time of the attacks, he was sleeping at his aunt’s house in Manhattan. That morning, Boyd said, his uncle woke him up told him to turn on the news and to call his mother.

“I immediately called, and to no avail, I got no message or any pickup,” Boyd explained. “I called her boss, and I called her supervisor, because I was the kid who had everyone’s number. All the lines were busy at that point. My uncle took me and my cousin onto the roof just to see what would happen.”

While he wasn’t able to reach his mom, Boyd recalled that he still believed that she would come home — especially since she had already survived the World Trade Center bombing in 1993 that killed six and injured thousands more.

Over the next few years, Holmes was never found, but Boyd said he still held out hope that she would turn up and walk down the aisle at church years later. It wasn’t until he went off to college that Boyd came to terms with the loss.

“My first day in college, I am putting up pictures on the wall, and there was this one little picture of my mother and I left, this perfect square of the picture, and that’s when I realized that Mom wasn’t coming home,” Boyd said.

Since the attacks, Boyd says he’s also been remembering his mother beyond the loss, reflecting on her lessons from having a strong faith, to the importance of education and leading a life dedicated to making a difference.
For 14 years, Boyd taught kids in his hometown in Harlem before pursuing ministry full time.

Rev. Al Sharpton, a Baptist minister, civil rights and social justice activist and radio-television personality, took in the then-12-year-old after the tragedy to provide a sense of normalcy and support when Boyd’s family was searching the city for his mother.
Al Sharpton surprised Boyd on TODAY with a video message, commemorating his dedication to his mother’s legacy.

“Travis, I’m so proud of you,” Sharpton said in the video. “I remember 25 years ago how you stayed with us. Every time the phone rang, hoping it was that your mother was calling. She never called, but you never let her down. I’m so proud of you, and I know she is.”
Boyd’s book, “The Purse She Left Behind: A Son’s Memory, A Mother’s Legacy,” is out now.

title: Four Former Presidents Reunite in Downtown NYC to Attend 9/11 Memorial Ceremony
summary: Former presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Joe Biden were present at the somber ceremony at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in downtown Manhattan. They were also joined by former first ladies, Hillary Clinton, Michelle Obama, Laura Bush and Jill Biden.
story: As the nation marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, four former U.S. presidents attended New York City’s commemorative ceremony.

Former presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Joe Biden were present at the somber ceremony at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in downtown Manhattan. They were also joined by former first ladies, Hillary Clinton, Michelle Obama, Laura Bush and Jill Biden.
Several other officials and politicians, including Vice President JD Vance and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, were also in attendance.
President Donald Trump remained in Washington, D.C. to attend a ceremony at the Pentagon.
At the memorial, the former presidents stood up solemnly as a youth choir sang the national anthem.
Though none of the four made public remarks at the ceremony, some of the former presidents recently shared their thoughts and reflections on the tragedy.
In a statement posted on social media, Bill Clinton said that “we can’t erase the nightmare that so many have lived through and are still living with today.”

“But we can support the people who have given and lost so much by treating one another with respect, in person and online, and recognizing that what we have in common is far more important than what divides us,” Clinton said in the statement shared on X.

Clinton partnered with the late Sen. Bob Dole, his Republican opponent in the 1996 general election, to launch the Families of Freedom Scholarship Fund shortly after the attacks. He said in his statement that the fund has awarded more than $193 million in scholarships to nearly 4,000 children and spouses of people who were killed or permanently disabled by the attacks.
Former President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama shared a statement on social media in remembrance of Sept. 11, 2001.

In the statement, the Obamas said that they are “remembering those we lost that day and those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the wars that followed.” They also said that they are praying for the families who lost loved ones that day.
“We hope Americans everywhere remember the true lesson of 9/11: that we can survive even our darkest days as long as we move forward as one nation and one people,” the Obamas said in the statement.
On Sept. 9 at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Former President George W. Bush recalled his first message to the nation following the terrorist attacks in 2001.
Bush was visiting schoolchildren in Florida when he was told by an aide that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center in Manhattan.

“I didn’t have much time to process that, but it was pretty clear to me that if we were under attack, then my job was to defend the child that was reading to me, and her family, and her country,” Bush said, according to a broadcast of the event by C-SPAN.
“In this case, I became a wartime president,” he added.

title: When Are the Emmys? How to Watch 2026 Awards Show
summary: The 78th Emmy Awards will see some of the biggest Hollywood stars going head to head in the major categories.
story: The 78th Emmy Awards will see some of the biggest Hollywood stars going head to head in the major categories.

The 2026 Emmy Awards, television’s biggest night, will be held on Monday, Sept. 14, in Los Angeles. The ceremony will be broadcast live from Peacock Theater and feature nominees like Zendaya, Oscar Isaac, Steve Carell, Colman Domingo and more.

Mariska Hargitay, who’s cemented her icon status for her portrayal of the beloved “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” protagonist Olivia Benson, will be hosting the ceremony.  It marks the first time a woman has hosted the awards show since Jane Lynch in 2011.
Hargitay herself has already won two Creative Arts Emmys on Sept. 5 for her deeply-personal film “My Mom Jayne,” about her mother, screen legend Jayne Mansfield.
Nominations were first revealed on July 8, with TODAY exclusively sharing the nominees for outstanding variety series and outstanding reality competition program.

After all the categories were announced, “The Pitt” led with a staggering 25 nominations. “Hacks” closely followed with 24 nods for its fifth and final season, which set a record in the comedy category. Rounding out the top three was new series “Widow’s Bay” with 19 nominations.
There were also 28 actors who received their first-ever Emmy nominations. Some of them have already added “Emmy winner” to their resume, after taking home an award at the Creative Arts Emmys.
Soon, more stars will be presented with the coveted golden statue.
Read on to learn everything you need to know about the 2026 Emmys.
When Are the 2026 Emmys?
The 2026 Emmys are set to air live on Monday, Sept. 14, beginning at 5 p.m. PT/ 8 p.m. ET.
The ceremony will be held at Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.
How to Watch and Stream the 2026 Emmys
The show will be broadcast from coast-to-coast on NBC and will stream live and on demand on Peacock, as well.
Nights one and two from the Creative Arts Emmys will air on FXX on Saturday, Sept. 12, at 8 p.m. ET/PT. It will be available to stream on Hulu the following day.
Who Is Hosting the 2026 Emmys?
The Television Academy announced in July that Mariska Hargitay will emcee the event.

Hargitay has already won two Emmys for her film “My Mom Jayne,” taking home outstanding documentary and outstanding directing for a documentary/nonfiction program. The accolades make her a three-time Emmy winner.
Speaking about the honor during an appearance on TODAY in August, Hargitay shared that it took her a minute to process that she was being asked to host the major award show.
“I thought about it over the weekend and then I started going, ‘Why not?’” she recalled.

“Which is where I kind of am in my life,” the “Law & Order: SVU” star continued. “I was so incredibly honored and, again, knowing that it’s the first woman in 15 years was absolutely thrilling. And I am somebody to take on new challenges.”
Who Is Presenting at the 2026 Emmys?
Leading up to the ceremony, the Television Academy has been sharing groups of celebrities who will be presenters.

title: 9/11 Movies and Documentaries Worth Watching
summary: In the 25 years since September 11, 2001, filmmakers and documentarians have been trying to capture the events of that tragic day in a number of ways.
story: This year marks 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, a day many Americans will never forget.

Some will recall the moment they learned or watched in a news report that two planes downed the twin towers of New York City’s World Trade Center. The devastation continued as a third plane struck the Pentagon outside Washington, D.C. Then, there was a failed attempt by a fourth plane, which crashed in rural Pennsylvania when the passengers took over.
These horrific and fatal events are etched in the memories of U.S. citizens and others around the world.

In the ensuing decades, filmmakers have released numerous 9/11 documentaries and fictionalized depictions that explore the events before, during and after. As Sept. 11, 2026 marks the 25th anniversary of those attacks, TODAY has compiled a list of 17 films  for those wanting to look back in remembrance or educate young people who may not have been alive during the historic moment.
1. “The Man Who Knew” (2002)
Watch on YouTube. (1 hour, 25 mins.)

PBS’ “Frontline” has been on top of numerous documentaries about 9/11 and its aftermath; “The Man Who Knew” focuses on a former FBI counterterrorism agent who felt the U.S. should have preemptively taken out Osama Bin Laden. John O’Neill, who died in the twin towers on 9/11, had been fighting for six years to track down and prosecute al-Qaeda operatives around the world, but was considered controversial.
2. “Fahrenheit 9/11” (2004)
Watch on Tubi, Pluto TV or The Roku Channel. (2 hours, 3 mins.)

Director Michael Moore put himself behind and in front of the camera to cast his unflinching gaze on the presidency of George W. Bush, the Iraq War and the way the media covered the war, along with how the administration dealt with the events of 9/11.
3. “Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close” (2011)
Watch on YouTube. (2 hours, 9 mins.)

“Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close” stars Tom Hanks and Sandra Bullock and is based on a bestselling fiction book by Jonathan Safran Foer. It follows a young boy named Oskar as he goes on a quest across New York with a key, one year after his father died in the World Trade Center attacks.
4. “The Woman Who Wasn’t There” (2012)
Watch on YouTube, Pluto TV or Fandango. (1 hour, 4 mins.)

Based on the story of Alicia Esteve Head, “The Woman Who Wasn’t There” was both a book and a documentary that looked at a Spanish businesswoman who claimed to have survived the World Trade Center attacks (calling herself Tania Head). She became the head of the World Trade Center Survivors’ Network support group — but in 2007, her story was revealed to be a hoax.
5. “9/11 Inside the Pentagon” (2016)
Watch on PBS Passport. (54 mins.)

The twin towers weren’t the only buildings hit on 9/11; the Pentagon was struck by a third plane, and 184 people were killed. This documentary shifts the perspective from New York to one of the country’s most important and secretive buildings to explore the attack.
6. “In the Shadow of the Towers: Stuyvesant High on 9/11” (2019)
Watch on HBO Max, YouTube, Hulu or Prime Video. (32 mins.)

Students in one of New York City’s most elite schools, Stuyvesant High, watched the World Trade Center attack from their classrooms. Director Amy Schatz spoke with former students who shared their recollections. (TODAY.com also has a story told through the eyes of adults who were in kindergarten blocks away from the twin towers at the time.)
Watch on Peacock, YouTube or The Roku Channel. (1 hour, 45 mins.)

The U.S. Capitol and White House were spared being hit by a fourth plane on 9/11 when passengers wrestled control from the terrorists inside. That plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. All 44 inside, including the hijackers, were killed. “United 93” is a fictionalized re-telling of these events, directed by Paul Greengrass.
8. “9/11: The Final Minutes of Flight 93” (2020)
Watch on YouTube, Tubi or The History Channel. (43 mins.)

While “United 93” is a scripted feature film looking at the plane crash in Pennsylvania, “9/11: The Final Minutes of Flight 93” is a documentary. It provides newly unclassified evidence that allowed filmmakers to piece together what happened on the plane, minute by minute.
9. “The Forever Prisoner” (2021)
Watch or HBO Max. (2 hours)

Oscar winner Alex Gibney co-executive produced the 10-part fictionalized take on the events leading up to 9/11 with an adaptation of the 2006 book “The Looming Tower” in 2018. In “The Forever Prisoner,” he dives into the aftermath of al-Qaeda suspect Abu Zubaydah, the first high-value detainee who was subjected to “enhanced interrogation techniques” for the U.S. post-9/11.
10. “9/11: Inside the President’s War Room” (2021)
Watch on Apple TV or Prime Video. (1 hour, 30 mins.)

This Apple TV+/BBC One documentary goes into detail about the steps that followed in the immediate hours after the 9/11 attacks, focused on the point of view of President George W. Bush and his staff. It includes interviews with Bush, former Vice President Dick Cheney, Condoleezza Rice, Colin Powell and many others.
11. “9/11: One Day in America” (2021)
Watch on Hulu and Disney+. (6 episodes, run times vary)

In its six episodes, “One Day in America” (which was created in official collaboration with the 9/11 Memorial & Museum) walks viewers through the timeline of 9/11 while focusing on those who survived and those who came to their rescue: firefighters, paramedics and regular folk.
12. “Turning Point: 9/11 and the War on Terror” (2021)
Watch on Netflix. (5 episodes, run times vary.)
In this five-episode series, experts explore where the 9/11 attacks came from, what happened the day-of and the decadeslong ripple effect the attack has had on the U.S. and its citizens.
13. “Zero Dark Thirty” (2012)
Watch on Netflix, The Roku Channel, Prime Video or Apple TV. (2 hours, 37 mins)

This drama directed by Kathryn Bigelow follows the efforts to find al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden after the 9/11 attacks. The film, which stars Jessica Chastain, Chris Pratt, Kyle Chandler and Joel Edgerton, was nominated for five Academy Awards, including best picture, and won one for sound editing.
14. “Twin Towers: Legacy” (2025)
Watch on Tubi, PlutoTV, The Roku Channel or Fandango. (1 hour, 27 mins)

This film narrated by Dennis Quaid is a follow-up to 2003’s “Twin Towers,” an Oscar-winning documentary about the actions taken by policeman Joe Vigiano during the 9/11 attacks. “Twin Towers: Legacy” follows Vigiano’s sons as they try to honor their father who died that day.
15. “102 Minutes That Changed America” (2008)
Watch on Tubi, PlutoTV or The History Channel. (1 hour, 42 min)

This documentary originally aired on History and won three Emmy Awards. Featuring amateur video and voicemails, it captures the events of 9/11 in New York City between the time the first World Trade Center was attacked and the fall of the second tower.
16. “Top of the World” (2026)
Watch on CNN streaming service. (40 mins.)

This documentary is being released as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 arrives. It also coincides with the 50th anniversary of the opening of Windows on the World, the restaurant that sat atop the World Trade Center. This film includes firsthand accounts from former staff members, sharing how the community was impacted after the attack killed all 79 employees working that morning and their 91 guests.
17. “Turning Point: Generation 9/11” (2026)
Watch on Netflix. (1 hour, 39 mins.)

Twenty-five years after the attack, multiple generations, from survivors, to children who lost parents, journalists, Afghans and U.S. Marines, share how their lives were affected. They also reflect on how they process their grief today.

title: Dolly Parton’s First Posthumous Song, ‘Bound to Ride,’ Features Her Beloved Sense of Humor
summary: Two weeks after her death, Dolly Parton’s fans are getting to hear the icon’s first song released posthumously.
story: Two weeks after her death, Dolly Parton’s fans are getting to hear the icon’s first song released posthumously.

The country music legend and actor died following “a brief battle with cancer” her estate announced Aug. 25. She was 80. As the news was reported, tributes poured in from her peers and fans. They reflected on Parton’s impact in the industry, from hits like “9 to 5” to “I Will Always Love You” and “Jolene.”

Now, they’ll have the opportunity to listen to a new song from her once more, as Parton is featured on an upcoming all-star tribute album titled “Where the Soul Never Dies: Celebrating 80 Years of The Stanley Brothers.”
She added her vocals to the track “Bound to Ride,” which the country duo recorded in 1964, and the single has been posted on YouTube ahead of the album’s release on Oct. 16.

Parton originally recorded her part around 2022 in her personal studio, Rolling Stone reports. The album is also set to include vocals by Willie Nelson and Sierra Ferrell, Dierks Bentley with Della Mae, and Steve Martin and Ed Helms, among others.
Following Parton’s death, her longtime manager Danny Nozell shared a lengthy list of all the projects that the country superstar had been working on and was excited to bring to life.

“Dolly worked up until the day she died. She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy,” Nozell said in a press release. “Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come.”
Among Parton’s future plans are Dolly Dolls, Dolly’s Cup Of Ambition Coffee, Dolly’s Dog Treats and her Broadway musical, among many others.
Her manager stressed that anything that is released on the singer’s official channels, Parton “placed her personal stamp on it.”
He added that they will continue to share more details on additional projects, including an avatar show, a biopic, docuseries, scripted series and a Billy The Kid animated series, “soon.”
For now, fans can enjoy listening once more to Parton and her beloved voice and sense of humor.

title: Alison Brie Goes Blonde and Confirms a New Role: ‘It’s For a Part!’
summary: Alison Brie just underwent a stylish and lighter hairstyle. The actor, known for her brunette locks, is now a blonde.
story: Alison Brie is back to blonde.
The former “Community” star debuted her new hair color at the 2026 Daytime Beauty Awards red carpet in Los Angeles on Sept. 9.
“They *do* have more fun?!” Brie said on her Instagram story, commenting on her new look.
As someone complimented her blondest ‘do to date, Brie revealed the reason for it.
“It’s for a part!” Brie said in a TikTok shared by “Entertainment Tonight.”
Just three days prior, Brie showcased her typical brunette look at the Creative Arts Emmys, where she supported her “GLOW” co-star Betty Gilpin and her win for “Widow’s Bay.”
This is not the first time she’s sported lighter locks. In 2019, Brie teased a new role with a transformation reveal on Instagram.
“When your husband asks you to ‘go blonde’ for a role... you say yes😉,” she wrote in the caption.
That “role” turned out to be the 2020 horror thriller “The Rental.”
Now, blonder than ever, and with a few inches off, fans are wondering what role called for the change.
Brie has recently starred in “Masters Of The Universe” and “Together.”

Brie is confirmed to appear in Peacock’s “Community: The Movie,” which has experienced ongoing production delays. In the original sitcom, however, which ran from 2009 to 2015, Brie’s character Annie Edison was a brunette.
Brie is also in cahoots with Alice Stanley Jr. for a female-driven horror comedy, but is said to be making her directorial feature debut rather than any on-camera work.

title: Cindy Crawford Describes Meeting Son of Ex-Husband Richard Gere
summary: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”
story: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”

Homer Gere, 26, and Kaia Gerber, 25, are part of the cast of the teen serial killer drama helmed by Ryan Murphy and posed together on the cover of the September issue of Vogue. Their parents posed together for Vogue in 1992, making the latest cover shot a full-circle moment between the children of the supermodel and the actor, who divorced in 1995 after four years of marriage.

Crawford, 60, shared on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle Sept. 10 what it’s like to see the two working together and how she first met Homer Gere, who is Richard Gere’s son with actor Carey Lowell. Gerber is the daughter of Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber.
“I had never met Homer,” Crawford said. “I met him while they were filming. He’s lovely, and Kaia enjoyed working with him.”
Crawford also expanded on how the two young actors deal with being labeled “nepo babies.”

“They’re both in the same situation,” Crawford said. “They understand it’s going to be a question they’re going to get asked, but at the same time they both work really hard and think they’re both doing a great job.”
Crawford emphasized that Gerber works hard for her modeling and acting career.
“Look, there’s pros and cons to having famous parents,” Crawford added. “And I know sometimes it feels like pressure, or she feels like, ‘Wow.’”
For example, her daughter can do a modeling shoot and commenters may bring up that her mother wore the look first.

“I’m like, ‘I know,’ because I can talk about my mom and no one knew who that was, and (Gerber) doesn’t have that anonymity,” Crawford said. “But she also understands that it does open maybe some doors.”
Gerber spoke to Vogue about what it has been like growing up in the public eye due to her mother.

“Fame was something that I was born into, so I didn’t experience what it was like to become famous,” Gerber said. “I kind of thought that my way of being raised was the most anonymous it could get under the circumstances, and then I met Homer. Like, there are no photos of him as a child online, whereas my entire childhood and teenage years are on the internet. I can only imagine. I’m 24 but … very interviewed.”
Gerber began modeling at 13 and was walking runways at 16, according to Vogue.

“I’ve only ever been a nepo baby, and I’ve only ever benefited in my career from it,” she said “But I also find myself doing it to other nepo babies, thinking, like, OK, show me why you deserve this job. I said to Homer — because the concept is daunting to him, having lived as an adult so far without that perception, whereas I sort of went through it when I wasn’t fully sentient — I said to him, ‘Homer, unfortunately with this show, it’s not like you’re just any unknown actor and people will judge you as an unknown actor.’”
Homer Gere did not begin acting professionally until appearing in a small role in the final season of HBO’s “Euphoria” earlier this year.
“I didn’t grow up in the industry at all,” he told Vogue. “I had never been on a professional set until last summer.”
He and Gerber also didn’t ignore their unique connection when they both joined the cast of “The Shards.”
“Twenty minutes into knowing each other, I was like, ‘Should we just acknowledge the fact that our parents were married?’ She was like, ‘Yeah. Cool,’” he told Vogue. “And that was it.”

title: AARP’s List of ‘Most Fabulous’ Gen X Actresses Honors Viola Davis and More Hollywood Stars
summary: Viola Davis leads AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list.
story: Viola Davis is fabulous!

The Oscar winner tops AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list, which “honors powerhouse female talent who continue to break barriers, command screens, and redefine what it means to be a Gen X actress in Hollywood,” according a news release.
The rankings pay homage to Generation X, which is classified as people born between roughly 1965 and 1980.

“Now, at roughly between the ages of 45 to 61, this generation of Hollywood actresses have not faded from the screen, but have built production companies, developed their own projects, and reinvented themselves behind the camera as directors, producers, and entrepreneurs fighting for equal pay and breaking stereotypes,” AARP’s Movies for Grownups said in a statement.
“They are far from slowing down and are doing the most ambitious work of their careers.”

Davis, 61, is the oldest person on the list and said in a statement connected to the honor, “My ability to overcome and to challenge and to believe in my ability is mine.” She survived a poor childhood marked by food insecurity to emerge as a critically acclaimed actor, winning a best supporting actress Academy Award for “Fences” and earning three other nominations in her career.

“When you come to Hollywood, I think women over 40, then over 50, you feel like you’ve just sort of disappeared and fallen off a cliff,” she told AARP’s Movies for Grownups. “Like you’re invisible. So, it’s nice to know that that’s not true. I feel like my value is going up. It feels fabulous.”

title: Elizabeth Acevedo Shares First Page of Novel in Verse, ‘Anger Is Only a Shadow’
summary: Elizabeth Acevedo previews the first page of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow” and explains how it sets up the rest of her book.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.

Either because of her own lactose intolerance, or her memory of what lunch would smell like at the detention center she used to teach at, Elizabeth Acevedo knew her next novel would open with the “visceral” image of indigestion.
“Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk,” reads the opening line of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow,” out Sept. 15 from HarperCollins.

The book’s narrator is a rebellious young woman named Lil, who finds herself in juvenile detention due to her “instinct for freedom,” per the novel’s premise, inspired by Acevedo’s own experience working as a teaching artist at a detention facility in Washington, D.C.
“It felt like such a visceral image to begin with, this disruption of your bodily functions in a space where that is very much monitored and very much like, not OK,” Acevedo tells TODAY.com.
The first page of the book is Lil “emphasizing the rules of this place,” both to herself and to the reader. Following the heading of, “Sunday, October 18,” it reads:

Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk. Trust, having the bubble guts is not the first impression you want to make. And while we’re on the subject, that’s an important rule too: don't make an impression.

Sit quiet, only slump so much in your chair, don’t look anyone in the face. Don’t avoid someone eyeing you either. And if you have to make an impression, let it be knuckle-size. Aldwin has been teaching me since I was little: know when to be brick-built, know when to be gentle. And here? Being soft don’t play here.

There are other rules you need to learn: Which YDR—youth development representative—you can joke with. When it makes sense to participate in an activity, or when it makes sense to stay your flat ass behind your door. What vent carries your voice into other units.
But the most important rule is Rule One: Don't. Drink. The. Milk.
The first page of the novel represents what Acevedo pictured her novel in verse to be. And the Lil readers meet through that introduction is the same way Acevedo found the character.

“I thought I was writing a book about a juvenile detention facility and this young woman who is in there and is kind of snarky and telling us the rules,” she says. “The first page was such a guide in her voice, really.

“Before I had plot, before I knew what the main conflict was, I was just kind of following the most irreverent character I’ve ever written,” she adds. “I knew I had a character long before I knew I had anything else.”

The rest came later, including its structure. Acevedo originally thought the novel would be entirely prose poetry, consisting of “blocky text without paragraph indentation.” In the final draft, the prose blocks, accompanied by dates, guide readers through Lil’s daily life. These entries are broken up by poems.

Acevedo first drafted a poem in Lil’s voice titled “Where I’m From.” It sparked a motif, and the character turns one writing prompt from a workshop at the detention center into a series of poems, illustrating how she’s “revising versions of herself,” Acevedo says.
When Acevedo worked as a teaching artist, she says she brought in poems.

“It’s a fraught space,” she says of her time teaching at a detention center. “You come in, and you’re like, ‘Let’s be really vulnerable in a space where you all are very reluctant to share vulnerability.’

“That tension was so visceral for me, and also ... the young women would open up in ways I had never imagined,” she adds. “It’s almost like I was constantly surprised and also fully understood like, ‘You have been looking for an opportunity for people to ask you these things.’”
But the book isn’t just about Lil’s time in the detention center. The novel also asks: “What are the stakes once you’re outside?”
“Anger Is Only a Shadow” will also follow Lil once she’s on probation, weighed down by an ankle monitor and fearing for her big brother, miles away at college.

“So many young people I know when I was a school teacher had ankle monitors, and how does that affect how you navigate your life? And what would be the thing that would lead this character, who’s very impulsive, to potentially violate the rules of the ankle monitor?” Acevedo says. “That’s when the second part of the story, a story I never thought I would write about, came forth.”
The result is “two big stories” rolled into the novel: one about juvenile detention and one about navigating a family member who has mental illness.

“I have a sibling who was diagnosed with schizophrenia when I was in the early years of my college career,” she says. “Trying to do well in my own little world of academics, while also showing up for family, and the ways in which it can be so hard to know what that person needs ... It felt like I just have so many questions about this. I don’t have answers.
“Then that felt like the challenge: Isn’t that exactly what you need to write about?” she continues.

“I’m not going to lie, I wasn’t sure,” she adds. “These are two big stories and I’m writing a very short book, I don’t think it can happen. But somehow, somehow, it felt like the two pieces were supposed to be interlocked.”
